items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.summary: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

items.title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
items.summary: >50% of tickets written by agents, the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR, and selling without SDRs or FDEs
items.full_text:
Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. "Issue tracking is dead" When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. The AI budget behind $100M in months The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. Linear threw out its 2025 enterprise roadmap Three weeks after joining in 2023, Cristina crossed "move upmarket to enterprise" off Linear's company goals. It had one salesperson. She went after growth-stage companies that would have to rip out an existing tool instead, the same way Stripe won new businesses long before it won switchers. Linear finally declared an enterprise push in 2025, with a roadmap full of features for large organizations. Then agents happened. Linear built an MCP server, an agents platform with a whole new set of APIs, and integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot. None of it was planned, and a lot of the enterprise work never got done. Cristina chose to race ahead anyway. Competitors waited, and enterprises started putting Linear on their shortlists. No SDRs, no forward deployed engineers Linear has never hired a single SDR. Cristina thinks the qualification call wastes the customer's time: they want a demo, not questions about their budget. AEs do their own outbound, with tooling to keep it personal. It doesn't do forward deployed engineering either. Linear should be easy enough to adopt that nobody needs access to your systems. Solutions engineers sell alongside enterprise AEs instead, sometimes building a working ServiceNow integration overnight to show a prospect it can be done. Cristina adds that an opinionated tool gives agents cleaner data than one where every team defines "bug" differently. Support stays in-house, and Linear won't let an LLM answer tickets on its own. AI drafts replies and a human decides what goes out. Customers sometimes assume the replies are AI because they arrive so fast. In three and a half years, Cristina has never had an escalation over a bad support experience. Everyone wants outcome-based pricing Cristina would love a model like Intercom's Fin, which charges for each support conversation its AI resolves. It's harder for Linear. What is auto-triaging a bug to the right team worth when one company thinks that's the PM's job and another doesn't? Until someone cracks that, Linear charges for what costs it money and keeps the rest free. Seats stay. Linear Agent chat is free even though it runs on frontier models. In coding sessions, users pick OpenAI or Anthropic models and harnesses, and Linear passes through the published API price plus a small markup. Loops run on AI credits. Linear doesn't start charging for things that used to be free. New AI features launch as free betas with notice that pricing is coming, and prices start high and come down rather than the other way around. Why not hire 100 salespeople? Cristina says Linear runs on about half the headcount of companies at its stage and revenue. A sales team bigger than the rest of the company would have cost it the trust engineering now has in sales. From Stripe she brought a 40% rule: at least 40% of the company should be engineering, product, design and data. If sales wanted more people, it helped recruit engineers first. Linear has no hard rule, but one of the first things she built was a headcount spreadsheet by function, and she still watches the ratio. Hiring is slow on purpose. Candidates do a work trial on a real problem. Hers was writing Linear's go-to-market plan for the next six to twelve months, which then became her job. At about 170 people, the only C-suite is the founders and her. items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.summary: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() . Via Lobste.rs Tags: mysql , postgresql , replication , scaling , wikipedia , ai-security-research

A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() .

items.title: Genie 4 is now available on the Gemini API.
items.summary: Build interactive 720p worlds with Genie 4 on the Google Gemini API. Generate coherent environments with native audio and real-time controls. Get started.
items.full_text: Following yesterday's Genie 4 launch , Genie 4 is now available for developers through the Gemini API (via the Interactions API) and Google AI Studio . Starting from a text prompt, a reference image, or both, developers can experiment with generating continuous 720p worlds at 24fps with synchronized native audio — from ambient soundscapes and sound effects to character dialogue. Using real-time keyboard controls alongside live text prompts, you can navigate environments and change weather, lighting, objects, or events on the fly. Gemini reasoning keeps the world state consistent and coherent throughout. Whether you’re prototyping interactive experiences, visualizing designs for spatial concepts, or training robotics and AI agents, Genie 4 opens up a blank canvas for you to test ideas and define new possibilities. As a reminder every output includes imperceptible SynthID watermarking. Try the interactive canvas and starter apps in Google AI Studio . Review pricing details and explore the Gemini API documentation to begin building.

items.summary: November 18, 2026 — Google’s middle tier scores 61 on the Intelligence Index. Plus, Anthropic prices its IPO at $83.
items.full_text: ← AI News AI News Gemini 4 Neon: GDM's Opus/Sol Contender November 18, 2026 — Google’s middle tier scores 61 on the Intelligence Index. Plus, Anthropic prices its IPO at $83. Google DeepMind shipped Gemini 4 Neon , its fourth Gemini 4 model in about seven weeks. If you’re confused about the naming, you’re not alone; the 1.5 month old Argon is now retired , the old Pro and Flash from Gemini 1-3 are dead, and if you’re thinking the names are based on atomic weights, Neon (10), the midtier model is faster/cheaper than Carbon (6). This is a helpful guide to the current leading models and sizes: Because of how distillation, RL, and benchmarking works, Neon technically outperforms Carbon by some measures despite being a smaller model… Also today, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share , above its initial range, and Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute in a $4.5B all-stock deal . Anthropic · Palo Alto Networks Pricing and specs. Neon costs $3 for input, $0.15 for cached input and $15 for output per million tokens. It has a 1M-token context window and four effort levels. Vals reports a maximum output limit of 1M tokens. Google · Vals Rollout. Neon is coming to the paid Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio, Gemini for business, and Antigravity for Pro and Ultra subscribers. In the Gemini app, Pro and Ultra users can select it as “Deeper analysis,” including for Tasks. Google’s rollout · Gemini app Day-one integrations. Cursor , GitHub Copilot across its app, CLI and VS Code, and LangChain Managed Deep Agents . Release cadence. Arena counted gaps of 28 days between Argon and Carbon, 15 between Carbon and Hydrogen, and six between Hydrogen and Neon. Arena High versus xhigh. At high effort, Neon matched Carbon’s 60 on the Intelligence Index for $3.74 per task. On GDP.pdf it scored 33.4% at high and 28.0% at xhigh. Artificial Analysis Agent Arena. Neon debuted second with 1,336 points across about 4,200 sessions. It had a $2.82 median task cost and placed second on steerability. Carbon still leads the separate Text Arena. Agent Arena · Text Arena Vals. Neon placed second on the Vals Index at 70.9%, about 0.4 points behind Fable 5.2 at less than half the cost per task. On Code Migration it averaged 160 turns, fewer than Carbon’s 234 or Hydrogen’s 574, and scored below both. Vals Index · Code Migration CursorBench 4.1. Neon scored 63.7% at default effort, up from Hydrogen’s 57.3%. Cursor Steering and capacity. In 13 early Antigravity sessions, Kimmonismus recorded 762 tool calls and a 93% input-cache hit rate. When told to avoid the terminal, Neon ran zero shell commands in those tests. The logs also recorded 57 capacity errors and four stalled runs. Test logs How teams use it. Theo says he’s now using Neon for copy, Fable to implement changes, and Astra to playtest. Jeremy Howard praised Neon while saying he was reverting Solveit’s Astra and Sol options to their pre-6.2 versions. Theo · Jeremy Howard Math and formal proof. Astra and Sol took the top two spots on MathArena. Astra solved 42 of 53 ArXivLean problems. Vals separately reports what it believes is the first formalization in Lean of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem, with the proof checked by an independent kernel replay. Tim Gehr · Vals Agent Arena. Astra debuted sixth. Sol placed eleventh at a $0.90 median task cost. On the separate Code Arena WebDev board, Astra placed third at a 42% lower median cost than its predecessor. Agent Arena · WebDev Background discounts. OpenAI opened a public beta for GPT-6.2 Responses API jobs that can wait. Two-hour and eight-hour targets for the first response come with 30% and 40% discounts per token, respectively. OpenAI Developers What changed after launch. OpenAI’s Tibo Sottiaux says early reviewers used builds from before the final few days of changes. Artificial Analysis found Astra’s responses got shorter and it was less likely to admit uncertainty in its behavioral evaluation. Sottiaux · Artificial Analysis Open weights and inference Correction to yesterday’s Pi adapter numbers. Yesterday’s issue cited 15 to 32 solves on the 51 hardest SWE-bench Pro tasks. Hugging Face reran affected tasks after finding a tunnel outage that hit nine base-model runs. The corrected result is 20 to 33 solves , or 39.2% to 64.7%. It also released an OpenCode adapter that moved Qwen3.8-27B from 35.3% to 51.0% on the same subset with thinking off. Corrected model card · OpenCode release Tencent releases Hy4 Flash weights. The 224B-parameter multimodal MoE activates 12B parameters per token, supports 1M context and includes a roughly 64B n-gram embedding table. Tencent released instruct, FP8 and base checkpoints. Tencent repository · vLLM vLLM 0.34.0. The extensible KV cache is on by default and Model Runner V2 is the sole GPU runner. The team reports up to 1.95× faster NVFP4 decoding on GB200. vLLM Inference capacity grew faster than peak compute. Epoch estimates that the capacity of chips sold for a fixed basket of agent workloads grew 4.6× from Q2 2025 to Q2 2026, while peak 8-bit compute grew 2.6×. Epoch AI Runway cuts serving hardware in half. It reports serving a 57B video model at 24 fps on four GPUs, down from eight. Runway Agent tooling. Prime Intellect launched Model Factory for RL, supervised fine-tuning, serving and evals. Hugging Face released the message dataset from its 1,000-agent PyBot project. Prime Intellect · Hugging Face OpenAI models help redesign AMD circuits. OpenAI reports up to 14% improvement against optimized baselines on blocks of AMD’s flagship GPU design. The team used Synopsys tools to check that rewritten circuits preserved behavior and to measure power, performance and area. Some changes made it into a design sent for manufacturing. OpenAI Measuring research acceleration. OpenAI published an update on internal agent use and research task completion, and proposed regular disclosure of indicators for AI research acceleration. OpenAI Smaller harness edits can save tokens. In a 40-issue held-out test, a gated approach that edited one module at a time scored 40.0% on SWE-bench Lite at 46.7K tokens per task. A full rewrite scored 42.5% at 451.6K tokens. DAIR research summary Agent teamwork. MAC Bench finds most gains from eight agents came from exploring in parallel. Opus 5.5 was the sole tested model to show an added gain from coordination. Bespoke Labs Genie 4 reaches Project Genie. Google’s world model adds native audio and lets users change the world with text mid-session. Access is rolling out to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers. Google DeepMind Turn detection and transcription. Inworld released weights for a voice-isolation model and its SAVA turn detector, which it says detects completed turns in a median 71 ms. AssemblyAI split its 3.7 release into models for voice agents, live transcription and recordings. Inworld · AssemblyAI Kling Image 4.0. It placed seventh in Artificial Analysis’s text-to-image rankings and sixth in editing. Artificial Analysis Anthropic prices its IPO at $83. The offering covers 980M shares, about $81.3B at the offer price. About $79.4B of that comes from shares sold by Anthropic before fees. Nasdaq trading under ANT is expected November 19. Anthropic Palo Alto Networks agrees to buy Applied Compute. The $4.5B all-stock deal gives Palo Alto a platform for post-training and serving open-weight models. The companies expect to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal Q3 2027, subject to regulatory clearance and other conditions. Palo Alto Networks AI Reddit Recap Blue TTS v3. A developer says their MIT-licensed model generates audio at about 50× real time on CPU. The thread’s headline number is a throughput claim about that setup. Code and demos · Discussion Inworld voice isolation. The release includes a 64M-parameter model for offline use and a 58M model for real-time use, both at 48 kHz. Weights · Local tests and discussion AudioGhost. A local interface for Meta’s SAM-Audio lets users describe a sound in text and separate it from the rest of a recording. Project discussion Local inference and coding Experts from an SSD. TokenWing’s developer claims it can stream a majority of routed experts from SSD. A user reported 45–50 tok/s on a 120B MoE with 12 GB of VRAM and 32 GB of RAM. LocalLLM thread One job, two models. A developer paired GPT-6.2 Astra for planning and review with local Qwen3.8-27B for implementation. The reported API bill fell from $7.40 to $1.62 on that run. Workflow and discussion Neon’s place in the line-up. Readers discussed whether Neon becomes the everyday replacement for Gemini 3.1 Pro, now that Google has separate tiers for fast work and harder projects. Launch discussion · Tier discussion Thanks for reading Stay a little ahead of the curve. Fresh ideas, original reporting, and deep conversations in your inbox. Subscribe to Latent Space

items.summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.38 Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon . I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse. Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price , and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires. The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up: So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen. Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st. I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high. I dropped Argon from my Gemini 4 comparison grid - here's the new Gemini 4 lineup, where the Neon pelicans do look better than Hydrogen and worse than Carbon: As I've done with several recent models , I also fired the following prompt against Gemini 4 Neon on "extra" effort level in Google Antigravity: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's the result . items.title: Genie 4 is now available
items.summary: Introduction to Genie 4
items.full_text: Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. Experience Genie 4 in Project Genie With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. Discover new Genie 3 capabilities While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Extended sessions and world chaining: Explore for up to 3 minutes per generation (up from 60 seconds), or link multiple worlds together for longer journeys. 360-degree panorama image grounding: Seed new worlds from 360-degree panorama images. Real-time in-world events: Dynamically change the environment with natural-language prompts while you explore. Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command. Create new interactive experiences The new Project Genie agent takes creation beyond a single text or image prompt. Now crafting an interactive universe is as effortless as having a conversation. Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood. You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds. Turns a natural language prompt into an interactive spacewalk, then an alien spaceship appears on command Remix a hillside cafe into a glass pavilion in the desert. Publish custom worlds to the gallery for others to explore and remix. Explore the new gallery When you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. Transform personal photos into explorable spaces in “Living Memory,” wander through rich prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas in “Dino Field Guide,” or pit themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini serving as your real-time referee in “Rock Paper Scissors.” Browse curated and community-built worlds and jump straight into exploring. “Villa Giallo,” created with Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, uses Genie 4 to turn a gothic manor into an interactive, room-by-room mystery. “The Life of Ants,” built with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, uses Genie 4’s photorealism to let you navigate a colony from an ant’s perspective. The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism. Beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix. Learn how we are building responsibly We are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings. Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. For a deeper look into model limitations and our progress on these fronts, read our Genie 4 model research overview . Try Project Genie today Eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers can try the new Project Genie experience starting today, and Google AI Pro members can join the waitlist on the same page.

items.title: datasette-arrows 0.1a0
items.summary: Release: datasette-arrows 0.1a0 Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats. I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it. Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot. Add the plugin to Datasette ( datasette install datasette-arrows ) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option: This screenshot is from Datasette's main branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release. Tags: datasette , projects

items.summary: November 17, 2026 — GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol lower benchmark costs. Early testers disagree on what Astra is like to work with.
items.full_text: ← AI News AI News GPT-6.2 Astra, the #2 Frontier Model is better and 20%-600% cheaper, but has mixed reviews; 6.2 Sol likely main workhorse November 17, 2026 — GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol lower benchmark costs. Early testers disagree on what Astra is like to work with. What’s more unusual about this launch is the STRONGLY negative influencer feedback… We think that some of this is overreacting and normal influencer tendency to either have everything be 🤯🤯🤯 or the literal WORST.MODEL.EVER, BUT also that some of the criticisms are valid, and the RL artefacts are noticeable and downright bizarre (don’t even get us started about the terrible launch video ). However, we still use it to automate our work and that’s all that matters in the end. Great ship, but Anthropic’s IPO is unaffected and that will be probably the headline of the week/year/decade (until OpenAI IPO’s….) Today’s AI News is brought to you by SerpApi! Retrieve public web pages by URL as LLM-ready Markdown or structured JSON. Map sites and run bounded crawls with one API. Pair with 100+ SerpApi search APIs for search-to-content workflows. Check them out to support LS, and contact business@latent.space for feedback! Availability. Today’s models are rolling out to ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu, and to developers through the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . OpenAI API prices per million tokens. Astra is $8 input, $0.40 cached input and $40 output. Sol keeps its predecessor’s pricing at $2, $0.10 and $10. Both have 1M context and a 128K output limit. Vals · Ultrafast pricing and rollout Astra for Law. The Enterprise configuration adds a legal search index. Artificial Analysis measured 20.8% on Harvey LAB-AA, versus 15.0% for base Astra. Artificial Analysis Preparedness. OpenAI rated Astra High for AI Self-Improvement, a first for one of its externally released models. On a separate measure, Vals’ RSI-Index rose from 27.07% to 29.01%, with 50% denoting its human reference. System card · Vals FrontierMath Erdős. Epoch verified seven solutions in Lean out of 68 problems. The previous best was three. Epoch What the benchmarks measure Agents’ Last Exam 1.1. OpenAI reports Astra at xhigh gained 5.2 points over GPT-6 Astra at max, using less than a third of the cost per task. It reports a 5.5-point lead over Fable 5.2 at about 5% of the cost on that test. On GDPval v2, it says Astra used 22% fewer output tokens than its predecessor. OpenAI’s results Long engineering runs. Mercor’s OpenWorldEngineer puts Astra at 67.2%, Fable 5.2 at 54.6%, and GPT-6 Astra at 44.2%. On Vals’ multi-turn Vibe Code Bench, Astra was first and Sol was third. Mercor · Vals 3D and robotics. Astra led AA-3D with 1,318, ahead of Fable at 1,271 and Sol at 1,259. On Artificial Analysis’s robotics preview, Astra scored 79 and Sol 78, ahead of Fable at 75. Artificial Analysis Research agents. On Perplexity’s WANDR, Astra scored 0.783 at about $12.54 per task. Sol reached 0.746 at about $2.65. Perplexity Matt Shumer called the models “essentially unusable” after weeks of testing and said his Opus and Fable agents rejected much of Astra’s subagent work. Review · Workflow details Pietro Schirano attributed many of his early issues to the harness. Arena’s Peter Gostev tested Astra against Fable on visual coding and singled out Astra’s SVG peacock. Schirano · Gostev The demos. Gabriel Chua built a walkable Singapore using more than 100 Codex threads. Simon Willison ran the same three.js mech prompt through several models, including Astra, Sol, Carbon and Fable. Singapore build · Same-prompt comparison Microsoft Ignite and Gemini Microsoft ships its own coding models. MAI Code 2 is for multi-step coding, and Code 2 Flash is for quicker edits. Both are available in GitHub Copilot’s model picker, Copilot Fusion and Foundry. Microsoft also announced a multimodal upgrade to its Decision model. Microsoft Copilot Fusion. Microsoft reports 71.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 with its multi-model harness, at 88% lower cost than Claude Fable 5.2 in that comparison. Jay Parikh Image editing. Artificial Analysis ranks MAI Image 2.7 first on its editing benchmark, at $34.82 per 1,000 images. Artificial Analysis Gemini Tasks. Hydrogen now powers free Tasks in six countries, including tasks that need a phone call or a text. Google also showed a new Antigravity robotics plugin with MuJoCo simulation. Sundar Pichai · Google DeepMind Agent harnesses and inference Hugging Face’s Pi adapter. A small adapter trained inside pi lifted Qwen3.8-27B from 15 to 32 solves on the 51 hardest SWE-bench Pro tasks. Across that subset it made 55% fewer tool calls per task. Model card and paired results Harness costs vary sharply. Baseten measured up to a 4.4× spread in cost per passing task across its benchmark of 22 harnesses and five open models. Baseten The harness may specialize to its model. Google’s SIM keeps the rationale and outcome of prior harness edits. A harness it evolved on Opus scored 68.41 on Gemini, versus 73.89 for the starting harness. Research summary More multi-agent products. Cognition launched persistent Devin Bots. Perplexity reported that its mixed-model teams beat four instances of the lead model on Terminal-Bench and WANDR. Replit reported diminishing returns from 16 to 32 agents on NumPy tasks. Cognition · Perplexity · Replit Coordination dominated a 1,000-agent run. Hugging Face says only 40–60 agents were calling the model at any moment. They read roughly 130 tokens for every token they wrote, with merges and tests contributing to the bottleneck. Thomas Wolf A small fraction of cache misses can dominate the bill. SemiAnalysis reports that 1.8% of uncached requests accounted for roughly 15% of spend in its sample. SemiAnalysis Marin and K2 Horizon opened up their training runs. Marin released 57 intermediate Mochi checkpoints from its 535B-A23B run. The K2 report compares four model sizes trained on the same 22T tokens and describes a decoding adapter that the team says reaches 2.2× speedup. Marin · K2 Horizon Zyphra’s long-context attention. Isomorphic Labs Genesis AI raises $500M. The Series A values the robotics company at $3.5B post-money. It plans to use the funding to deploy its Eno robot and expand training and data collection. Zhou Xian AI Reddit Recap Local models and hardware A 9B model with layers that run twice. SenseNova-Loop-9B runs 24 of its 32 layers a second time. The model’s authors report GAIA rising from 37.86 in the preview to 69.90 in the release. Local users asked how much memory remains for the KV cache at long context. Its sparse attention still retains the full-history KV cache, which is what local users want measured before they commit hardware. Model card · Discussion Olala mini 7A1B. items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.summary: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. items.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
items.summary: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" items.title: How genome mapping can help researchers better understand disease
items.summary: Glowing DNA double helix made of light particles, with floating A, C, T, and G letters on a dark background.
items.full_text: Your genome is your body’s instruction manual: the blueprint that informs how your body functions. It contains 3 billion base pairs of DNA. Because this DNA is responsible in part for switching genes on and off, it could be the difference between developing a disease and avoiding one. Determining which DNA changes cause diseases (and other outcomes) is like finding a needle in a haystack. Illustrative. Your genome, one point at a time. Decoding the DNA sequence is the goal behind AlphaGenome , a model from Google DeepMind. AlphaGenome can take a partial DNA sequence of 1 million base pairs in length, and make thousands of predictions. By comparing these predictions for DNA changes, scientists can find that needle faster. We talked to Google DeepMind research scientist Žiga Avsec to learn more. What do you do at Google? ŽA: I’m a research scientist overseeing our genomics initiative. Basically, I lead a team that builds models to help us better understand the genome. How is your team making it easier for scientists to predict and understand diseases? It really all comes down to how the genome works. It contains 3 billion DNA base pairs. And each pair contains two bases, which we call “letters.” These letters — A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine), G (guanine) — act like a biological alphabet, spelling out the genetic instruction manual that makes someone who they are. Since you can replace any of those letters with three other letters, there are 9 billion possible single-letter changes. Many genetic diseases are caused by just one of these letters changing. But scientists don’t have time to run billions of studies to figure out which changes make a difference. So we used AlphaGenome to predict the outcomes of all 9 billion single-letter changes, and we created a massive dataset — AlphaGenome Atlas — so scientists can decide what to research faster. Illustrative. The letters are invented for this example. What’s holding scientists back from better understanding the genome? While science can read all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA, we still haven’t fully deciphered the semantics of the genetic code — particularly the non-coding "dark matter" that regulates gene expression and disease risk. Experimental research, or as it’s also called, wet-lab research is the best way to help us reach breakthroughs in our understanding, but it’s expensive and time-consuming. A single breakthrough could take years. Let’s say you sequence DNA from a patient with a rare disease. You might end up with 4 million variants — 4 million ways their DNA differs from the standard reference human genome. But the question is: Which variant is causing their condition? Maybe you narrow the list to only include rare variants. But even then, you could be left with hundreds or thousands of options. When scientists use AlphaGenome Atlas, they get a single, easy-to-read score — the AVI (AlphaGenome Variant Impact) score — which instantly indicates the potential impact of a variant across the full genome. This helps them prioritize and more easily find the most disruptive changes to follow up on. Illustrative. Each dot stands for many variants. Scores are invented. Can you give me some examples of how AlphaGenome impacts everyday people? Tools like AlphaGenome move us from merely reading DNA to helping us better understand the molecular mechanisms behind a disease, giving researchers new leads to test and taking an important step towards someday digitally simulating a complete human cell. There are several ways that will have an impact. It can accelerate research that could help society improve our ability to diagnose and personalize treatment for patients suffering from rare or previously uncharacterized genetic disorders. It could also speed up drug discovery pipelines by helping pharmaceutical researchers identify and validate high-probability therapeutic targets faster. Beyond healthcare, AlphaGenome’s model architecture could help researchers tackle broader societal challenges, including breeding climate-resilient crops. Illustrative. Possible ways AlphaGenome can help. What kinds of breakthroughs has AlphaGenome enabled? AlphaGenome is still pretty new. We launched it in June 2025, and we just introduced AlphaGenome Atlas in September this year. But researchers are already using it to advance science. Gareth Hawkes, a Medical Research Council fellow at the University of Exeter, used AlphaGenome Atlas to narrow down a list of 1 billion genetic variants. By focusing on the most impactful 1%, he identified 19 variant groups linked to body mass index to prioritize in his research. And Laura Covill, a Broad Institute research fellow, used the AVI score to prioritize genetic variants in their research of unsolved rare diseases. AlphaGenome Atlas identified a critical variant in a gene linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, providing crucial supporting evidence that drove their subsequent research, including solving the case. What are you hoping to do next? We just launched our latest model, AlphaGenome 2 , which tackles one of the key limitations of AlphaGenome: cell type specificity. While AlphaGenome is state-of-the-art, it was trained mostly on data from whole tissues or cell lines. We know that individual cell types in those tissues have a very specific role and can malfunction in disease. AlphaGenome 2 moves beyond tissue-level averages to predict how genetic variants disrupt these individual cell types, helping researchers pinpoint the cellular drivers of disease. We’re also actively researching better ways to measure how confident our model is in its predictions so researchers know how much to trust each result. From early analyses, we see that variants with strongly predicted effects are quite good and achieve high levels of accuracy. As always, anyone using AlphaGenome should interpret its predictions with other sources of information. What's the ultimate goal of your work in biology? In the short term, we’d like to use AI to better understand the grammar of the genome and accurately predict the effects of mutations. In the long term, we’d like to build on this foundation towards a fully functioning digital simulation of a human cell. This will allow researchers to computationally model disease mechanisms, understand rare genetic conditions, and test candidate therapies.

items.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
items.summary: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io : Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. As an example, consider the following URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this: That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table. Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing: https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins. &url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists , because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file. &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file . The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file. #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it ( %23 is a URL-encoded # ) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data. That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year. The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README . I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite: Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty. Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score How this works, using service workers Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022 , originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value. The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack . It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML . This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files. The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers . These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead. Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this: /app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS) Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about? The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs. Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another. The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure. Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session. (We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!) I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here's my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README: This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production! Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite . Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then. Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues. In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process. WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab. datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this: pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl That's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version. Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1 , resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it. Once I'd built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29)">this bonus tool for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here's an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1: This should work for every other Python app, too Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs. C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026. One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden. I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem. Tags: javascript , projects , python , urls , datasette , webassembly , service-workers , pyodide , datasette-lite
