Let’s break down that URL to see what it’s doing: https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins. &url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers —I host files like this in Gists , because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file. &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file . The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file. #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette—here it’s loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it ( %23 is a URL-encoded # ) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data. That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year. The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README . I’ve already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here’s a recent issue describing a pagination bug—I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite: Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score —click next and the second page is empty. Here’s that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score How this works, using service workers Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022 , originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value. The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack . It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML . This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don’t execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files. The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers . These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead. Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this: /app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS) Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What’s that about? The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs. Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another. The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure. Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session. (We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!) I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here’s my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README: This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn’t until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production! Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite . Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then. Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues. In the past I’ve used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it’s not a trivial process. WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab. datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this: pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl That’s for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version. Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1 , resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it. Once I’d built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29)">this bonus tool for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here’s an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1: This should work for every other Python app, too Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick—running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs. C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026. One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden. I’d love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.summary: Cloudflare made its name speeding up the web. Now it's building System One models to make decisions and pull data in milliseconds.
items.full_text: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction . In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings . “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince . “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company : from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Jev as the “east wind” Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here , that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.” Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company — speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow more work to be done by smaller, faster models , where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds. Clairic and what extraction models do While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with an original twist on System One with Clairic , launched last month as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.” “What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation. In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “overkill” and didn’t always return the right answer. One of the problems they settled on was that LLMs don’t always deal well with unstructured input. Because LLMs are autoregressive, Chen explained, they are prone to hallucinate and they sometimes return malformed JSON. “So we used the same System One principles [as Jev/Clef] there, and decided on extraction.” Some examples of system one use cases at Cloudflare. She used the example of an invoice, where an LLM will sometimes get an important detail wrong — like the order number. “When you send it [the order] to an LLM, they're like, wait, I think the order number's three, maybe it's four, maybe it's five. But it's like, the number's right there, you just have to read it! ” So the idea with Clairic is that it will extract a typed value — like a number — from unstructured data, in one forward pass. Why Cloudflare is in the lab now Using the label “neolab” sounds a bit like a marketing gimmick, but it also makes a ton of sense for Cloudflare to produce system one models — and even, in future, reasoning models. “Being a neolab means that we can create what we are missing,” Chen said in her presentation. In our interview, she also mentioned that creating their own models allows Cloudflare to derisk its AI operations. “I think there's a lot of risk in the AI space , because just like Jev was closed source and we couldn't run it, there [are] a lot of models out there [with] maybe regulatory risks coming up, like the Chinese open source models. I think lots of model labs want to actually make money, as well — so enforcing quite expensive licenses.” If you look at Cloudflare’s product page now, it resembles what Amazon’s cloud computing product page looked like at the height of Web 2.0 — i.e. there’s a lot there! But there’s still room for several more models.

items.title: [AINews] Perplexity hits a $1B revenue run rate, up 4x in 2026
items.summary: November 16, 2026 — Computer gets Teammates, Perplexity ships Monitor API, and a new research lab launches.
items.full_text: ← AI News AI News Perplexity hits a $1B revenue run rate, up 4x in 2026 November 16, 2026 — Computer gets Teammates, Perplexity ships Monitor API, and a new research lab launches. Gathering up some recent Perplexity launches for those catching up: Computer. September’s Automations let it pick up recurring tasks where it left off. November’s Teammates take on ongoing jobs. Computer also runs fully locally on supported Macs. Monitor API. Watch a topic or page and get a webhook when something relevant changes. Frontier Research. The new research lab has access to 10,000+ GPUs and plans to publish papers, data, models, and code. Sponsored by Deepgram Deepgram is the voice AI infrastructure behind natural conversation—bringing speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice-focused LLMs, and agents to teams building with voice AI. For any stack and any tools you already love building with, Deepgram slots in as your foundational voice AI technology. So you have control. And we have the context to listen, understand, and speak like a human. Learn more about the Real-time Context Standard . Friday’s Qwen4-Max preview is now a shipping model. At the highest reasoning setting, Qwen4-Max scored 43 on the Intelligence Index, up from 34. Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task. Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens, and the model generated about 39% fewer of them. Kimi K3.1 Pro cost $3.68 per index task and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to Qwen’s 48%. Artificial Analysis Inside the model. Alibaba kept the total parameter count at 2.4T and reduced the number active per token by 25% to 71B. The model takes images and text, with a 1M-token context window. Smaller open-weight Qwen4 models are still to come. Alibaba Arena and Vals : Arena ranks it #14 overall on Agent Arena, the top Chinese model, with +7.5% net over 14.7k sessions ( Arena ). WebDev : It placed #6 in Code Arena WebDev at 1750, +74 over its predecessor ( WebDev ). It also placed #6 in Image-to-WebDev, just above Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol ( I2WebDev ). Vals Index : It is #11 overall, with large gains in coding and finance ( Vals ). Legal-benchmark caveat : On HLAB it gets 95.7% of checklist items right but passes only 21.3% of tasks, and its output tokens rise 3.6x ( HLAB ). Vision results (independent) : Roboflow calls it underwhelming on its VLM benchmark, with Google, OpenAI and Anthropic now far ahead. At high reasoning effort, however, it is ~4.5x faster and ~68% cheaper per image than Qwen3.8-Max ( Roboflow ). Safety, alignment and eval integrity OpenAI embedded assessments : OpenAI is giving Apollo, METR, Transluce and Goodfire internal access to its models and systems ( OpenAI ). Scope by group : Apollo places six evaluators onsite for four months ( Rundown ). METR reviews OpenAI's largest RL run, with access to transcripts, monitor records and checkpoint snapshots ( METR ). Transluce runs a six-week audit of post-training alignment evals, with a fuller follow-up in early 2027 ( Transluce ). Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs ( Goodfire ). Limits : METR says its scope excludes the misalignment incidents OpenAI has disclosed and is narrower than METR proposed ( scope ). Criticism of the access terms : Critics say the deals fall short of Sam Altman's promise of "employee-like access." Reported gaps : Assessors get no Slack access, OpenAI selects which staff they interview, and they cannot access weights or run training-based elicitation ( Neel Nanda , Alex Mallen ). Former-employee account : Mikita Balesni says assessors cannot quote employees, even anonymously, and some may be barred from publishing on internal-only models ( balesni ). Goodfire acquisition talks : The Information reports OpenAI explored buying the interpretability startup for more than $5B. Goodfire reportedly wanted to stay independent so it could sell to multiple labs ( report ). Other integrity signals : Benchmark contamination : Claude appears to have memorized details of the LinuxArena control eval ( Karvonen ). Incident taxonomy : OpenAI published a v0.1 framework for classifying AI control incidents ( framework ). Disclosure policy : Anthropic is cutting its coordinated disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities ( policy ). Inference systems and agent infrastructure Together moves on from hand-tuned megakernels. Its first design made it into production for one customer. Agents now search for smaller groups of GPU operations to fuse. Together reports 28% higher throughput on Llama 3.2 1B on B200. Engineering writeup DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Vera Rubin : vLLM with Dynamo on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmark shows 63.4x per-chip throughput over GB300 NVL72 at 400 tok/s/user, and 93.3x at 600 ( vLLM ). Batch-1 latency : SGLang-adjacent work reaches ~2,500 tok/s at batch size 1 on TP4, 1.7x its GB300 result ( saltyph ). Baseten reports a similar 1.7x over its 4xB300 numbers ( Baseten ). Agent-driven optimization : An agent shared Engram tables across HBM via NVLink symmetric memory to recover prefix-cache capacity ( Liu ). Another team says agents found optimizations that made its B300 step time 10% faster ( Halex ). Agentic serving research : MIT's Evolving Infra replaces fixed prefill/decode disaggregation with online adaptation. Against NVIDIA Dynamo on up to 256 GB300s, it reports up to 4.1x lower latency and 14x lower P95 TTFT ( Evolving Infra ). Pipeline-parallel prefill : Inferact finds PP2 on MiniMax-M3.1-Flash sustains 23% more requests per GPU than DEP2 at a 2s TTFT target ( Inferact ). Prefix-cache pitfalls : Ollama found that a single system-prompt timestamp or a change in reasoning effort can wipe the cache ( Ollama ). Sandboxes and training : External sandboxes : Simon Willison describes running agents on a Mac while executing their code in WebAssembly, QEMU or Apple Container sandboxes. The pattern includes allow-list proxies and credential replacement ( post ). MLPerf : In MLPerf Training v6.1, a GB300 NVL72 trained GPT-OSS-20B in 19.7 minutes, 2.86x faster than H100 ( Lambda ). One endpoint for open models. Hugging Face Inference Providers now runs on OpenRouter using the same endpoint and token. Hugging Face Research, benchmarks and evals PyBot : A swarm of 1,000 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash agents spent a week writing a rule-based chatbot with no neural network ( lewtun ). Self-improvement and training : AutoRL : Agents supervising a live RL run lifted Qwen3 on AIME 2024 from 46.67% to 66.67% ( omarsar0 ). Benchmark-gaming caveat : A roundup warns that many self-improving agent gains come from learning the benchmark rather than the task ( TuringPost ). Weight-space programming : Opus 5.5 hand-wrote transformer weights that solved algorithmic tasks with a median of 166 parameters ( dair_ai ). Data curation : DatologyAI published the tech report behind its claimed 6x pretraining compute multiplier ( Datology ). Distillation reproduction : A small-scale replication confirms perturbed-input distillation helps when the student trains from scratch, but finds it hurts when distilling into a pretrained student ( Maini ). New benchmarks : GradeBench : The best frontier model agrees with instructors only 57% of the time when grading handwritten physics answers ( GradeBench ). Time to First Audio : AA's new TTS latency benchmark finds a median of 376 ms for streaming models versus 2.0 s for non-streaming ones ( AA ). SpeedRunBench : Inkling-2-Small cleared SuperTux 1-1 in 1,988 frames, ahead of Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol ( SpeedRunBench ). Science models and developer tools Gemini 4 Carbon : DeepMind says Carbon powered AlphaProof Code agents that verified Signal's cryptographic code. It also spotted wet-lab errors and found 40x more related protein sequences ( details ). Science access : Google expanded free Carbon access for 10,000 scientists through Antigravity ( program ). Context window : Antigravity doubled the context window for Argon, Carbon and Hydrogen, cutting compaction 3.5x per user turn ( Mohan ). User reports (anecdotal) : One researcher says Carbon solved a problem that waves of Astra and Fable attempts had not ( anecdote ). OpenAI for science and health : OpenAI is opening free frontier access to up to 200,000 scientists, with applications from Nov 23 ( program ). Productivity study : OpenAI reports scientists roughly doubled their productivity in a study of 1,800 participants ( study ). Physics showcase : Physicist Nathaniel Craig used GPT-6 Astra to develop a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model ( blog ). Healthcare : ChatGPT for Healthcare adds computer-use agents and more than 20 plugins ( healthcare ). Claude Code : The desktop app now runs iPhone Duo in the iOS simulator and can fold and unfold the device to test layouts ( ClaudeDevs ). Verification : The team published how it uses cheap tests, benchmarks and end-to-end runs to let Claude verify its own work ( blog ). Unreleased model (unconfirmed) : A "Silicon 2" entry spotted in Devin is suspected to be an Anthropic model ( rumor ). Liquid d1.2-ultra : It ranks #1 on AA's Decision Index at $0.042 per M input tokens ( AA ). Sage S2.1 Flash : The open-weight science model reports leading MLE-bench Lite and OfficeQA Pro results ( Sage ). FLUX-mimic-x : A 7B video-action robotics model ranks #1 on RoboLab among real-time models ( mimic ). Unsloth computer use : Local models can now drive desktop apps and game engines through Unsloth ( Unsloth ). Nvidia. The US Commerce and Justice departments issued a joint statement on the Megaspeed investigation. Commerce Financing and M&A : Noeri : Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin's continual-learning lab raised $110M ( Choi ). Corma : The cyber-defense model company raised a $125M Series A at a $1B valuation ( Corma ). World Labs : The team is joining AMD ( Fei-Fei Li ). Market data : Anthropic's S-1 shows $16.3B revenue in H1 2026 and compute costs falling from 251% to 48% of revenue ( The Batch ). AI Reddit Recap Local models and hardware What fits in 16 GB? Unsloth expects a smaller Qwen4-27B to run in 16 GB. Local users want to see the quantization and how much memory is left for the context window. One developer already splits coding jobs between Opus for specs and a local Qwen3.8-27B for implementation. Memory discussion · Local workflows Hy4 Flash. Tencent’s multimodal model has 224B parameters and activates 12B per token. At $0.070 per million input tokens and $0.281 per million output tokens, it gives developers a cheaper way to try Hy4’s 1M context window. Tencent’s release · Discussion EUROPA. A reported test run on the JUPITER supercomputer trained a roughly 952B-parameter mixture of experts with 32.8B parameters active per token. The local-model community’s question is why the team chose that scale for its first model. Training run and discussion Where do two quantizations diverge? inside-llm loads two GGUFs with the same tokenizer and lets you step through their predictions side by side. Watch the first token where they disagree, then compare the probabilities they assigned to the alternatives. Project · Demo and discussion Basalt’s 770 tokens/sec headline depends on what you generate. The developer reports up to 776 tokens/sec for structured output from Qwen3.8-27B, 262 in chat and 194 for prose. Readers asked for longer quality tests of the 4-bit prefill. Basalt · Benchmark thread An FPGA running Qwen 27B. Valley Semiconductor reports 7.9 tokens/sec on short prompts and about 5.5 in live chat. Its 50 tokens/sec target at 20 W is a projection for a future chip. Live demo · Hardware discussion Claude Meetings. A CTO describes inviting Claude into a 30-minute Google Meet. It updated project records in Notion and called the team’s own tools to update bids during the meeting. Field report A Minecraft test for Hydrogen. A developer asked Gemini 4 Hydrogen to recover missing source and build a datapack for 11 Minecraft versions. The agent reportedly launched two graphical clients to test fixes for dropped items and raycasts. Developer’s account What teams hire a harness developer to do. One example from the discussion: a coding agent can propose a change, while the harness decides which repository it may write to, which CI test counts as passing and when a person needs to approve the next step. Claude Code discussion Testing a video model’s physics. After a second MiniMax H3 demo, commenters proposed a harder test: describe the scene, leave the outcome out of the prompt and see whether the model predicts what the objects will do. Demo and discussion Thanks for reading Stay a little ahead of the curve. Fresh ideas, original reporting, and deep conversations in your inbox. Subscribe to Latent Space

items.name: LoopForge
items.description: Self-hosted workflows for coding-agent delivery. Orchestrate CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code with scripts and human approval gates. Includes Local workflows for coding assistants.
items.readme_text:
English · 简体中文

Two ways to work · Quick start · SOPs · Features · Local (Legacy) · FAQ · Docs

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8af401d9-1aae-427c-b4bc-455c12d17beb

80-second product tour (1080p, with sound).

**LoopForge** is a self-hosted workspace where your team ships software with coding agents. Describe what you need to **Main Bot** in chat: it opens a Docker sandbox, checks out your repositories, delegates to project roles, and opens the PR. When a way of working proves itself, save it as an **SOP** (a standard workflow of agents, scripts and human gates) so the next requirement is delivered the same way, with review and approval built in. Coding-agent CLIs do the work: CodeBuddy, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Antigravity, Kimi Code, Pi, DeepSeek Harness and ZCode. LoopForge adds the roles, sandboxes, checkpoints and history around them, all on your own infrastructure under the MIT license. ## Two ways to work | | **Chat with Main Bot** | **Run an SOP** | | --- | --- | --- | | Best for | Exploring, quick fixes, iterating with the agent | Repeatable delivery with fixed stages and sign-off | | How it runs | Main Bot opens a [conversation workspace](docs/conversation-workspaces.md) (a Docker sandbox with your repos) on demand and calls project roles as subagents | The engine runs Agent, Script, Human-gate and sub-SOP nodes in order, in their own sandbox | | You stay in control by | Queuing or steering messages mid-reply, and pausing, resuming or taking over a running SOP from chat | Approving at human gates, sending work back to a chosen step, retrying or rerunning from any node | | Delivers | A PR/MR, or a direct merge into a shared branch (`mode=direct`) | Documents, code or a PR, plus per-node artifacts and logs | Both paths track the same **requirements**, so every change, whether made in chat or by an SOP, links back to what was asked for and counts toward delivery and cost reports.

The chat home. Type a request, @ a role, skill, requirement, SOP or repository, and pick the executor, model and permission mode per conversation.

## Why LoopForge Ask a coding agent to "fix this bug" and the result depends on that run. It might skip the plan, forget the tests, review its own code, or stop halfway without anyone noticing. That's fine for a demo, but it isn't how a team ships. - **Repeatable.** Same SOP, same stages, same checks for every requirement. Start from built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs. - **Separated roles.** Planning, implementation, review and testing each get their own prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools. A role works as an SOP node or as a subagent in chat. - **Human on the loop.** Agents run on their own while you supervise. Pause, steer or take over anytime, and approval gates stop the run where a human must decide: approve, or send the work back to a chosen step. - **Observable and resumable.** Node status, tool traces, logs and artifacts in one place. Pause, retry a failed step, or rerun from any node. - **Your stack, your servers.** Ten coding-agent CLIs as executors, from CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code to OpenCode, Cursor CLI and more. GitHub, Skills and MCP as tools. Docker sandboxes or your own machine as the runtime. ## Quick start Install **Git** and clone the repository first. The installer checks Docker, Compose, Python 3 and curl and offers to install missing components. Python/curl installation supports apt, dnf and yum on Linux; the Compose plugin supports x86_64/arm64 and verifies the official release SHA-256. macOS needs a working Python 3 and Docker Desktop; Homebrew can install missing components. Ordinary Linux users are supported through Docker group access or sudo. Set `LOOPFORGE_YES=1` to accept installation prompts. Package and image downloads require internet access. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Tencent/LoopForge.git cd LoopForge ./start.sh ``` `./start.sh` pulls the GHCR release image pinned in `compose.yaml` without building locally (`bash scripts/install.sh` does the same). It creates the MySQL and platform services, generates configuration and session secrets, and installs the built-in sandboxes, starter SOPs and welcome project. Host Go and Node.js installations are not required. Configure model API keys and GitHub authorization after startup. Use `./start.sh logs`, `stop`, `restart` or `pull` to manage it, and `./start.sh dev` to build the checkout from source. If downloads from `ghcr.io` stall, set `MIRROR` to a registry host that can stand in for `ghcr.io`. `./start.sh` pulls from that host and tags the image back to the name pinned in `compose.yaml`. Setting `MIRROR` trusts that host, because the download is tagged with the official name. The GitHub Release records the digest; `docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/tencent/loopforge:` should show the same digest after `@`. Without `MIRROR`, `./start.sh` still pulls `ghcr.io` directly, and `compose.yaml` stays unchanged. Upgrade with the same variable and `./start.sh pull`. [ghcr.nju.edu.cn](https://doc.nju.edu.cn/books/e1654/page/ghcr) is one such host. A Docker `registry-mirrors` entry such as `https://docker.nju.edu.cn` only accelerates Docker Hub and is not a value for `MIRROR`. ```bash MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn ./start.sh ``` Open the address printed by the installer and create your account; the first one becomes the administrator. The service listens on `0.0.0.0:8090` by default. On a cloud host, the installer reads the public IP from the provider's metadata service and prints it; allow the port in your security group, or put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front. Restrict access to your own IP until the administrator account exists. The home page's quick-access guide walks you through adding a model key, connecting a repository and choosing an SOP. For GitLab, Gitea, Gogs and other Git hosts, [set up Git SSH](docs/deployment.md#git-repositories-over-ssh) to check out and push branches with a personal key. PR/MR and Issue automation requires a hosting API token or a separately configured MCP. ### Try it without an API key New accounts join the **LoopForge demo project**, which includes an SOP made only of a script and a human gate: 1. Switch to the demo project, open **Templates**, and open **Platform check · script & approval**. 2. Click **Run SOP**. A real script writes a report, then the run waits for you at the approval step. 3. Approve it from **Needs review** or the run page, and watch the run continue to its final artifact. ### What you need for real work | I want to… | You need | | --- | --- | | Run the script + approval demo | Nothing | | Chat with Main Bot, generate a document or a new project | An API key for the selected executor | | Change an existing repository (in chat or via an SOP) and open a PR | Model credentials and a GitHub repository (connect GitHub in personal settings) |
More setup details: executors, GitHub, sandboxes, access model
- **Executors.** Pick one of ten CLIs beside the home composer, then a model. Every SOP role can choose its executor independently (built-in roles default to CodeBuddy). Requirement clarification, AI notification summaries, Bot replies and run evals currently use CodeBuddy, so their model pickers list CodeBuddy models only and the server refuses a model of another CLI instead of switching it to CodeBuddy; scheduled assistant tasks run on the CLI the task selects. | Executor | Credentials | Installation | | --- | --- | --- | | **CodeBuddy** | Personal key, or a shared key an administrator configures for chat and SOP runs | In the Docker image | | **Codex** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | In the Docker image | | **Claude Code** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **OpenCode · Kimi Code · Pi** | Personal key only | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **DeepSeek Harness** | Personal key only | In the Docker image | | **Cursor CLI** | Personal key only | Provider installer on first chat use; not installed into SOP sandboxes | | **Antigravity** | Personal key, or the connected execution machine owner's existing account login | Install the official CLI on the execution machine and in Docker images used for SOP runs | | **ZCode** | Personal key only | Not bundled; install it on the service or execution machine PATH | The seven agent CLIs after Claude Code keep their model and MCP configuration in a private home directory per run. Antigravity can reuse the execution machine owner's account login in conversation workspaces and native or Docker SOP sandboxes. Its official CLI refreshes the credential copy, and the Runner saves the refreshed login back to its original local store. Gemini API keys use separate API billing. The other agent CLIs use the responsible user's own key and Base URL from personal settings, including on a connected execution machine. First-use installs need npm or provider access; [native deployments](docs/deployment.md#workers-and-runners) need the CLI for the executor you choose. - **GitHub is optional.** All built-in generic SOPs run without a repository: product SOPs deliver documents, and new frontend/backend projects deliver source files in the task workspace. Bug fixes still need source code and reproduction details. Connect a repository when you work on existing code or want PRs. - **Delivering to a repository.** Choose **Connect GitHub** in personal settings, approve the device code on GitHub and pick your repository (the LoopForge OAuth App is built in; no PAT required, manual PAT entry still works). Set executor credentials (or bind a local execution machine), then either run a project SOP or ask Main Bot to change the code and submit a PR/MR. - **Sandboxes.** In the default Compose installation, SOP runs and conversation workspaces both use Docker sandbox containers started through the host Docker socket. Default sandboxes reuse the installed runtime image, so nothing extra is built after installation; custom Dockerfiles still build their own images. Docker socket access grants control of the host daemon, so this setup is for trusted teams, not untrusted multi-tenant isolation. See [deployment boundaries](docs/deployment.md#accounts). Re-running the installer keeps your data. - **Accounts and access.** New installations listen on all interfaces (existing bind settings are kept) and are designed for a trusted team: signed-in users can read project data across the instance, and teammates can sign up from the login page (`AGENTFLOW_ALLOW_SIGNUP=false` in `.env` turns that off). Read the [account and access model](docs/deployment.md#accounts) before exposing it beyond your team. - **Remote access, HTTPS, separate workers.** See [Deployment](docs/deployment.md). - **Hacking on LoopForge itself?** `bash scripts/dev.sh` runs it natively (Go 1.26.11+).
## How SOPs work An **SOP** is the workflow a delivery follows. Agents, scripts and people take part in the same run:

The SOP designer with the built-in bug-fix SOP. Each step picks a role; failed checks can send the work back to an earlier step.

| Node | What it does | | --- | --- | | **Agent** | A role (prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools) that designs, implements, reviews or tests. | | **Script** | A deterministic shell step: build, test, lint, generate a report. No AI where AI is not needed. | | **Human gate** | Pauses the run until someone checks the artifacts and approves, or sends the work back to a step. | | **Sub-SOP** | Runs another SOP as a sub-workflow. | | **Preview build** | Builds a static site and archives it for review. | Each node declares its artifacts and dependencies, and the engine starts each step once its dependencies complete. Start from a built-in SOP, adapt its roles, rules and environment to your project, and publish versions as it evolves.

A run waiting at a human gate: approve and continue, add context and rerun the step, or send the work back upstream.

**A delivery we actually ran:** four CodeBuddy roles planned a Python fix, implemented it, reviewed it independently and summarized the delivery. Three real tests passed; the run waited for human approval, then verified the accepted code had not changed. The [reusable acceptance case](e2e/api/45-delivery-model.test.mjs) checks the files and results. See the [validation record](docs/validation.md) for scope and known gaps. ## Features | Area | What you get | | --- | --- | | **Chat workbench** | Main Bot with per-conversation executor, model and permission mode. `@` references for roles, skills, requirements, SOPs and repositories. Messages queue while a reply runs; *Steer* interrupts and sends now. Generated files open in a side panel with preview, source and download. | | **Conversation workspaces** | On-demand Docker sandboxes with the project's repositories checked out, project roles as native subagents, and direct control of a running SOP workspace: pause, resume or take over. | | **SOP designer** | Visual canvas with Agent, Script, Human gate, Sub-SOP and Preview nodes, rework-on-failure edges, validation, version history and publishing. Built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs. | | **Roles** | Reusable definitions: prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills, MCP tools, artifacts and gates, shared across SOP nodes and chat subagents. | | **Requirement → delivery** | Requirements tracked end to end, whether shipped by an SOP or straight from chat, with PR/MR status tracking, merge detection and direct-branch merges. | | **Runs & approvals** | Live node status, tool traces, worker logs, per-node artifact snapshots and workspace previews. A single **Needs review** inbox for every gate waiting on you. | | **AI scheduled tasks** | Recurring agent tasks with full workspace, SOP and MCP access; a shared market of versioned, parameterized task templates; automatic SOP dispatch for new requirements. | | **Insights & cost** | Engineering metrics, business-domain reports with static HTML/SVG export, and token/cost accounting for SOPs and conversations at public list prices. | | **Execution environments** | Platform workers, Docker sandboxes, or a connected local execution machine using your own tools and repositories. | | **Team-ready** | Password accounts, projects and members, light/dark/system themes, an OpenAPI-described HTTP and MCP API. Management pages are in English and Chinese; the chat workbench is Chinese for now. |

Built-in SOPs are read-only blueprints; copy one into your project to run and edit it.

## LoopForge Local > **Legacy.** Previously published versions of LoopForge Local (`loopforge-cli`) remain available. The [Local guide](docs/local/usage.md) covers installing a fixed version and keeping existing workflows and artifacts. To use platform projects and SOPs from a coding assistant, [connect CodeBuddy to your LoopForge instance over MCP](docs/local/usage.md#connect-to-loopforge-with-mcp). Local continues to run its built-in workflows inside the coding assistant without a LoopForge server. | | Platform | Local (Legacy) | | --- | --- | --- | | Best for | Teams sharing chat workspaces, SOPs, approvals and history | One developer inside an IDE or CLI | | Needs | Docker + Python 3 | Node.js 20+, Python 3.8+ and a coding assistant | | Workflows | Chat with Main Bot + custom SOPs on a visual canvas | Built-in Classic / Portable workflows | | Evidence | Shared run details, approvals and metrics in the web workspace | Artifacts under `artifacts/{task_slug}/` + optional local dashboard | ## FAQ **Do I need an API key to try it?** No. The demo SOP uses only a script and a human gate. Chat and agent steps need a key for the executor you pick. Model usage is not included; you bring your own credentials. **Do I need GitHub?** No. Chat, documents and new projects run in the task workspace. Connect GitHub when you want to change an existing repository or open PRs. **Should I use chat or an SOP?** Use chat to explore and iterate; Main Bot can still open a PR. Once you find a way of working you want every requirement to follow, with fixed reviewers, tests and sign-off, put it in an SOP. Main Bot can start, pause and take over SOP runs, so the two paths work together. **How is this different from Dify, n8n or Flowise?** Those are general-purpose AI and automation workflow builders. LoopForge is built for **software delivery with coding agents**: implementer and reviewer roles, Docker sandboxes with real repositories, GitHub delivery, human acceptance gates and run evidence. **How is this different from using Claude Code, Codex, CodeBuddy or another coding CLI directly?** LoopForge doesn't replace them; it orchestrates them. Each agent step and each chat turn runs one of those CLIs. LoopForge adds what surrounds it: who does what, in which sandbox, in which order, with which checks, and who signs off. **Is it safe to expose on the internet?** New installations listen on all interfaces and target a trusted team. Read the [account and access model](docs/deployment.md#accounts) and set up HTTPS before opening it up. Report vulnerabilities privately via the [security policy](SECURITY.md). ## Documentation | I want to… | Start here | | --- | --- | | Deploy, manage accounts, connect execution machines | [Deployment](docs/deployment.md) | | Understand chat workspaces, scheduled AI tasks and token pricing | [Conversation workspaces](docs/conversation-workspaces.md) · [AI scheduled tasks](docs/ai-scheduled-task-capabilities.md) · [Token pricing](docs/token-pricing.md) | | Maintain an existing Local installation | [LoopForge Local](docs/local/usage.md) · [Editions](docs/local/editions.md) | | Extend the platform or use the HTTP / MCP API | [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) · [API reference](docs/api/README.md) · [Shared schedules API](docs/api/shared-schedules.md) | | Contribute to the UI | [Frontend design conventions](design.md) (Chinese) | | Check functional coverage and release readiness | [Validation record](docs/validation.md) · [Acceptance matrix](docs/testing/acceptance-matrix.md) · [Release review](docs/release-readiness.md) | | Understand source provenance and maintenance | [Public scope](docs/open-source-scope.md) · [Upstream synchronization](docs/upstream-sync.md) | ## Community Scan the QR code to join the LoopForge community group. ## Contributing Issues and PRs are welcome: share a use case, report a bug, or improve workflows, integrations and the platform experience. Start with the [contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md). Security issues go through the [security policy](SECURITY.md). If LoopForge is useful to you, a star helps others find it. ## License [MIT](LICENSE). Third-party components keep their own licenses and notices; see [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

items.name: evalscope
items.description: A streamlined and customizable framework for efficient large model (LLM, VLM, AIGC) evaluation and performance benchmarking.
items.readme_text:
中文 ｜ English

📖 中文文档 ｜ 📖 English Documentation ｜ 🌐 Product Website

> ⭐ If you like this project, please click the "Star" button in the upper right corner to support us. Your support is our motivation to move forward! ## 📝 Introduction EvalScope is a one-stop LLM evaluation framework built by the [ModelScope Community](https://modelscope.cn/). Just one command to start — it supports model capability evaluation, inference performance stress testing, and result visualization. ```bash pip install evalscope evalscope eval --model your-model-name --api-url $OPENAI_API_BASE_URL --api-key $OPENAI_API_KEY --eval-type openai_api --datasets gsm8k --limit 5 ``` ## ✨ Key Features - **📚 Comprehensive Evaluation Benchmarks**: Built-in multiple industry-recognized evaluation benchmarks including MMLU, C-Eval, GSM8K, and more. - **🧩 Multi-modal and Multi-domain Support**: Supports evaluation of various model types including Large Language Models (LLM), Vision Language Models (VLM), Embedding, Reranker, AIGC, and more. - **🧭 System One Evaluation**: Evaluate text Choice decision models via `--eval-type systemone_api`, with task instructions, few-shot examples and structured probabilities/confidence. See the [usage guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/systemone.html). - **🚀 Multi-backend Integration**: Seamlessly integrates multiple evaluation backends including OpenCompass, VLMEvalKit, RAGEval to meet different evaluation needs. - **🤖 Agent Evaluation Mode**: Drives benchmarks (e.g. GSM8K, AIME, SWE-bench Agentic) inside a controlled multi-turn AgentLoop with pluggable strategies and tools, plus Docker or [E2B remote sandboxes](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/sandbox.html#e2b); full per-sample Agent Trace is recorded and visualizable. - **⚡ Inference Performance Testing**: Provides powerful model service stress testing tools, supporting multiple performance metrics such as TTFT, TPOT. - **📊 Interactive Reports**: Provides a Web Dashboard for multi-dimensional model comparison, report overview and detailed inspection. - **⚔️ Arena Mode**: Supports multi-model battles (Pairwise Battle), intuitively ranking and evaluating models. - **🔧 Highly Extensible**: Developers can easily add custom datasets, models and evaluation metrics. ## 📊 Visualization Preview EvalScope provides an interactive Web Dashboard for multi-dimensional model comparison and in-depth analysis.

Dashboard Overview

Model Comparison

Report Overview

Prediction Details
For details, please refer to [📖 Visualizing Evaluation Results](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get_started/visualization.html). ## 🎉 What's New - 🔥 **[2026.11.12]** Added **E2B remote sandboxes** with support for official E2B and Aliyun Agent Sandbox. Run benchmarks such as SWE-bench Agentic, HumanEval and LiveCodeBench in the cloud without local Docker. See the [sandbox guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/sandbox.html#e2b). - 🔥 **[2026.10.09]** Added **System One Choice evaluation** and **ANLI**, **BoolQ**, **BANKING77**, **ContractNLI**, **RewardBench v1** benchmarks. All five default to ModelScope and also support standard LLM evaluation. See [System One Evaluation](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/systemone.html). - 🔥 **[2026.08.24] v1.11.0** Introduced published evaluation versions for reproducible benchmark results; improved report semantics and incomplete-run handling; strengthened multimodal media loading and task-config validation. - 🔥 **[2026.08.13]** Improved evaluation reports with unified metric semantics and more reliable Agent Trace step grouping and tool-call/result linking. - 🔥 **[2026.08.10]** Added **AutomationBench**, **JobBench**, **MiniWoB**, **OmniDocBench-v1.6**, **PerceptionBench**, **ScreenSpot-Pro**, **PLawBench**, **PMC-VQA**, **HiPhO**, **LogicVista**, and **CC-OCR-V2** benchmarks. - 🔥 **[2026.07.21]** Added **Claw-Eval**, **ResearchRubrics**, **Toolathlon** (agent), **TVBench** (video), **WideSearch**, and **PerspectiveGap** benchmarks. - 🔥 **[2026.07.03]** Added **CharXiv** & **BabyVision** (chart understanding, visual cognition) and **ERQA** & **WorldVQA** (entity-recognition QA with LLM-judge + CoT) multimodal benchmarks. - 🔥 **[2026.06.23]** Major agent & code evaluation expansion: added **BigCodeBench**, **SWE-bench Multilingual**, **BrowseComp**, **MCP-Atlas**, **GDPval** benchmarks; added **OpenCode** / **OpenHands** runners; refactored adapter architecture with `AudioLanguageAdapter`, unified `FunctionCallAdapter`, and public `run_agent_loop` API. - 🔥 **[2026.06.16]** Added full-reference **image quality metrics** (SSIM, PSNR, etc.), long-context benchmarks (**LoCoMo QA**, **LongMemEval**), **Caption** & **Maritime-OCR-Bench** benchmarks; perf module now supports unified `--data-source` and parallelized request generation. - 🔥 **[2026.06.02]** Refactored **RAG evaluation** module: upgraded to MTEB 2.x and RAGAS 0.4.x, with unified Pydantic-based configs. See the [RAGEval guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/backend/rageval_backend/index.html). - 🔥 **[2026.05.27]** Added **Trie agentic trace replay** for perf benchmarking: three new dataset plugins (`trie_agentic_coding` / `trie_code_qa` / `trie_office_work`) replay real multi-turn agent traces with per-turn token caps and tool-call latency simulation. Also introduced a `--duration` wall-clock budget for all benchmark modes and a `Turn` dataclass for per-turn overrides. - 🔥 **[2026.05.27]** Added **Vendor Verifier benchmarks** (`k2_verifier`, `kimi_verifier`, `minimax_verifier`) for validating whether third-party API deployments faithfully reproduce official model behavior, with a shared `FunctionCallAdapter` base class. - 🔥 **[2026.05.26]** Added the [GAIA](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/third_party/gaia.html) agent benchmark (multi-turn ReAct + `bash` in a Docker sandbox, official rule-based scorer) and generic [MCP server](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/agent/native.html#mcp-server-tools) support — any `NativeAgentConfig`-driven benchmark can now plug in stdio / HTTP / SSE MCP servers (`fetch`, web search, GitHub, ...) without per-benchmark wiring. - 🔥 **[2026.05.22]** Introduced the **External Agent Bridge** mode: evaluate off-the-shelf agent CLIs such as Anthropic's [Claude Code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code) and OpenAI's [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) directly through EvalScope. The bridge transparently forwards each CLI's LLM traffic (Anthropic Messages / OpenAI Chat / OpenAI Responses, including SSE streaming) to your evaluation model, while recording the full trajectory as an `agent_trace`. Bring-your-own-runner via `@register_runner`. See the [External Agent Bridge guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/agent/bridge.html). - 🔥 **[2026.05.19]** Added support for [SWE-bench_Pro](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/third_party/swe_bench_pro.html) and [τ³-bench](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/third_party/tau3_bench.html): SWE-bench_Pro is a more challenging multilingual long-horizon software-engineering benchmark from Scale AI (recommended over the original SWE-bench for less data contamination and broader language coverage; per-instance Docker images are pulled directly from DockerHub, no local image build required); τ³-bench is the v1.0.0 release of the tau-bench family, extending τ²-bench with a new `banking_knowledge` retrieval domain (RAG), 75+ task fixes across existing domains, and pluggable retrieval pipelines (BM25 / embeddings / rerankers / sandbox shell).

More historical updates - 🔥 **[2026.05.15]** Introduced **Agent Evaluation Mode**: any benchmark based on `DefaultDataAdapter` (GSM8K, AIME, IFEval, etc.) can now be driven through a multi-turn AgentLoop with pluggable strategies (`function_calling` / `react` / `swe_bench_*`), tools (`bash` / `python_exec` / `submit`) and `local` / `docker` environments. Per-sample `agent_trace` is recorded and rendered step-by-step in the dashboard's Predictions tab. See the [Agent Evaluation guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/agent/native.html) for details. - 🔥 **[2026.05.08]** Partnered with [LightSeek](https://lightseek.org/) to launch [TokenSpeed](https://lightseek.org/blog/lightseek-tokenspeed.html), a speed-of-light LLM inference engine for agentic workloads. EvalScope provides the SWE-smith benchmarking pipeline — using real coding-agent traces to measure per-GPU throughput (TPM) and per-user latency (TPS) — serving as the official benchmark tool for TokenSpeed performance evaluation. Refer to the [SWE-smith usage guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/stress_test/multi_turn.html#swe-smith) to get started. - 🔥 **[2026.05.07]** Replaced the Gradio-based WebUI with a new React + Vite web interface for better performance and user experience. - 🔥 **[2026.04.23]** Added support for recording performance (perf) metrics during evaluation tasks, enabling simultaneous tracking of model accuracy and inference efficiency metrics such as TTFT, TPOT, and throughput in a single evaluation run. - 🔥 **[2026.04.17]** Added support for multi-turn conversation performance stress testing, enabling load testing of dialogue-based model services with multi-turn context. Refer to the [usage documentation](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/stress_test/examples.html). - 🔥 **[2026.04.10]** Added support for [TIR-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01833) (Thinking-with-Images Reasoning Benchmark), a multimodal benchmark evaluating agentic visual reasoning capabilities of vision-language models. - 🔥 **[2026.03.24]** Added support for Agent Skill. Any agent model that supports Skill/Tool calling can use natural language to drive EvalScope for model evaluation, performance benchmarking, and result visualization. - 🔥 **[2026.03.09]** Added support for evaluation progress tracking and HTML format visualization report generation. - 🔥 **[2026.03.02]** Added support for Anthropic Claude API evaluation. Use `--eval-type anthropic_api` to evaluate models via Anthropic API service. - 🔥 **[2026.02.03]** Comprehensive update to dataset documentation, adding data statistics, data samples, usage instructions and more. - 🔥 **[2026.01.13]** Added support for Embedding and Rerank model service stress testing. - 🔥 **[2025.12.26]** Added support for Terminal-Bench-2.0, which evaluates AI Agent performance on 89 real-world multi-step terminal tasks. - 🔥 **[2025.12.18]** Added support for SLA auto-tuning model API services. - 🔥 **[2025.12.16]** Added support for audio evaluation benchmarks such as Fleurs, LibriSpeech; added support for multilingual code evaluation benchmarks such as MultiplE, MBPP. - 🔥 **[2025.12.02]** Added support for custom multimodal VQA evaluation; added support for visualizing model service stress testing in ClearML. - 🔥 **[2025.11.26]** Added support for OpenAI-MRCR, GSM8K-V, MGSM, MicroVQA, IFBench, SciCode benchmarks. - 🔥 **[2025.11.18]** Added support for custom Function-Call (tool invocation) datasets to test whether models can timely and correctly call tools. - 🔥 **[2025.11.14]** Added support for SWE-bench_Verified, SWE-bench_Lite, SWE-bench_Verified_mini code evaluation benchmarks. - 🔥 **[2025.11.12]** Added `pass@k`, `vote@k`, `pass^k` and other metric aggregation methods; added support for multimodal evaluation benchmarks such as A_OKVQA, CMMU, ScienceQA, V*Bench. - 🔥 **[2025.11.07]** Added support for τ²-bench, an extended and enhanced version of τ-bench that includes a series of code fixes and adds telecom domain troubleshooting scenarios. - 🔥 **[2025.10.30]** Added support for BFCL-v4, enabling evaluation of agent capabilities including web search and long-term memory. - 🔥 **[2025.10.27]** Added support for LogiQA, HaluEval, MathQA, MRI-QA, PIQA, QASC, CommonsenseQA and other evaluation benchmarks. Thanks to @[penguinwang96825](https://github.com/penguinwang96825) for the code implementation. - 🔥 **[2025.10.26]** Added support for Conll-2003, CrossNER, Copious, GeniaNER, HarveyNER, MIT-Movie-Trivia, MIT-Restaurant, OntoNotes5, WNUT2017 and other Named Entity Recognition evaluation benchmarks. Thanks to @[penguinwang96825](https://github.com/penguinwang96825) for the code implementation. - 🔥 **[2025.10.21]** Optimized sandbox environment usage in code evaluation, supporting both local and remote operation modes. - 🔥 **[2025.10.20]** Added support for evaluation benchmarks including PolyMath, SimpleVQA, MathVerse, MathVision, AA-LCR; optimized evalscope perf performance to align with vLLM Bench. - 🔥 **[2025.10.14]** Added support for OCRBench, OCRBench-v2, DocVQA, InfoVQA, ChartQA, and BLINK multimodal image-text evaluation benchmarks. - 🔥 **[2025.09.22]** Code evaluation benchmarks (HumanEval, LiveCodeBench) now support running in a sandbox environment. - 🔥 **[2025.09.19]** Added support for multimodal image-text evaluation benchmarks including RealWorldQA, AI2D, MMStar, MMBench, and OmniBench, as well as pure text evaluation benchmarks such as Multi-IF, HealthBench, and AMC. - 🔥 **[2025.09.05]** Added support for vision-language multimodal model evaluation tasks, such as MathVista and MMMU. - 🔥 **[2025.09.04]** Added support for image editing task evaluation, including the [GEdit-Bench](https://modelscope.cn/datasets/stepfun-ai/GEdit-Bench) benchmark. - 🔥 **[2025.08.22]** Version 1.0 Refactoring. Break changes, please [refer to](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get_started/basic_usage.html#switching-to-version-v1-0). - 🔥 **[2025.07.18]** The model stress testing now supports randomly generating image-text data for multimodal model evaluation. - 🔥 **[2025.07.16]** Support for [τ-bench](https://github.com/sierra-research/tau-bench) has been added. - 🔥 **[2025.07.14]** Support for "Humanity's Last Exam" ([Humanity's-Last-Exam](https://modelscope.cn/datasets/cais/hle)). - 🔥 **[2025.05.13]** Added support for the ToolBench-Static dataset, DROP and Winogrande benchmarks. - 🔥 **[2025.04.29]** Added Qwen3 Evaluation Best Practices. - 🔥 **[2025.04.27]** Support for text-to-image evaluation. - 🔥 **[2025.04.10]** Model service stress testing tool now supports the `/v1/completions` endpoint. - 🔥 **[2025.04.08]** Support for evaluating embedding model services compatible with the OpenAI API has been added. - 🔥 **[2025.03.27]** Added support for AlpacaEval and ArenaHard evaluation benchmarks. - 🔥 **[2025.03.20]** The model inference service stress testing now supports generating prompts of specified length using random values. - 🔥 **[2025.03.13]** Added support for the LiveCodeBench code evaluation benchmark. - 🔥 **[2025.03.11]** Added support for the SimpleQA and Chinese SimpleQA evaluation benchmarks. - 🔥 **[2025.03.07]** Added support for the QwQ-32B model evaluation. - 🔥 **[2025.03.04]** Added support for the SuperGPQA dataset. - 🔥 **[2025.03.03]** Added support for evaluating the IQ and EQ of models. - 🔥 **[2025.02.27]** Added support for evaluating the reasoning efficiency of models. - 🔥 **[2025.01.20]** Support for visualizing evaluation results. - 🔥 **[2025.01.07]** Native backend: Support for model API evaluation. - 🔥🔥 **[2024.12.31]** Support for adding benchmark evaluations. - 🔥 **[2024.12.13]** Model evaluation optimization. - 🔥 **[2024.11.26]** The model inference service performance evaluator has been completely refactored. - 🔥 **[2024.10.31]** The best practice for evaluating Multimodal-RAG has been updated. - 🔥 **[2024.10.23]** Supports multimodal RAG evaluation. - 🔥 **[2024.10.8]** Support for RAG evaluation. - 🔥 **[2024.09.18]** Documentation added blog module. - 🔥 **[2024.09.12]** Support for LongWriter evaluation. - 🔥 **[2024.08.30]** Support for custom dataset evaluations. - 🔥 **[2024.08.20]** Updated the official documentation. - 🔥 **[2024.08.09]** Simplified the installation process. - 🔥 **[2024.07.31]** Important change: The package name `llmuses` has been changed to `evalscope`. - 🔥 **[2024.07.26]** Support for **VLMEvalKit** as a third-party evaluation framework. - 🔥 **[2024.06.29]** Support for **OpenCompass** as a third-party evaluation framework. - 🔥 **[2024.06.13]** EvalScope integrates with SWIFT; Integrated the Agent evaluation dataset ToolBench.
## 🚀 Quick Start ### Installation Requires **Python >= 3.11**. ```shell pip install evalscope ``` > For detailed installation instructions (source install, extra dependencies, etc.), please refer to the [📖 Installation Guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get_started/installation.html). ### Method 1. Evaluate an Online Model API (Recommended for beginners, no GPU required) Supports any OpenAI API-compatible model service. Just set `$OPENAI_API_BASE_URL` and `$OPENAI_API_KEY` and you are ready to go: ```bash evalscope eval \ --model your-model-name \ --api-url $OPENAI_API_BASE_URL \ --api-key $OPENAI_API_KEY \ --eval-type openai_api \ --datasets gsm8k arc \ --limit 5 ``` ### Method 2. Evaluate a Local Model Evaluate a local model (auto-downloaded from ModelScope): ```bash evalscope eval \ --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \ --datasets gsm8k arc \ --limit 5 ``` ### Method 3. Using Python Code ```python from evalscope import run_task, TaskConfig task_cfg = TaskConfig( model='your-model-name', api_url='https://your-openai-compatible-endpoint/v1', api_key='your_api_key', eval_type='openai_api', datasets=['gsm8k', 'arc'], limit=5 ) run_task(task_cfg) ```
💡 Tip: run_task also supports dictionaries, YAML or JSON files as configuration. **Using Python Dictionary** ```python from evalscope.run import run_task task_cfg = { 'model': 'Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct', 'datasets': ['gsm8k', 'arc'], 'limit': 5 } run_task(task_cfg=task_cfg) ``` **Using YAML File** (`config.yaml`) ```yaml model: Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct datasets: - gsm8k - arc limit: 5 ``` ```python from evalscope.run import run_task run_task(task_cfg="config.yaml") ```
### Output Results After evaluation completion, you will see a report in the terminal in the following format: ```text ┌───────────────────────┬───────────┬────────────┬───────────────┬───────┬─────────┐ │ Model │ Dataset │ Metric │ Subset │ Num │ Score │ ├───────────────────────┼───────────┼────────────┼───────────────┼───────┼─────────┤ │ Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct │ gsm8k │ Accuracy ↑ │ main │ 5 │ 40% │ ├───────────────────────┼───────────┼────────────┼───────────────┼───────┼─────────┤ │ Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct │ arc │ Accuracy ↑ │ ARC-Easy │ 5 │ 80% │ ├───────────────────────┼───────────┼────────────┼───────────────┼───────┼─────────┤ │ Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct │ arc │ Accuracy ↑ │ ARC-Challenge │ 5 │ 40% │ └───────────────────────┴───────────┴────────────┴───────────────┴───────┴─────────┘ ``` **Launch the visualization dashboard**: ```bash pip install 'evalscope[service]' evalscope service ``` Visit `http://127.0.0.1:9000` to open the visualization interface. ## 📈 Advanced Usage ### Custom Evaluation Parameters You can fine-tune model loading, inference, and dataset configuration through command line parameters. ```shell evalscope eval \ --model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --model-args '{"revision": "master", "precision": "torch.float16", "device_map": "auto"}' \ --generation-config '{"do_sample":true,"temperature":0.6,"max_tokens":512}' \ --dataset-args '{"gsm8k": {"few_shot_num": 0, "few_shot_random": false}}' \ --datasets gsm8k \ --limit 10 ``` - `--model-args`: Model loading parameters such as `revision`, `precision`, etc. - `--generation-config`: Model generation parameters such as `temperature`, `max_tokens`, etc. - `--dataset-args`: Dataset configuration parameters such as `few_shot_num`, etc. For details, please refer to [📖 Complete Parameter Guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get_started/parameters.html). ### ⚔️ Arena Mode Arena mode evaluates model performance through pairwise battles between models, providing win rates and rankings, perfect for horizontal comparison of multiple models. ```text # Example evaluation results Model WinRate (%) CI (%) ------------ ------------- --------------- qwen2.5-72b 69.3 (-13.3 / +12.2) qwen2.5-7b 50 (+0.0 / +0.0) qwen2.5-0.5b 4.7 (-2.5 / +4.4) ``` For details, please refer to [📖 Arena Mode Usage Guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/arena.html). ### 🖊️ Custom Dataset Evaluation EvalScope allows you to easily add and evaluate your own datasets. For details, please refer to [📖 Custom Dataset Evaluation Guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/advanced_guides/custom_dataset/index.html). ## ⚡ Inference Performance Evaluation Tool EvalScope provides a powerful stress testing tool for evaluating the performance of large language model services. - **Key Metrics**: Supports throughput (Tokens/s), first token latency (TTFT), token generation latency (TPOT), etc. - **Result Recording**: Supports recording results to `wandb` and `swanlab`. - **Speed Benchmarks**: Can generate speed benchmark results similar to official reports. For details, please refer to [📖 Performance Testing Usage Guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/stress_test/index.html).

## 🧪 Other Evaluation Backends EvalScope supports launching evaluation tasks through third-party evaluation frameworks (we call them "backends") to meet diverse evaluation needs. - **Native**: EvalScope's default evaluation framework with comprehensive functionality. - **OpenCompass**: Focuses on text-only evaluation. [📖 Usage Guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/backend/opencompass_backend.html) - **VLMEvalKit**: Focuses on multi-modal evaluation. [📖 Usage Guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/backend/vlmevalkit_backend.html) - **RAGEval**: Focuses on RAG evaluation, supporting Embedding and Reranker models. [📖 Usage Guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guides/backend/rageval_backend/index.html) - **Third-party Evaluation Tools**: Supports evaluation tasks like [ToolBench](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/third_party/toolbench.html).
🏛️ Overall Architecture


EvalScope Overall Architecture.

1. **Input Layer** - **Model Sources**: API models (OpenAI API), Local models (ModelScope) - **Datasets**: Standard evaluation benchmarks (MMLU/GSM8k etc.), Custom data (MCQ/QA) 2. **Core Functions** - **Multi-backend Evaluation**: Native backend, OpenCompass, MTEB, VLMEvalKit, RAGAS - **Performance Monitoring**: Supports multiple model service APIs and data formats, tracking TTFT/TPOT and other metrics - **Tool Extensions**: Integrates Tool-Bench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, etc. 3. **Output Layer** - **Structured Reports**: Supports JSON, Table, Logs - **Visualization Platform**: Supports Web Dashboard, Wandb, SwanLab
## ❤️ Community & Support Welcome to join our community to communicate with other developers and get help. [Discord Group](https://discord.gg/xc66bMxc4h) | WeChat Group | DingTalk Group :-------------------------:|:-------------------------:|:-------------------------: | | ## 👷‍♂️ Contributing We welcome any contributions from the community! If you want to add new evaluation benchmarks, models, or features, please refer to our [Contributing Guide](https://evalscope.readthedocs.io/en/latest/advanced_guides/add_benchmark.html). Thanks to all developers who have contributed to EvalScope!



## 📚 Citation If you use EvalScope in your research, please cite our work: ```bibtex @misc{evalscope_2024, title={{EvalScope}: Evaluation Framework for Large Models}, author={ModelScope Team}, year={2024}, url={https://github.com/modelscope/evalscope} } ```
