items.name: agent-foundation
items.description: a13n - Build, run, and manage AI agents at scale on your own infrastructure. Open source, with a built-in harness, durable execution, multi-provider support, and a management console. Built With Love 💜 @converge-ai-labs
items.readme_text:
Agent Foundation (a13n)

[![CI](https://github.com/converge-ai-labs/agent-foundation/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/converge-ai-labs/agent-foundation/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Documentation](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-agent--foundation-blue)](https://a13n.dev/docs/) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.13%2B-blue)](https://www.python.org/) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-green)](LICENSE) [![Slack](https://img.shields.io/badge/Slack-Join%20the%20community-4A154B)](https://join.slack.com/t/a13n/shared_invite/zt-4embv13zr-JfXjmJQop4Y9y6K3NH0kDQ) **Build, run, and manage AI agents at scale on your own infrastructure.** a13n Service is an open-source runtime for managing and running agents. Use Console, its web interface, to configure an agent, try it in a conversation, and debug its tool calls. Your application can then call that same agent through the [HTTP API](docs/a13n-service/connect-application.md) or a [Python, TypeScript, Go, or Rust SDK](docs/a13n-service/sdks.md). Service handles execution and recovery for those requests. - **Long-running tasks:** Agents keep working when clients disconnect. - **Durable execution:** Interrupted runs can resume from saved checkpoints after worker failures. - **Run visibility:** Inspect runs from your application in Console and track workspace usage and cost. Choose your [providers](#providers-and-integrations) for models, sandboxes, web search, and memory. Bring your own keys. ## Run Service [![Console showing six managed agents, their model providers, and status](.github/assets/console-managed-agents.jpg)](.github/assets/console-managed-agents.jpg) Console with fictional demo data. See [run details from a scripted demo](.github/assets/console-run-details.jpg) and [workspace usage](.github/assets/console-usage.jpg). ### Quickstart with Docker Compose Install Docker and Docker Compose, then run: ```bash mkdir a13n-service && cd a13n-service curl -fL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/converge-ai-labs/agent-foundation/main/deploy/docker/compose/a13n-service.yaml -o a13n-service.yaml docker compose -f a13n-service.yaml up -d --wait --pull always ``` Open : 1. Create your administrator account. 2. In **Models**, select **Add model** and configure a model using an API key or an eligible [ChatGPT subscription](docs/a13n-service/models.md#chatgpt-subscription-provider). 3. Create an agent with that model and select **Try agent** to send it a message. 4. Open **Connect to app** on the same agent to get its ID, Service URL, and an API key. Call the agent from your application through the [HTTP API](docs/a13n-service/connect-application.md) or a [Python, TypeScript, Go, or Rust SDK](docs/a13n-service/sdks.md). The stack runs Service, Console, PostgreSQL, and Redis. Agent environments use your host Docker Engine. See the [Compose guide](deploy/docker/compose/README.md) for configuration. ### Production on Kubernetes Deploy to Kubernetes with our [Helm chart](deploy/kubernetes/README.md#other-clusters). Configure API and worker replicas and shared storage for [high availability](docs/a13n-service/operations.md#process-roles). ## Providers and integrations [![Bring your own stack. Self-host a13n with your choice of models, environments, web data providers, and app connections.](.github/assets/a13n-architecture.webp)](https://a13n.dev/docs/#providers-and-integrations) [Models](docs/a13n-service/models.md) · [Sandboxes](docs/a13n-service/environments.md) · [Web search](docs/a13n-service/tools.md#web-search-and-scrape) · [Memory](docs/a13n-service/memory.md) · [App connections](docs/a13n-service/tools.md#connections) ## Use Harness directly Service is built on Harness, which handles tool use, Skills, memory, and subagents. You can also use it without deploying Service: - **In your application:** [Embed Harness](docs/a13n-harness/getting-started.md) in your Python code. Your application manages execution and storage. - **On your machine:** Use [Harness UI](docs/a13n-harness-ui/index.md) to work with agents in a terminal or browser. **Benchmarks:** Harness scored **58.06%** on 62 Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks, compared with **58.77%** in published Codex results using the same model and reasoning effort. See the [methodology](https://github.com/converge-ai-labs/agent-foundation/discussions/1015) and [FrontierHarness evaluation](https://github.com/converge-ai-labs/agent-foundation/discussions/1064). ## Documentation - [Service documentation](docs/a13n-service/index.md) - [HTTP API and application integration](docs/a13n-service/connect-application.md) - [Deployment and operations](docs/a13n-service/operations.md) - [Examples](examples/README.md) These guides track `main`. For an installed release, use its release notes and package metadata. Ask questions on [Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/a13n/shared_invite/zt-4embv13zr-JfXjmJQop4Y9y6K3NH0kDQ) or [open an issue](https://github.com/converge-ai-labs/agent-foundation/issues) for bugs and feature requests. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) before submitting changes. You can self-host a13n under the [Apache 2.0 license](LICENSE). See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) to report a vulnerability.

items.name: computer-use-linux
items.description: Native Linux desktop control for AI agents (MCP, Pi, CLI): semantic AT-SPI trees, screenshots, window targeting, and input across GNOME, KDE, Hyprland, niri, COSMIC, i3, Sway, labwc and other wlroots compositors, and X11.
items.readme_text:
computer-use-linux

Native Linux desktop control for AI agents over MCP, Pi native tools, and CLI.

> Running open models for your company? [**Tiyuvta**](https://tiyuvta.ai/services/) helps with model choice, deployment and optimization, and fine-tuning on your hardware or cloud account.

Built and maintained with a lot of agent tokens and hours. If it saves you time, sponsoring helps keep it going.

`computer-use-linux` gives AI agents real, structured control of a local Linux desktop: semantic AT-SPI accessibility trees, bounded screenshots, compositor-aware window targeting, Wayland/X11 input synthesis, and single-round-trip post-action verification across **GNOME, KDE Plasma/KWin, Hyprland, niri, COSMIC, i3, Sway, labwc and other wlroots compositors, and X11/EWMH**, plus a click-through on-screen activity indicator on GNOME and on Wayland compositors with wlr-layer-shell. ## Quick start Pick the setup that matches your agent or shell workflow: | Host / workflow | Install command | | --- | --- | | **Claude Code** (plugin + skill) | `claude plugin marketplace add agent-sh/computer-use-linux && claude plugin install computer-use-linux@computer-use-linux` | | **Codex CLI** (plugin + skill) | `codex plugin marketplace add agent-sh/computer-use-linux && codex plugin add computer-use-linux@computer-use-linux` | | **Pi Coding Agent** (native lazy-loaded tools) | `pi install npm:@agent-sh/computer-use-linux` | | **Hermes Agent** (CLI + skill + MCP server) | `npm install -g @agent-sh/computer-use-linux && hermes skills tap add agent-sh/computer-use-linux && hermes skills install agent-sh/computer-use-linux/computer-use-linux && hermes mcp add computer-use-linux --command computer-use-linux --args mcp` | | **CLI + any stdio MCP client** (npm) | `npm install -g @agent-sh/computer-use-linux` | | **CLI + system setup from source** | `git clone https://github.com/agent-sh/computer-use-linux && cd computer-use-linux && ./install.sh` | | **Rust crate (`crates.io`)** | `cargo install computer-use-linux` | Verify desktop readiness from the shell (after installing the CLI on `PATH` via `npm install -g @agent-sh/computer-use-linux`, `./install.sh`, or `cargo install computer-use-linux`): ```bash computer-use-linux doctor | jq .readiness computer-use-linux setup # enable AT-SPI accessibility bridge if needed computer-use-linux setup-window-targeting # install GNOME Wayland window-control extension if needed ``` > **Plugin-only or Pi-only installs:** The Claude Code / Codex plugin launcher and `pi install` manage private cached binaries and do not add `computer-use-linux` to `PATH`. Either run the MCP `doctor` / `setup_accessibility` / `setup_window_targeting` tools (or `computer_use_linux_doctor` in Pi) directly from your agent, or also install the CLI above when you want shell subcommands on `PATH`. The Rust crate is published as [`computer-use-linux`](https://crates.io/crates/computer-use-linux) and the npm package as [`@agent-sh/computer-use-linux`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@agent-sh/computer-use-linux). Prebuilt `x86_64` and `aarch64` Linux binaries ship with the [latest release](https://github.com/agent-sh/computer-use-linux/releases/latest). They need glibc 2.28 or newer: RHEL 8 and its rebuilds, Debian 10, Ubuntu 20.04, and anything later. On an older system, build from source with `cargo install computer-use-linux`. > Need an **isolated** desktop where the agent never touches your real mouse, keyboard, or focused window? Use the sibling project [**`agent-workspace-linux`**](https://github.com/agent-sh/agent-workspace-linux) alongside this one. ## What this is `computer-use-linux` is a Rust MCP server and CLI for Linux desktop control. It ships three binaries: the main `computer-use-linux` server/CLI, the `computer-use-linux-cosmic` Wayland toplevel helper for COSMIC, and the `computer-use-linux-indicator` click-through activity overlay. Any MCP host (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Codex Desktop's Linux build, [Pi Coding Agent](#pi-coding-agent), [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent), Claude Desktop, or your own client) can spawn it to inspect accessibility trees, list and focus windows, take screenshots, click, drag, scroll, type, and invoke semantic accessibility actions. Most computer-use MCP servers are macOS-only (they lean on AppKit, AXUIElement, CGEvent). The few that target Linux either drive `xdotool` against an X11 root window or shell out to OCR over screenshots. It differs in five ways: - **Wayland actually works.** On Wayland, pointer actions use `/dev/uinput` or `org.freedesktop.portal.RemoteDesktop`. ydotool sends only untargeted wheel events there, and a coordinate action with neither route is refused. Literal text prefers KDE clipboard integration on Plasma, `wtype` on compatible Wayland compositors, and portal keysyms on other Wayland sessions, including GNOME with ydotool installed. Portal text startup or conversion errors fail the call without replaying text through ydotool. Raw ydotool text accepts printable ASCII, tab and newline only, and its physical US key positions can produce different text under the active layout. Screenshots use the GNOME Shell DBus screenshot method when present, `org.freedesktop.portal.Screenshot` otherwise, then on a native X11 session a root-window `GetImage` (device pixels, no toolkit scaling), and finally spawn `gnome-screenshot` for background/systemd contexts where the DBus paths are denied. - **Window targeting is compositor-aware.** The window registry tries GNOME Shell extension, GNOME Shell Introspect, COSMIC Wayland helper, KWin DBus scripting, Hyprland `hyprctl`, the niri IPC socket, the `umbriel` CLI, i3 IPC, labwc's `labwc.sock`, wlr-foreign-toplevel-management, and generic X11/EWMH in order, then reports exactly which backend won or why each backend failed. Terminal windows are enriched with their controlling TTY and foreground process so agents can target "the terminal running `pytest`" directly. Every `window_id` fits JavaScript's exact integer range (at most 2^53-1), so JSON clients can pass it back unchanged; a larger value is rejected with a prompt to re-run `list_windows`. - **Semantic selectors first, pixel coordinates when needed.** Tools like `click`, `perform_action`, and `set_value` accept `role` / `name` / `text` / `states` selectors or `element_index` values backed by AT-SPI, and every mutating tool can return a post-action screenshot and updated accessibility tree in the same round trip. Pixel coordinates remain available for rendering-only surfaces (canvas, games, X clients without ATK). - **Visible to humans, invisible to screenshots.** While an agent acts, `computer-use-linux-indicator` renders a click-through overlay with a per-agent cursor glide, click ripple, keycaps/typing banner, screen-edge glow, and status pill, and hides automatically under a shared capture lock before any screenshot is read. - **One JSON readiness report.** `computer-use-linux doctor` returns a structured document covering platform, portals, AT-SPI, windowing, input, and a `readiness` summary with explicit blockers and a recommended next step. MCP hosts can render or surface that to the user without parsing prose. The crate was extracted from [`codex-desktop-linux`](https://github.com/avifenesh/codex-desktop-linux) (the Linux distribution of Codex Desktop), which bundles this backend for its native Computer Use feature. This standalone repo is the upstream. ## MCP tools & features | Category | Tool | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | **Diagnostics & setup** | `doctor` | Single-shot JSON readiness report (platform, portals, accessibility, windowing, input, readiness summary, and capability map). | | | `setup_accessibility` | Enables and verifies GNOME's `org.gnome.desktop.interface toolkit-accessibility` setting so toolkit apps expose AT-SPI trees. | | | `setup_window_targeting` | Installs and enables the bundled GNOME Shell extension. GNOME Wayland needs it for exact window activation and move/resize; every GNOME session needs it for the on-screen indicator. | | **Discovery & observation** | `get_app_state` | Combined screenshot + compacted AT-SPI accessibility tree with stable `element_index` handles. Scope with `app_name_or_bundle_identifier` or a window target (`window_id`, `pid`, `app_id`, `wm_class`, `title`). | | | `get_tree_page` | Page through the latest cached tree by node offset, for trees too large to return inline when the host cannot read the spill file. Pass `snapshot_id` to refuse a page from a tree a later snapshot replaced. | | | `screenshot` | Bounded PNG or JPEG capture of the full desktop (`full_screen: true` or no target), a raised and cropped target window (`window_id`, `pid`, `app_id`, `wm_class`, `title`, `raise_window`), or one monitor (`monitor`, a 0-based index in reading order: rows of monitors top to bottom, each row left to right) at its own resolution, with its origin in the caption for click coordinates. | | | `list_windows` | Compositor windows with `window_id`, title, `app_id`, `wm_class`, PID, focus state, client type (`wayland`/`x11`), bounds, and terminal TTY/process metadata. | | | `focused_window` | The window currently holding keyboard focus. | | | `list_apps` | Running desktop applications visible to the AT-SPI registry. | | **Input** | `click` | Click by `element_index`, semantic selector (`role`/`name`/`text`/`states`), or desktop/window-relative coordinates (`left`/`right`/`middle`, `click_count`). | | | `drag` | Desktop coordinate drag from `(start_x, start_y)` to `(end_x, end_y)`. | | | `scroll` | Page-based vertical/horizontal scroll on an element, window, or pixel coordinate. | | | `press_key` | Single keys or chords (`Ctrl+L`, `Alt+F4`, `Return`), optionally focusing a target window or terminal first, or with `delivery: "background"` to an element, browser tab or terminal without moving keyboard focus. | | | `type_text` | Literal text entry, optionally targeted at a window or terminal (`tty`, `terminal_pid`, `terminal_command`, `terminal_cwd`), or with `delivery: "background"` to an element, browser tab or terminal without moving keyboard focus. | | **Semantic actions** | `perform_action` | Invoke any AT-SPI action exposed by an element (`Press`, `Activate`, `Toggle`, `Jump`, …); defaults to the primary action. | | | `set_value` | Write directly to a settable accessibility element (text fields, sliders, spinners). | | **Window management** | `activate_window` | Focus a window by `window_id`, `pid`, `app_id`, `wm_class`, `title`, or terminal selectors. | | | `move_window` / `resize_window` | Reposition or resize a window in desktop coordinates (GNOME Shell extension and X11/EWMH backends). | | **Opt-in host tools** | `complete_interaction` | Parameter-free desktop completion notification (`notify-send`); registered only when `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_NOTIFY_ON_COMPLETE=1`. | | | `run_shell` | Bounded non-login `/bin/sh -c` execution; registered only when `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_ENABLE_SHELL=1` (absent by default). | Every tree result carries a `snapshot_id`: `get_app_state`, an `include_tree` observation, and `get_tree_page`. The server caches one tree, and each new tree replaces it. Pass the `snapshot_id` with an `element_index` (or a selector, except on `scroll`) to `click`, `scroll`, `perform_action` or `set_value`, and to `get_tree_page`: if a later tree replaced that snapshot, the call is refused before any window is raised or input is sent, since the index could name another element by then. A full capture-space `x`/`y` point does not come from the tree, so it is not checked. A `coordinate_space: "atspi"` click maps through its element, so it is checked. Without `snapshot_id`, the element resolves in the latest tree. An `element_identifier` names the AT-SPI object itself and is not checked against a snapshot. Ids differ between server processes, so an id from before a restart is refused. `click`, `scroll`, `perform_action`, and `set_value` take an optional app target (`pid`, `window_id`, `app_id`, `wm_class`, `window_title`). With one, an `element_index` (or a selector, where the tool takes one) from another app's `get_app_state` snapshot is refused; call `get_app_state` for the target app first. When the window backend reports no pid for a target window (i3 without `xprop`, COSMIC, other wlroots compositors), the snapshot must have been taken for that window, or the call is refused. `perform_action` and `set_value` do not focus the target window. An `element_identifier` is refused when its owner on the accessibility bus is a different pid than the target; it is not checked when either pid is unknown. ### Post-action observation in one round trip All mutating tools (`click`, `drag`, `scroll`, `press_key`, `type_text`, `perform_action`, `set_value`, `activate_window`, `move_window`, and `resize_window`) accept optional post-action observation parameters so an action and its verification complete in a single MCP tool call: - `screenshot_after: true | "screen" | "window" | false`: capture after the action is dispatched and the indicator overlay is hidden (`true` or `"screen"` for full desktop, `"window"` cropped to the action's target window or the focused window when untargeted) - `format`, `quality`, `scale`, `max_width`, `max_height`, `max_bytes`: same screenshot payload controls as `screenshot` and `get_app_state` - `screenshot_file_path`: save the post-action screenshot to this new file instead of returning it as image content (see [Screenshot files](#screenshot-files)) - `include_tree: true`: include a fresh compacted AT-SPI accessibility tree and its `snapshot_id`; it replaces the cached tree, so later `element_index` values come from it When post-action screenshot capture succeeds, the image is returned as the first MCP `image` content block alongside the JSON action summary and `screenshot` metadata. If the action succeeds (`ok: true`) and only the post-action screenshot or tree capture fails, `ok` remains `true` and the error is reported in `screenshot_error` / `accessibility_error` and appended to `message`. ### Screenshot sizing & coordinate scaling Screenshot payloads are size-bounded by default before they are returned to the MCP host: max 1920 px width/height and 2 MiB image bytes, with hard caps even when callers request more. Agents that need more detail can pass `max_width`, `max_height`, `max_bytes`, `scale`, `format: "jpeg"`, or `quality`, preferably with a window target or crop. PNG remains the default; JPEG lets callers trade lossless pixels for a smaller payload before the byte cap forces further resizing. Returned screenshot metadata includes `coordinate_width`, `coordinate_height`, `scale`, `format`, and `quality` so callers can convert from a downscaled preview to desktop coordinate pixels. ### Screenshot files `screenshot`, `get_app_state` and the `screenshot_after` capture of mutating tools take `screenshot_file_path`. With it, the image is saved to that file and no MCP image content is returned, so a capture costs no image tokens until the agent reads the file. The metadata stays the same (`width`, `height`, `coordinate_width`, `coordinate_height`, `scale`, `format`, `quality`, `bytes`) plus `file_path`: in the `screenshot` caption, and in `screenshot.file_path` for the other tools. - The path must be absolute, and its parent directory must exist. Directories are not created. - The extension must match `format`: `.png` for png (the default), `.jpg` or `.jpeg` for jpeg. - The path must end with the file name, so a trailing `/` or `/.` is refused. - File output creates a new file and never replaces one. Any existing entry at the path is refused: a file, a directory or a symlink. - The image is written to a temp file in the same directory, then moved into place with a step that fails if anything exists at the path (`renameat2` with `RENAME_NOREPLACE`, or `link` where that is unsupported). A reader never sees a partial file, and an entry created meanwhile is neither followed nor replaced. The file is created with mode 0600. - A bad path is refused before anything is captured or any input is sent. - A failed write is never answered with the image inline. `screenshot` returns an error, `get_app_state` sets `screenshot_error`, and a mutating tool sets `screenshot_error` and keeps the action's `ok`. - Over stdio the path is on the machine that runs the server. Over HTTP (`mcp --listen`) the parameter is refused, so a remote client gets no way to write files on the host. ### Input & semantic targeting contracts For a plain left `click` by element index or selector, the element's first AT-SPI action takes precedence over bounds when it is `click`, `press`, or `toggle`. Entry `activate` and slider `jump` must be requested explicitly with `perform_action`; they are never a substitute for a pointer click, even when bounds are missing. This avoids pointer conversion for GTK3 HiDPI extents and GTK4 zero-origin bounds when the element exposes such an action. The preference does not substitute an arbitrary action name for a coordinate click. Explicit `x`/`y`, right clicks, and double/multiple clicks retain pointer semantics. Re-check application state after either kind of activation. On KDE Wayland, element clicks that need pointer dispatch match the cached AT-SPI frame to a coherent KWin window/output snapshot, then map the target separately to physical capture pixels (uinput) and logical desktop coordinates (portal). Client-local and decorated frames, actual decoration offsets, and nonzero or negative output origins are supported when the geometry and uniform output scale can be verified. Ambiguous windows, mixed or unknown scales, overlapping outputs, or stale pointer geometry fail before input. These clicks get no off-screen or monitor-gap warning, since KWin maps the point onto an output; the uinput route still reports a clamp. Explicit `x`/`y` defaults to `coordinate_space: "capture"` (raw screenshot pixels). To click a global AT-SPI screen point, pass `coordinate_space: "atspi"` together with its `element_index` or semantic selector; KDE Wayland then applies the same native KWin decoration and scale conversion as an element-bounds click, including when the AT-SPI window frame is client-local. This mode requires both coordinates and element identity and cannot be combined with `relative: true`. Other calls keep their existing coordinate behavior. For coordinate `click` or `scroll` with `relative: true`, select a target window and measure from its clipped screenshot crop origin. Divide preview `x` and `y` by the returned screenshot `scale` before passing them. These are not raw GDK surface or widget-local coordinates; decorations and clipping can change the origin. A missing window target is rejected. **X11 text fidelity:** `xdotool`/XTEST can silently substitute symbols under non-US XKB layouts (reported with Brazilian `br`/ABNT2) or changing keymap state, even when `type_text` returns `ok: true`. Every successful xdotool text dispatch includes a layout warning. XKB layout replacement events, persistent mapping/group changes, and keyboard focus/grab transitions detected across a call return an error after dispatch, without replaying the text. Keyboard grabs can divert characters without changing the polled focused-window ID. If monitoring cannot start, xdotool still dispatches and the response explicitly warns that layout-change and keyboard interception detection were unavailable. PointerRoot focus is unsupported because pointer motion can redirect input without a detectable focus event. This also detects a `setxkbmap` layout changed and restored during one call. Temporary raw remaps or group switches restored within a call and dropped text with a stable map remain unverified. Re-observe the actual text before pressing Enter, submitting it, or treating it as delivered. Use `include_tree: true` for AT-SPI readback when the application exposes the text, or `screenshot_after: true` to inspect it. These observations do not automatically compare the field to the requested text. Do not retry blindly. Targeted `press_key`/`type_text` results append focused-element feedback from AT-SPI (role, name, editable); `type_text` also warns when a concrete non-terminal focus is not editable. Terminals accept keyboard input without an EditableText interface; re-observe the contents to confirm input. Click/screenshot/input results warn when the target window or coordinate is partially or fully off-screen. A click, scroll or drag coordinate between monitors, where monitors of different sizes or offset rows leave part of the screenshot uncovered, gets a warning too: the server reads the monitor layout once per screenshot (from the portal session, KWin, the GNOME Shell extension, Hyprland, kscreen, Sway, COSMIC, niri or wlr-output-management, and from RandR on X11 only) and checks the point in screenshot pixels. Without a layout that fits the screenshot, only its outer rectangle is checked. The warning says what the route did. The portal sends nothing. X11 keeps the pointer on the screen, so a point off the screenshot lands at an edge. On X11 and the uinput pointer, a point between monitors lands at a monitor edge or on no visible pixel. A failed X11 click or scroll gets no warning, since nothing was sent. A failed drag gets none either, though it may have pressed and released before it failed. A drag checks its start and end points, and each warning names the endpoint. On the uinput pointer, a drag result also says where an off-screen endpoint was clamped to, as a click result does. Points along the path are not checked: the portal moves them onto the nearest shared monitor, and on X11 and uinput the drop goes to the end point. `get_app_state` returns a compact readiness block by default; pass `verbose: true` for the full diagnostics report. Tree nodes use a compact encoding: null, empty, zero and false fields are left out, containers do not carry the U+FFFC placeholder text Chromium gives them, and `actions` lists action names (pass one as `perform_action`'s `action`). `verbose: true` returns the full encoding, with every field and action descriptions and keybindings. `interactive_only: true` returns only nodes with an action, editable text or a value, plus headings, status and live regions, windows and dialogs; containers are collapsed, so `parent_index` names the nearest kept ancestor. Its `element_index` values are the same as in the full tree. When `title` or `window_id` names one of several windows under one AT-SPI application root (Chromium puts every browser window under one), the tree covers that window plus the app's popups and dialogs, and drops its other named windows; `message` says so. It also reports `tree_scoped` (false when no app target narrowed the AT-SPI tree, with a warning in `message`) and `accessibility_tree_truncated` (true when the node, depth, read, or time budget stopped traversal with unread elements left). When a result would pass 32,000 bytes, the tree comes back as its leading nodes plus `accessibility_tree_spill` (`path`, `node_count`, `bytes`, `inline_node_count`). `path` is a private JSON file holding the whole tree with the same `element_index` values, in `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/computer-use-linux/trees` when that runtime directory is private, otherwise under `~/.cache` (directories 0700, file 0600). Search the file instead of requesting the tree again; hosts that cannot read files page through the same tree with `get_tree_page`. The file lasts until the next snapshot or until the server exits; after a crash it is swept at the next start or after an hour. An `app_id` may be a full desktop ID or its final dot-separated segment; matching is case-insensitive, ambiguous aliases are rejected, and an unresolved explicit `app_id` returns an empty scoped tree rather than the desktop. `set_value` on editable text reads the full contents back after dispatch. `verified: true` means an exact match; mismatches and readback failures return `ok: false` without replaying the mutation. Password fields return `verified: false` because masked content cannot prove the write. Re-observe after any mismatch; the contents may have changed. On X11, text input sends LF and CRLF line endings as Return, with one newline per CRLF pair. On GNOME, a read-only keymap preflight rejects the whole string before input if a character is absent or requires a modifier level Mutter cannot synthesize. The background reader cannot establish the active layout group, so every configured group must support the text. This can reject text that works in one of several groups. Then the text goes into the focused editable field of the verified target window through AT-SPI EditableText: it is inserted at the caret, replaces a selection, and counts as typed (`ok: true`) only when the field reads it back with the rest of its text unchanged (in a field over 4096 characters, the 32 on each side of the insert). The field must be in the AT-SPI window that matches the target and that window must be active, so a field left focused in another window of the app is not used. A password field, focus outside an editable field, and text with a newline, tab or other control character keep the refusal; send keys with `press_key`, or fill the field with `set_value`. The check parses the keymap in pure Rust, with no system XKB library, and stops after a two-second keymap read deadline. It does not cover held modifiers or a keymap changed concurrently with typing. ### Background keyboard delivery `type_text` and `press_key` take `delivery: "background"` to reach a target without moving the user's keyboard focus ([#480](https://github.com/agent-sh/computer-use-linux/issues/480)). The target picks the route. Naming an element or a `browser_tab` selects background delivery on its own, and `delivery: "focus"` with one is refused. The result's `background` field says what happened: `{"requested": true, "used": true, "route": "..."}` when a background route delivered it. When no route serves the target because the desktop or app lacks one (below, "no route"), the call is not blocked. The first such call in a server session sends nothing and returns a notice: `ok: false` without `isError`, `background: {"requested": true, "used": false, "delivered": false, "reason": "...", "retry_to_continue": true}`, and a message with the reason (and the setting that would open a route, where there is one), that normal input moves the user's keyboard focus and pointer, and that [agent-workspace-linux](https://github.com/agent-sh/agent-workspace-linux) gives the agent its own session. Repeating the call sends it through normal focused input, as without `delivery`, and so does every later call with no route, with only `background: {"requested": true, "used": false}` in the result. For an element, focused input first gives the element keyboard focus with AT-SPI `GrabFocus` and then types into its window (the target fields, or the snapshot's window); for a `browser_tab`, it targets the one window whose title contains the tab's name (with window fields, that window must show it). With Hyprland background mode on, normal input to a window is the same sendkeystate route, so a call with no route there stays an error. A wrong, ambiguous or stale target (an unmatched or ambiguous element, tab, tty or window, a replaced snapshot, a terminal whose pty belongs to another devpts instance, a point outside the target window or screen), the X server's Ctrl+Alt+F-key and Ctrl+Alt+BackSpace chords on the agent seat, and a failure after input started stay errors. - **Element (AT-SPI).** Pass `element_index` with `snapshot_id`, `element_identifier`, or `role`/`name`/`states`, plus the app target to check the snapshot against, as for `set_value`. `type_text` inserts through EditableText at the element's caret, or at its end when the caret is not in it, and succeeds only when the field reads the text back with the rest unchanged. A selection is left alone and the caret is not moved. A line feed or tab goes in only on a multi-line element; other control characters have no route. A password field takes the text but cannot be read back, and the result says so, as with `set_value`. `press_key` runs the AT-SPI action the key means: Enter or space on a button or menu item, space on a check box, radio button or toggle, Enter on a link, and Enter on a single-line field that has an `activate` action. Other keys and chords with modifiers have no route there. - **Browser tab (DevTools).** Start Chrome, Chromium or an Electron app yourself with `--remote-debugging-port` and its own `--user-data-dir`, and set `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_DEVTOOLS` to the port or to the path of its `DevToolsActivePort` file. The server connects only to that port on 127.0.0.1, only when its listener belongs to the same user, and never starts or restarts a browser. `browser_tab` names the tab: a target id, or text in one tab's URL or title. Text goes in with `Input.insertText` at the tab's focused element, as typing would, and an input or textarea must read it back. Keys go with `Input.dispatchKeyEvent`. The tab needs a focused field for text. Shortcuts the browser handles outside the page, such as Ctrl+T, do not run this way. A field inside a frame from another origin is refused. - **Terminal.** Pass `tty`, `terminal_pid`, `terminal_command`, `terminal_cwd`, or a terminal window. The server finds the program on that tty and tries, in order: kitty remote control (the `KITTY_LISTEN_ON` socket kitty gives its shells; needs `allow_remote_control` and `listen_on` in kitty.conf), `wezterm cli`, tmux (a pane on the tty, or the active pane of a client attached on it), GNU screen (the current window of a client on the tty, when no other client may be attached to its session; a screen window's own tty is refused, since window numbers can be swapped), TIOCSTI where `dev.tty.legacy_tiocsti` is 1 and the server has CAP_SYS_ADMIN, and the terminal's pty master through `pidfd_getfd` where ptrace rules allow it. The result names the channel it used. Text reaches kitty, wezterm and tmux on stdin and screen through a private file and its `^_` register, which is cleared after the paste, never as a process argument. A tty taken from a window must have its pty master held by that window's terminal, so a container's pts with the same number is refused. When nothing works, there is no route, and the reason names the terminal found and the setting that would open one. GNOME Terminal, Ptyxis and other VTE terminals and Ghostty have no remote input command, and Konsole's D-Bus route is not supported yet, so a program in them needs tmux or screen. Writing to `/dev/pts/N` only prints on the screen, so the server never does it. On Hyprland with `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_HYPRLAND_BACKGROUND=1`, a window target with `delivery: "background"` goes through `send_key_state` as in background mode, and so does a terminal window that no terminal channel reaches. - **Whole window (agent seat).** A window target that is not an element, a browser tab or a terminal some channel above reaches goes through the agent's own keyboard focus, on desktops that ship one. On X11 the server adds an XInput 2 master pointer and keyboard named `computer-use-linux agent `, focuses the target with `XISetFocus` for that keyboard only, and types through its XTEST device; the user's master keeps its focus and cursor. Keys come from the user's keymap (first two levels), so a character it lacks has no route, and neither does a key or chord another client grabs on the root window (a window manager shortcut such as openbox's Alt+F4), since through the agent seat the grab would act on the user's session. The check takes and drops a passive grab of each key back to back; a key the user presses in that instant goes nowhere. On sway 1.10 and later the server creates an `ext-transient-seat-v1` seat, focuses the target on it with `zwlr_foreign_toplevel_handle_v1.activate`, and types through a virtual keyboard with its own keymap; `seat0` keeps its focus and its workspace (a target on a workspace the user is not viewing still gets the keys), and sway removes the seat when the server disconnects. Xwayland windows have no route, because Xwayland feeds every seat into one X keyboard that follows the X focus, and neither do scratchpad windows, because activating one shows it on the user's workspace; if seat0's focus moves anyway, no keys are sent. Alt and Super chords, and chords the sway config binds (its included files too), have no route, because sway runs its bindings for the agent seat too. The agent keymap uses keycodes above any real keyboard's, so `bindcode` and `bindsym --to-code` bindings never match an agent key. On Hyprland the route is `sendkeystate`, as in Hyprland background mode below, without the environment variable. On X11 the master appears on first use and goes away after ten idle minutes or when the server exits. On sway the transient seat lives for one call (each call waits 100 ms after creating it, so clients can bind the new seat before input arrives; a client busy for longer misses the input), so no other program sees it between calls: wtype, for one, binds the last seat it sees, and a password or autotype helper using it would otherwise type into the agent's window. The X11 master's name carries a window owned by the server's X connection, so a master left by a killed server is removed by the next one. When input fails partway, the result says it may have been partly delivered and the seat is rebuilt. `click` and `scroll` take `delivery: "background"` too, with `x` and `y` in screenshot capture pixels and a window target: the agent seat's pointer moves and clicks, and the user's pointer stays. The point must be over that window (on sway, on a visible workspace), or nothing is pressed. On X11 this needs a session with no window manager, because a window manager answers a click from any pointer by focusing that window for the user (openbox did); with one running, background clicks have no route and background keys still work. On sway the click also focuses the window on the agent seat only. | Desktop | Agent seat | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | X11 (EWMH window managers) | Keys; pointer only without a window manager | XInput 2 multi-pointer is part of the X server. Checked with xterm, GTK 3 and Chrome under openbox, and the pointer without a window manager. | | sway 1.10+ | Keys and pointer | [ext-transient-seat-v1](https://wayland.app/protocols/ext-transient-seat-v1) plus foreign-toplevel activation on a named seat ([sway view.c](https://github.com/swaywm/sway/blob/master/sway/tree/view.c)). GTK 3, GTK 4 and Chromium bind only the seats that exist when they start ([gdkdisplay-wayland.c](https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gtk/-/blob/gtk-3-24/gdk/wayland/gdkdisplay-wayland.c), [wayland_seat.cc](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:ui/ozone/platform/wayland/host/wayland_seat.cc)), so they never see the agent seat and have no route; foot and other clients that bind new seats get the keys. Xwayland windows have no route. Older sway has no transient seats. | | Hyprland | Keys (`sendkeystate`, US layout) | One seat; `sendkeystate` is its per-window key dispatcher. No second pointer. | | GNOME | Pointer through a virtual pen (below); no keys | One seat, and Mutter has no per-window input request. A tablet has its own cursor. | | KDE Plasma (KWin) | None | One `SeatInterface` and no per-window input request. KWin 6.2+ gives a tablet its own cursor too, but maps a tablet with no configured output to the active output, which follows the user's pointer. | | COSMIC | None | cosmic-comp creates one seat and has no transient-seat protocol. | | niri | None | One seat and no transient-seat protocol. | | labwc, river-classic, other wlroots compositors | None | One seat (labwc activates foreign toplevels on it; river-classic lists multiple seats as a TODO). | Where there is no agent seat, a window-targeted background call has no route (the notice, then focused input); element, browser tab and terminal targets still work. For full isolation, with its own keyboard and pointer, run the app in an [agent-workspace-linux](https://github.com/agent-sh/agent-workspace-linux) workspace; the notice points there. `doctor` lists the routes this machine has in `capabilities.background_input` (`seat` when the agent seat is available) and the seat's route, pointer support or the reason it has none in `capabilities.background_seat`. `capabilities.background_pointer` shows the GNOME pen route and its limits, or why there is none. On GNOME Wayland (and KDE Plasma, below), background `click`, `drag` and `scroll` go through a virtual pen and a virtual touchscreen instead of the user's pointer ([#480](https://github.com/agent-sh/computer-use-linux/issues/480); the idea and the tested approach are [@Ondra-Zik](https://github.com/Ondra-Zik)'s). Mutter gives a tablet tool its own cursor and sends its events through the tablet protocol, not `wl_pointer`, so the user's mouse stays where it is. Clicks are pen taps (left), the upper barrel button (right) and the lower one (middle); `click_count` repeats them. GNOME 48 and later default the lower button to a right click and the upper one to a middle click, so before each action the server sets its own pen's button actions to match the buttons it presses, and resets them when the pen goes away. A drag is the pen tip pressed at the start, moved and lifted at the end. The pen leaves proximity after each action: libinput pairs a pen with a touchscreen and ignores that screen's touches while the pen is near, and that screen can be the user's. A scroll is a one-finger touch pan, 60 logical pixels per wheel notch (5 notches per page), split into strokes that stay inside the window and 48 pixels from the monitor's edges, where GNOME Shell starts its edge swipes; the finger rests before it lifts, so the app does not fling further. Before any input, the server checks through the GNOME Shell extension that the point is on the target window, on the workspace the user sees, and that no window stacked above it covers the point; both ends of a drag and every pan stroke must be on the window, and a pan always starts at the point. The results report the route as `gnome-pen` or `gnome-touch`. The devices need write access to `/dev/uinput`, as the uinput pointer does; without it, or without the extension, the call gets the notice and then focused input. Limits: - A pen tap or a touch focuses the window it lands on, as a click does, so the user's typing goes there after it. The result says when the keyboard focus moved. - The window check sees windows, not GNOME Shell's own UI. The call is refused while the screen is locked, while no window has focus (the overview may be open), and when the target is not on the workspace of the focused window, but a Shell dialog, notification banner or open menu over the point is not seen. - Mutter sends tablet events only to clients that support the tablet protocol (GTK 3 and 4, Qt, Chromium, Firefox and Xwayland do). Other clients never see the pen, and the call cannot tell: re-observe the window. This is also why the pen is not the default route: the uinput pointer reaches every client. - A drag stays inside one window. A touch pan scrolls only where the app pans on touch. - The pen leaves proximity right after each action, so hover effects such as tooltips end with it. - Mutter maps an unconfigured tablet across the whole layout, and an unconfigured touchscreen to the builtin panel. When a device maps elsewhere than the point needs, the server writes that device's `output` setting (`org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.tablet` or `.touchscreen`, at the path keyed by the devices' own vendor and product ids, `6375:7065` and `6375:7463`), waits for mutter's `org.gnome.Mutter.InputMapping` to confirm the new mapping, and resets the setting when the device goes away. No other device's setting is touched. - The devices appear on first use and go away after ten idle minutes or when the server exits. On KDE Plasma Wayland with KWin 6.3 or later the same route runs as `kwin-pen` and `kwin-touch`. KWin gives a tablet its own cursor from 6.3 (it tracks the tablet cursor itself and moves it whether or not the client under it supports tablets). KWin maps a tablet with no setting to the active output, which follows the user's pointer, and a touchscreen to the internal panel or the first output. So before input the server sets the pen's `mapToWorkspace` and the touchscreen's `outputName` (the output under the point) through `org.kde.KWin.InputDevice`, reads them back, and once the devices are gone removes what KWin wrote for them into `kcminputrc` (the groups keyed by these devices' vendor, product and name) with `kwriteconfig6`. The window check goes through KWin scripting: the point must be on the target, on the desktop and activity the user sees, not minimized or hidden, with no window, panel, popup or notification stacked above it. The call is refused while KWin shows the desktop or runs a full-screen effect such as the Overview (`org.kde.kwin.Effects.activeEffects`), and when another setting for the device moves where input lands (calibration, input or output area, rotation). A scroll reads the output's rotation with `kscreen-doctor` and refuses a rotated or flipped output; without `kscreen-doctor` there is no touch route. There is no route at all when KWin's `SyncWithMouse` tablet option (`kcminputrc` `[Tablet]`) is on, since it moves the user's pointer to where the pen was, when KWin runs with `KWIN_WAYLAND_EMULATE_TABLET`, which sends pen input over apps without tablet support through the user's pointer, or without `kreadconfig6` and `kwriteconfig6`. Some clients mishandle a second `wl_seat` (Zed, [zed-industries/zed#66735](https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/issues/66735)); that is one more reason the sway seat exists only during a call. A menu the agent opens on sway closes when its call ends, since the seat that opened it goes away. While sway is in a binding mode other than `default`, background keys have no route, since the mode's bindings would take them. ### On-screen indicator While an agent acts, the server drives `computer-use-linux-indicator`, a click-through overlay that shows what it is doing: a software cursor tinted per agent that glides to each coordinate `click`, `drag`, or `scroll` target and ripples on click (AT-SPI actions such as `perform_action`, `set_value`, and element clicks show in the pill without moving it, since no pointer moves); keycaps for `press_key` and a typing line for `type_text`; a glow along every screen edge; and a status pill such as *Claude is using your computer · click*. Pointer actions wait 350 ms so the cursor lands before the real input. While `screenshot` or `get_app_state` captures the screen, the overlay draws nothing, so agents never see it: not their own, not one shown for another agent, and not one that another agent starts mid-capture. This holds with `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_INDICATOR=0` too, which only stops a server from showing its own actions. The capture waits for the compositor only when something was on screen. The agent name comes from the MCP client's `clientInfo`. The server starts the indicator on the first action and it exits after ten idle minutes. It stays hidden between bursts of activity. Compositors with `wlr-layer-shell` use the shared-memory overlay. GNOME uses native Shell actors through the bundled extension. X11 sessions other than GNOME show no indicator. Run `setup_window_targeting` once, then log out and back in after installing or updating the extension. Both renderers use the same capture lock and acknowledgement protocol. Set `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_INDICATOR=0` to turn it off. Screenshot processing uses one blocking worker per server. Captures enter one pipeline before reading pixels, so concurrent requests do not queue decoded full-screen images. A source can contain up to 134,217,728 pixels; serial processing bounds decoded-image memory while letting MCP answer other requests during resizing and encoding. Session discovery is reused after a successful probe and refreshed when session variables change. Failed discovery is retried. Captures require the shared capture lock and, when an overlay is running, its acknowledgement that it has hidden. A missing or invalid acknowledgement, a stalled socket, or a failed lock returns a capture error. Concurrent captures keep separate holds; their acknowledgements are exchanged in order. ### MCP safety contract `computer-use-linux` is not a read-only data source. It can observe the local desktop and, when a mutating tool is called, can change real application state. The `tools/list` response includes MCP `ToolAnnotations` so hosts can surface this distinction before invocation: | Class | Tools | Contract | | --- | --- | --- | | Read-only observation | `doctor`, `list_apps`, `list_windows`, `focused_window`, `get_app_state`, `get_tree_page` | `readOnlyHint=true`; may reveal app, window, accessibility, and screenshot contents. `get_app_state` may trigger the desktop screenshot portal prompt. Its `screenshot_file_path` file output creates a new file and never replaces one. | | Local setup mutators | `setup_accessibility`, `setup_window_targeting` | `readOnlyHint=false`, `destructiveHint=false`, `idempotentHint=true`; modifies user desktop configuration by enabling accessibility or installing/enabling the GNOME window-targeting extension. | | UI state mutators | `activate_window`, `move_window`, `resize_window`, `scroll`, `screenshot` | `readOnlyHint=false`, `destructiveHint=false`; changes focus, geometry, or scroll position in the live desktop, or raises a window to capture it. `screenshot_file_path` file output creates a new file and never replaces one. | | Desktop action mutators | `click`, `drag`, `press_key`, `type_text`, `perform_action`, `set_value` | `readOnlyHint=false`, `destructiveHint=true`, `openWorldHint=true`; can trigger arbitrary actions in whatever local application is targeted. | | Conditional notification | `complete_interaction` | Absent unless `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_NOTIFY_ON_COMPLETE=1`; when enabled, `readOnlyHint=false`, `destructiveHint=false`, `idempotentHint=false`, `openWorldHint=true`. Sends a desktop notification. | | Conditional host-code execution | `run_shell` | Absent unless `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_ENABLE_SHELL=1`; when enabled, `readOnlyHint=false`, `destructiveHint=true`, `idempotentHint=false`, `openWorldHint=true`. Runs with the MCP server user's host permissions. | Annotations are safety hints, not an authorization system. MCP hosts should still ask the user before calls that could submit, delete, send, purchase, overwrite, or otherwise commit state. `run_shell` is an explicit trust-boundary opt-in, not a restricted command runner. Enabling it grants an approved MCP call the same file and network authority as the user running the server. The tool clears the ambient environment and inherits only a small desktop/runtime allowlist (`PATH`, home/user/locale fields, display/session-bus fields); additional variables must be supplied in the visible call payload. Commands use a fixed non-login `/bin/sh`, an existing canonical working directory, a 30-second default / 120-second hard timeout, process-group cleanup, and stderr audit records keyed by the command SHA-256 rather than command text. Collected streams up to 8 MiB are returned with a 512 KiB per-stream response cap and truncation flag; exceeding 8 MiB on either stream fails the call without partial output. These controls bound accidental leakage and runaway work; they do not make arbitrary shell code safe. The binary also exposes the same capabilities from the CLI for scripting and debugging: ``` computer-use-linux mcp # stdio MCP server computer-use-linux mcp --listen 127.0.0.1:5200 # streamable HTTP MCP; needs COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_MCP_TOKEN computer-use-linux doctor # JSON readiness report computer-use-linux setup # enable AT-SPI computer-use-linux guard-accessibility # explicit foreground GNOME accessibility guard computer-use-linux setup-window-targeting # install GNOME Shell extension computer-use-linux apps computer-use-linux state [APP_NAME] computer-use-linux screenshot # JSON screenshot summary computer-use-linux windows ``` ## Support matrix Validated manually on Ubuntu 25.10 (GNOME Shell 50.1, Wayland). niri window listing and exact focus were also validated on Ubuntu 26.10 (development), niri 26.04, with a single 2x output, through both CLI and direct IPC.
