Only manual prebuilt-binary installs need you to download all three release assets. ### Option A: `./install.sh` from a clone Installs system packages on Debian/Ubuntu, Fedora/RHEL-like, Arch-like, or Artix systems; installs Rust if needed; builds all three release binaries (`computer-use-linux`, `computer-use-linux-cosmic`, and `computer-use-linux-indicator`); installs them to `~/.local/bin`; configures `ydotoold` as a systemd user service when available; enables GNOME AT-SPI settings when running under GNOME; and installs the bundled GNOME Shell extension on GNOME Wayland. ```bash git clone https://github.com/agent-sh/computer-use-linux cd computer-use-linux ./install.sh # log out and back in if the GNOME extension was newly installed computer-use-linux doctor | jq .readiness ``` `ydotool` is an optional fallback. On X11, the installer includes `xdotool` as the required keyboard backend. If ydotool is unavailable from the configured repositories, the installer continues, but `doctor` still requires a keyboard-capable RemoteDesktop portal or `wtype` (on compatible compositors) on Wayland, or xdotool on X11; direct uinput provides absolute pointer input only. On non-systemd hosts, automatic `ydotoold` service setup is skipped and the installer prints a command suitable for a per-user supervisor. For an unrecognized distro, pass `--package-manager apt|dnf|pacman`; `--force-unknown-distro` auto-selects only when exactly one of those managers is available. ### Option B: `cargo install` (Rust binaries, no system setup) Installs all three Rust binaries from crates.io. You still handle the system-level pieces yourself: AT-SPI, desktop portals, the optional `ydotoold` fallback, and the GNOME extension if you need the GNOME Wayland exact-focus backend. ```bash cargo install computer-use-linux computer-use-linux doctor ``` For unreleased changes from `main`, install directly from Git: ```bash cargo install --git https://github.com/agent-sh/computer-use-linux ``` Then, as needed: ```bash sudo apt install ydotool at-spi2-core # ydotool 1.0.3+ when using this fallback sudo apt install wtype # optional Unicode typing on wlroots/Hyprland Wayland systemctl --user enable --now ydotool # only when doctor selects ydotool (Ubuntu's unit name) computer-use-linux setup # gsettings AT-SPI bridge computer-use-linux setup-window-targeting # GNOME Shell extension ``` ### Option C: npm wrapper (binary download) Good for users who already have Node.js and want a no-Rust install. The npm package downloads and verifies the matching `computer-use-linux`, `computer-use-linux-cosmic`, and `computer-use-linux-indicator` binaries during install, or on first launch when npm skipped the install script (npm 12 does for scripts it was not told to allow). The wrapper wires `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_COSMIC_HELPER` and `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_INDICATOR_BIN` to the bundled helpers automatically. ```bash npm install -g @agent-sh/computer-use-linux computer-use-linux doctor ``` You will still need AT-SPI enabled (`computer-use-linux setup`) and one input backend reported ready by `doctor`. Start `ydotoold` only when using the ydotool fallback. ### Option D: prebuilt binaries Linux x86_64 / aarch64 builds are published with each tag. Each binary ships a `.sha256` next to it. The `-gnu` builds need glibc 2.28 or newer; the `-musl` builds (`target=x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`) are statically linked for musl distributions such as Alpine. - Latest release: ```bash target=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu base=https://github.com/agent-sh/computer-use-linux/releases/latest/download for binary in computer-use-linux computer-use-linux-cosmic computer-use-linux-indicator; do asset="$binary-$target" curl -L -O "$base/$asset" curl -L -O "$base/$asset.sha256" sha256sum -c "$asset.sha256" install -D -m 0755 "$asset" "$HOME/.local/bin/$binary" done ``` You will still need AT-SPI enabled (`computer-use-linux setup`) and one input backend reported ready by `doctor` (start `ydotoold` only when using the ydotool fallback). ## Wire it into your MCP host The binary speaks MCP over stdio through `rmcp` 3.5, or over streamable HTTP with `mcp --listen` (see [Generic MCP client](#generic-mcp-client)). It answers `initialize` with the client's protocol version when that is 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18 or 2025-11-25, and with 2025-11-25 for any other. 2026-07-28 clients skip `initialize`: they send `server/discover` and carry the version in each request's `_meta`, on stdio or HTTP. For stdio, pass `mcp` as the only argument; everything else is configured through MCP tool calls. ### Claude Code and Codex plugin This repo is a plugin marketplace for both Claude Code and Codex. The plugin registers the MCP server and ships the `computer-use-linux` skill. On first start it downloads the release binaries pinned to the plugin version, checks each against its published `.sha256`, and caches them under `~/.cache/computer-use-linux/plugin/`. It needs `curl` or `wget`, and nothing else is installed. Claude Code: ```bash claude plugin marketplace add agent-sh/computer-use-linux claude plugin install computer-use-linux@computer-use-linux ``` Codex CLI: ```bash codex plugin marketplace add agent-sh/computer-use-linux codex plugin add computer-use-linux@computer-use-linux ``` Start a new session afterwards. To run your own build instead of the pinned release, set `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_BIN` to its path in the host's environment. System setup (`computer-use-linux setup`, `setup-window-targeting`, ydotoold) still applies; ask the agent to run the `doctor` tool to see what is missing. Codex passes only a short allowlist of environment variables to MCP servers, so the Codex manifest forwards the desktop session variables, the [server settings](#environment-variables), and every variable the Pi extension passes, such as the GLib and loader paths `gsettings` reads. Codex Desktop's Linux build already bundles Computer Use; do not install both there. ### Codex Desktop (Linux build) [`codex-desktop-linux`](https://github.com/avifenesh/codex-desktop-linux) includes a native `computer-use-linux` feature that embeds and stages this backend inside the app's unified Computer Use plugin. Enable `computer-use-linux` via `make setup-native` (or in `linux-features/features.json` followed by `make install-native`), then toggle **Settings → Computer use → Any App** in the desktop app. Do not register a second standalone `computer-use-linux` MCP server inside Codex Desktop when the native feature is enabled. ### Claude Code (CLI) The plugin above is the simplest route. To wire a binary you installed yourself, use the `claude mcp add` command to register the binary as a stdio MCP server. Pick a scope: - `--scope user`: available across all projects for your user. - `--scope project`: written to `.mcp.json` at the project root for team sharing. - `--scope local` (default): only the current project, stored in `~/.claude.json`. ```bash # User-wide install (recommended for desktop control) claude mcp add --scope user computer-use-linux -- computer-use-linux mcp # Verify the server is registered and reachable claude mcp list ``` If `computer-use-linux` is not on `PATH`, pass the absolute path (e.g. `~/.local/bin/computer-use-linux`). Inside a Claude Code session, run `/mcp` to confirm the tools are loaded. ### GitHub Copilot CLI Install the binary first using one of the methods above, then register it with Copilot CLI from your logged-in Linux desktop session: ```bash copilot mcp add computer-use-linux \ --env COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_ENABLE_SHELL=0 \ -- computer-use-linux mcp copilot mcp get computer-use-linux ``` This adds a user-scoped MCP entry; it does not install the backend or configure desktop permissions. If the binary is not on `PATH`, use its absolute path after `--`. Avoid registering a second controller if a plugin already supplies this server. Start a new Copilot session and use `/mcp` to confirm that the server's tools are loaded. Ask for the `doctor` tool first, then test one non-sensitive app with a specific target and visible-result check. Complete portal permission dialogs yourself. A ready doctor report is not capture/control permission; screenshots and app text can enter the model's context. To remove only this registration: ```bash copilot mcp remove computer-use-linux ``` These commands were checked with Copilot CLI 1.0.112. For other clients, use the generic stdio configuration below. ### Claude Desktop Edit `~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`: ```json { "mcpServers": { "computer-use-linux": { "command": "computer-use-linux", "args": ["mcp"] } } } ``` Restart Claude Desktop. The tools should appear in the tools list. ### Pi Coding Agent ```bash pi install npm:@agent-sh/computer-use-linux ``` Restart Pi or run `/reload`. The package exposes one small loader initially; the real tools keep their upstream schemas and are enabled only when Computer Use is needed: Native tools require Pi 0.84.4 or newer (Node.js 22.19 or newer). The standalone npm CLI wrapper continues to support Node.js 18 or newer. ``` computer_use_linux_tools({ tools: ["doctor", "list_windows"] }) computer_use_linux_doctor({}) computer_use_linux_list_windows({}) ``` You can also search by capability: ``` computer_use_linux_tools({ query: "observe a window and click a control" }) ``` Codemode scripts receive `{ text, images, isError }`. Each image is an MCP image block that can be passed directly to `image()`: ```js const result = await tools.computer_use_linux_screenshot({}); if (result.isError) throw new Error(result.text); text(result.text); for (const block of result.images) image(block); ``` No separate MCP adapter or manual MCP configuration is required. When npm skipped the package's install script (npm 12 does for scripts it was not told to allow), the first real tool call downloads the binary. Pi starts one computer-use-linux process lazily on the first real tool call, reuses it for the session so accessibility snapshots remain valid, serializes desktop actions, and closes it on reload, session switch, or exit. See the [Pi setup guide](skills/computer-use-linux/references/pi-setup.md) for migration from older adapter-based installs. ### Hermes Agent Install the companion Hermes skill so Hermes has the desktop-specific runbook: ```bash hermes skills tap add agent-sh/computer-use-linux hermes skills install agent-sh/computer-use-linux/computer-use-linux ``` The skill is optional but recommended for Hermes users. It teaches Hermes how to install, configure, verify, and call the Linux desktop MCP safely. It follows the same `skills//SKILL.md` tap layout used by Hermes community skills. Then add the stdio MCP server: ```bash hermes mcp add computer-use-linux --command computer-use-linux --args mcp hermes mcp test computer-use-linux hermes mcp configure computer-use-linux ``` `configure` opens Hermes' tool-selection UI for the server. The generated config holds `command`, `args` and `enabled`, plus `tools.include` when you pick a subset of tools. Hermes defaults to a 300-second tool-call timeout and a 60-second connect timeout; add `timeout` or `connect_timeout` under the server to change them. ```yaml mcp_servers: computer-use-linux: command: computer-use-linux args: ["mcp"] enabled: true ``` Subagents keep the parent's MCP tools by default (`delegation.inherit_mcp_toolsets`). If you installed the binary somewhere that is not on `PATH`, pass the absolute path as `--command`. Restart Hermes after editing the config. Hermes registers the tools as `mcp_computer_use_linux_` and creates the `mcp-computer-use-linux` runtime toolset. You can verify both sides before asking Hermes to use the desktop: ```bash computer-use-linux doctor | jq .readiness hermes skills inspect agent-sh/computer-use-linux/computer-use-linux hermes chat --toolsets mcp-computer-use-linux -q "List the current desktop windows." ``` For one-off installs without adding the tap first, Hermes also accepts `hermes skills install agent-sh/computer-use-linux/skills/computer-use-linux`. ### Generic MCP client Spawn the binary with `["mcp"]` as the argv tail. It speaks MCP (JSON-RPC over stdio) through rmcp, with the protocol versions [listed above](#wire-it-into-your-mcp-host); capability discovery happens through `tools/list` and the `doctor` tool. `mcp --listen ADDR:PORT` serves the same protocol over streamable HTTP at `/mcp` instead; without `--listen` no socket is opened. It needs a bearer token from the file named by `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_MCP_TOKEN_FILE` (for example a mounted Kubernetes Secret) or from `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_MCP_TOKEN`. Prefer the file, because a token in `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_MCP_TOKEN` stays readable in `/proc//environ` while the server runs, even though child processes do not inherit it. Clients send `Authorization: Bearer `; a missing or wrong token gets 401. `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `::1` are always accepted as the `Host`. A bind that is not loopback, including `0.0.0.0` and `[::]`, needs each name clients use as `--allowed-host NAME` (repeatable, any port, case-insensitive); another `Host` gets 403. Any request with an `Origin` header gets 403, because browser clients are not supported. `--listen` refuses to start while `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_ENABLE_SHELL=1`. Over HTTP, every `get_tree_page` call, and `click`, `scroll`, `set_value` and `perform_action` calls that pick an element by `element_index` or selector, must pass the `snapshot_id` of the caller's latest `get_app_state` or `include_tree` result; calls by `element_identifier` or capture-space `x`/`y` do not. Clients share one cached tree, so two clients that alternate `get_app_state` refuse each other's ids; call `get_app_state` again after a refusal. `screenshot_file_path` is refused over HTTP, so remote clients always get screenshots inline. Responses may be SSE (`text/event-stream`). 2024-11-05 and 2025 clients get sessions; 2026-07-28 requests run stateless. SIGTERM and SIGINT stop the listener cleanly with exit status 128 plus the signal number, and a connection that does not send its request headers within 10 seconds is closed. The port is plain HTTP: put TLS in front (service mesh, ingress or sidecar) when it leaves the host. The server normally needs no other MCP-specific configuration, but desktop runtime environment still matters (`DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`, `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, portals, AT-SPI, `ydotoold`, and optionally `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_COSMIC_HELPER`). Idle sessions expire after an hour. A `404 Session not found` means the session expired, so initialize again; the cached tree and its `snapshot_id` survive re-initializing. ### Selkies containers (linuxserver.io) linuxserver.io's Selkies desktop images (`webtop`, `chrome`, and others) can run the server inside the container, with the host's MCP client connecting over stdio through `docker exec`. Start the container with `PELORUS=true` so pixelflux serves screenshots and input. A small launcher joins the desktop session, because `docker exec` starts outside it. See the [Selkies container guide](skills/computer-use-linux/references/selkies-setup.md). ## First-run checklist 1. **Run `doctor`.** ```bash computer-use-linux doctor | jq .readiness ``` Aim for `can_register_mcp_tools`, `can_build_accessibility_tree`, `can_send_development_input`, and `can_query_windows` all `true`, with an empty `blockers` array. Doctor lists detected screenshot routes in `capabilities.screenshot`, but does not take a screenshot or request consent. Detected routes are always `screenshot_capture_status: "unverified"` and `can_capture_screenshots: false` in a doctor report. `get_app_state` records the result of its requested raw capture as `verified` or `failed`; only `verified` sets `can_capture_screenshots: true` in that response. If no route is detected, the status is `unavailable`. An unverified capture is a warning, not an installation blocker. 2. **If `accessibility.at_spi_bus.ok = false`**, run `computer-use-linux setup` (or call the `setup_accessibility` MCP tool). This sets: - `org.gnome.desktop.interface toolkit-accessibility true` You may need to restart toolkit-using apps for the change to take effect. 3. **If `windowing.can_list_windows = false`**, inspect `doctor.windowing.backends`. On GNOME Wayland, run `computer-use-linux setup-window-targeting` (or call `setup_window_targeting`) to install the bundled `computer-use-linux@avifenesh.dev` Shell extension, then log out and back in so GNOME Shell loads it. On KDE, Hyprland, niri, i3, Sway, COSMIC, labwc and other wlroots compositors, or generic X11, install or expose the matching compositor tool/helper shown in the backend details. 4. **Verify screenshot capture.** Call `get_app_state` or run `computer-use-linux screenshot`. The Screenshot portal may request consent for the caller's app ID. On GNOME, that dialog can be rejected when the app ID does not match the focused app. A detected portal interface alone does not prove capture permission. Inspect the full backend error and the desktop portal logs if capture fails; `gnome-screenshot` is an optional fallback when GNOME Shell or portal calls are denied. 5. **If doctor selects ydotool, confirm ydotool 1.0.3+ and `ydotoold` are running.** ```bash systemctl --user status ydotoold # install.sh's unit; Ubuntu's package names it ydotool ``` Its socket should appear at `/run/user/$UID/.ydotool_socket`. ## Environment variables Most setups need none of these: the server and installers detect backends and paths. They exist for overriding auto-detected paths and input backends. **Server runtime** (set in the MCP host's environment): | Variable | Effect | | --- | --- | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_NOTIFY_ON_COMPLETE` | Set exactly to `1` to expose the optional `complete_interaction` notification tool. Requires `notify-send` and a desktop notification service; disabled by default. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_COSMIC_HELPER` | Path to the `computer-use-linux-cosmic` helper when it isn't next to the binary or on `PATH`. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_INDICATOR` | Set to `0` (or `false`/`off`/`no`) to turn off the on-screen indicator. On by default. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_INDICATOR_BIN` | Path to the `computer-use-linux-indicator` overlay when it isn't next to the binary or on `PATH`. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_INDICATOR_HIDE_TEXT` | Set exactly to `1` to mask all typed text and keycaps in the indicator. `set_value` values are always masked. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_AGENT_NAME` | Name shown in the indicator instead of the one derived from the MCP client's `clientInfo`. | | `CU_DISABLE_ABS_POINTER` | Set exactly to `1` to disable the uinput absolute pointer. Wayland coordinate actions then need the RemoteDesktop portal; they refuse input rather than use ydotool's relative-motion approximation. Native X11 fallback is unchanged. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_FORCE_PORTAL_POINTER` / `…_KEYBOARD` | Set exactly to `1` to prefer the RemoteDesktop portal on Wayland, skipping auto-detection. Pointer forcing skips the absolute uinput backend. Forced ydotool or XTEST keyboard overrides take precedence; KDE literal text keeps its clipboard route. Portal startup and text conversion failures return errors without replaying through ydotool. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_PORTAL_SCROLL_INVERT` | Set to `1` to reverse vertical scrolling through the RemoteDesktop portal. Defaults to normal direction on both GNOME and KDE Plasma; horizontal direction is unchanged. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_DEVTOOLS` | The loopback DevTools port of a browser you started with `--remote-debugging-port`, or the absolute path of its `DevToolsActivePort` file. With it, `type_text` and `press_key` with `browser_tab` type into that browser's tabs without focusing it. The server connects only to 127.0.0.1 and never starts a browser. Unset, `browser_tab` calls are refused. See [Background keyboard delivery](#background-keyboard-delivery). | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_HYPRLAND_BACKGROUND` | Set exactly to `1` on Hyprland to work on a window without focusing it. `type_text` and `press_key` calls that name a target window send keys to it through Hyprland's `send_key_state` dispatcher instead of focusing it and typing, and `get_app_state` and `screenshot` capture an unfocused target alone with `grim -T` instead of raising it or using the portal. The user's focus, cursor and workspace do not change, so the target can sit on a hidden workspace. Text is mapped for a US layout: other keymaps and characters outside printable ASCII, tab and newline are refused before any key is sent. Browser accelerators such as Ctrl+R are ignored by an unfocused Chromium. Unset, input focuses the target as before. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_PERSIST_REMOTE_DESKTOP` | Set exactly to `1` to ask the RemoteDesktop portal to remember pointer and keyboard grants across processes. The first dialog still appears (on GNOME the remember box starts checked). Later processes reuse the single-use restore token from `Start`, stored mode `0600` under `$XDG_STATE_HOME/computer-use-linux/` (or `~/.local/state/computer-use-linux/`). Pointer and keyboard tokens are separate. Needs interface version 2. Unset, every new process is prompted. No effect when input is not using the portal. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_FORCE_YDOTOOL_POINTER` / `…_KEYBOARD` | Set exactly to `1` to always route pointer / keyboard through `ydotool`, skipping the portal and KDE clipboard paths; pointer forcing also skips the absolute uinput backend and native-X11 `xdotool` clicks, scrolls and drags. Coordinate pointer actions on Wayland then refuse input because ydotool cannot position them accurately; scrolling at the current pointer remains available. | | `YDOTOOL_SOCKET` | Explicit ydotool socket path. When unset, only an owner-only `.ydotool_socket` in the user's private runtime directory is accepted; the legacy shared `/tmp/.ydotool_socket` is never selected automatically. Setting this variable is an operator trust override for custom layouts. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_FORCE_XDOTOOL_KEYBOARD` | Set exactly to `1` to prefer `xdotool`/XTEST keyboard input when `DISPLAY` is available. `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_FORCE_YDOTOOL_KEYBOARD=1` takes precedence. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_XDOTOOL_TYPE_DELAY_MS` | Per-character delay for `xdotool type` in milliseconds (default `12`). `0` is faster but can deliver characters out of order on some X servers. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_SCREENSHOT_BACKEND` | Force a single screenshot backend, skipping the fallback chain. Accepts `gnome-shell`, `portal`, `x11`, `gnome-screenshot`, or `pixelflux`. `x11` works only on a native X11 session. `pixelflux` needs `PIXELFLUX_CU` and `PIXELFLUX_CU_TOKEN`. Pin `gnome-screenshot` for background/systemd contexts where the GNOME Shell and portal DBus paths are denied. | | `PIXELFLUX_CU` | Loopback port of a Selkies pixelflux computer-use server (`5000` or `127.0.0.1:5000`). With `PIXELFLUX_CU_TOKEN`, screenshots try pixelflux before the other backends, and click, scroll, drag, press_key, and type_text go there without a portal prompt. A closed port falls through. A server error does not. Anything other than loopback is ignored. | | `PIXELFLUX_CU_TOKEN` | Bearer token for `PIXELFLUX_CU`. Never logged. Both variables must be set. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_MCP_TOKEN_FILE` | Path of a file holding the `mcp --listen` bearer token, such as a mounted Kubernetes Secret. Surrounding whitespace is trimmed. Setting both this and `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_MCP_TOKEN` is an error. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_MCP_TOKEN` | The `mcp --listen` bearer token, when no token file is used. Clients send `Authorization: Bearer `. The token is never logged, and both variables are removed from the environment so child processes do not inherit them. Prefer `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_MCP_TOKEN_FILE`: a token passed here stays readable in `/proc//environ` for the server's lifetime. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_ENABLE_SHELL` | Set exactly to `1` before starting the MCP server to register the destructive `run_shell` tool. Unset by default. Do not enable for untrusted or unattended MCP hosts. | **Build-time identity overrides** (set while compiling a downstream embedded bundle): `CUL_GNOME_EXTENSION_UUID`, `CUL_DBUS_SERVICE`, and `CUL_DBUS_OBJECT_PATH` replace the default standalone GNOME Shell extension UUID and DBus endpoint in both the Rust probes and the generated extension files. **npm wrapper** (set during `npm install`, or before running). The package's install script downloads the release binaries. When npm skipped it (npm 12 runs only install scripts it is told to allow), the wrapper runs the same download on first launch, with its output on stderr. A download that receives no data for 30 s fails: | Variable | Effect | | --- | --- | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_BIN` | Run this binary instead of the bundled one. The CLI wrapper and the plugin launcher use the path as given and fail if it does not exist. The Pi extension uses it only when it is an absolute path to an executable. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_TIMEOUT_MS` | Pi native tools only: per-call timeout in milliseconds (default `60000`). Raise it for `run_shell` calls with `timeout_seconds` above 60. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_DOWNLOAD_BASE` | Override the GitHub release base URL the installer downloads from (mirrors, air-gapped hosts). | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=1` | Skip the binary download entirely, at install and at first launch. | | `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_LOCAL_BINARY` / `…_LOCAL_COSMIC_HELPER` / `…_LOCAL_INDICATOR` | Install from a local build instead of downloading (used by CI and local testing). | ## Architecture - **Accessibility tree**: [`atspi`](https://crates.io/crates/atspi) crate (tokio backend) talks to the AT-SPI registry on the user session bus. The tree is flattened to `(role, name, text, states, bounds)` tuples and indexed; element indices are stable for the duration of a `get_app_state` snapshot. A new snapshot is published only between input operations. `click`, `scroll`, `perform_action`, and `set_value` hold the input lock while they check and resolve an index, so a checked element cannot turn into another app's node mid-action. - **DBus where desktops expose it**: [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) for portal calls (`org.freedesktop.portal.Screenshot`, `…RemoteDesktop`, `…ScreenCast`), GNOME Shell screenshots (`org.gnome.Shell.Screenshot`), the bundled GNOME extension's `dev.avifenesh.ComputerUseLinux.WindowControl` service, and temporary KWin scripting. - **MCP transport**: [`rmcp`](https://crates.io/crates/rmcp) with the `transport-io` feature for stdio, and its streamable HTTP server on `axum` for `mcp --listen`. No socket is opened without `--listen`. - **Input fallback**: on X11, keyboard input prefers `xdotool`/XTEST and falls back only when xdotool cannot launch. On Wayland, literal text uses `wtype` when it is installed on a compatible compositor (not GNOME, KDE or COSMIC), unless `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_FORCE_PORTAL_KEYBOARD=1`; `wtype` supports Unicode through the virtual-keyboard protocol. Otherwise KDE uses its clipboard route and other Wayland sessions use portal keysyms, which never fall back to ydotool. ydotool 1.0.3+ with its `ydotoold` socket types only when the selected wtype is missing or cannot start, when KDE cannot read the Klipper clipboard, or when ydotool is forced. A wtype that started and failed is returned without replaying the text. `press_key` chords use the portal when ydotool is absent; on a session whose bus answers that it has no RemoteDesktop portal (wlroots compositors such as Sway, labwc, river or cage), they go through `wtype` instead. The route is chosen before any input is sent, so a failed or denied portal request is never replayed through wtype. `install.sh` can configure `ydotoold`; the `setup` command only enables the GNOME AT-SPI bridge. - **Hyprland background mode**: with `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_HYPRLAND_BACKGROUND=1`, a targeted `type_text` or `press_key` is sent as `hl.dsp.send_key_state` down/up pairs for the target's address, written straight to Hyprland's control socket in one `[[BATCH]]` request per 64 key presses (never through `hyprctl` arguments, so typed text cannot be read from `/proc//cmdline`), and the window is never focused. Hyprland answers each dispatch, so when every dispatch in a failed batch was answered the error states how many key presses were delivered (and whether a key was left down), and the caller can send only the remainder. An empty or incomplete reply, a timeout, or an ok after an error proves nothing about what ran, so the error gives the confirmed count and says the rest may have been delivered. The action indicator shows the input; it is masked unless an AT-SPI probe of the target app finds a non-secret editable field or a terminal. The dispatcher resolves a key name to its unshifted physical key and applies only the modifiers it is given, so text goes through a US-layout table (shifted symbols become SHIFT plus the base key); unmappable characters or a non-US main keymap refuse the whole call. An unfocused target is captured with `grim -T ` (ext-foreign-toplevel image capture). Hyprland stops sending frame callbacks to windows on hidden workspaces, so their buffer holds the last frame drawn on screen; each capture makes the client repaint, so a hidden-workspace target is captured every 150 ms until two consecutive frames match (at most 8 captures) and the result's `source` says whether it settled. - **Hyprland/Electron text**: for classified nonsecret fields on Hyprland, wtype passes one literal argument after `--` to avoid stdin keymap-refresh corruption. Argument text is visible in process listings; confirmed password fields are rejected. Terminals and ambiguous fields (with or without AT-SPI) use private stdin for at most 100 Unicode characters per call; split larger input into smaller calls or expose accessibility. The input probe has its own 1.5-second budget; the 250 ms indicator probe only masks text. Other compatible compositors retain their existing stdin path. NUL and text over 131,071 UTF-8 bytes are rejected before focus or indicators. Success confirms dispatch only; re-observe the field before retrying. - **Limited accessibility feedback**: when exact window focus was verified before input but AT-SPI reports no focused element, the result describes the missing feedback without claiming the input was lost. It still does not verify the field contents. A complete scoped tree containing only application/window containers adds an Electron/Chromium `--force-renderer-accessibility` hint; a truncated tree instead retains its traversal-limit guidance. - **Focused containers**: Chromium can mark a `document web` focused alongside its contenteditable editor. The focus probe keeps searching that document and reports the editor; a document that holds focus itself still gets a warning, which no longer claims the text was lost. An editor can carry the `editable` state without the EditableText interface (`supports_editable_text: false`): `type_text` can reach it, `set_value` cannot. Verify its text or a screenshot before submitting or retrying. - **Large embedded browser trees**: an app-scoped snapshot includes embedded browser documents, which can use up the node budget before the app's own controls. When `accessibility_tree_truncated` is true, a missing editor proves nothing: raise `max_nodes` (default 1000, hard cap 10000) and, if needed, `max_depth` (hard cap 64). A busy renderer may give only a few thousand nodes before the deadline. A snapshot stops reading at 10 seconds and returns what it read, marked truncated; if the editor is still missing, hide the embedded browser pane for the snapshot. - **Selkies pixelflux**: when `PIXELFLUX_CU` and `PIXELFLUX_CU_TOKEN` are set, screenshots and pointer/keyboard actions use the container's loopback computer-use server first. Element clicks scale AT-SPI bounds by the latest screenshot size over the logical layout (`wlr-output-management` on labwc, the existing desktop layout elsewhere). Coordinate clicks use screenshot pixels. A connection failure falls through to the backends below; an HTTP error does not. - **Wayland coordinate input.** Coordinate clicks, drags, and targeted scrolls require the absolute uinput pointer or an approved RemoteDesktop portal session. Targeted scroll sends the move and the wheel through the same uinput device, so the compositor routes the wheel to the point the move set, and it needs no ydotool daemon. If accurate positioning is unavailable, the call returns `ok: false` before sending coordinate input. The absolute pointer still requires a successful full-desktop capture when first created; an existing device does not need another capture. A device sized for an earlier screenshot is replaced at the next coordinate action. If that fails, the action is not sent, and the result says where a retry goes: a new device from a fresh screenshot, then the RemoteDesktop portal, ydotool, or a refusal on Wayland. Scrolling without a point or window/element target keeps using the current pointer position. Portal keyboard input preserves the receiving window or app target before consent, then restores and verifies its focus after consent. If focus cannot be verified, no text or key chord is sent. Untargeted portal keyboard calls therefore require working window introspection. GNOME Introspect only verifies an already focused app; if consent changes focus, refocus the app manually or install the Shell extension. - **Native X11 coordinate clicks.** Eligible native X11 sessions use one supervised `xdotool mousemove -- X Y click --repeat N BUTTON` command for left, middle, and right clicks; native X11 does not initialize the system-wide uinput device. Missing or failed xdotool commands return an error without routing input to another display. `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_FORCE_YDOTOOL_POINTER=1` skips this xdotool path. - **Native X11 scroll.** The same sessions send one `xdotool` command, `mousemove -- X Y click --delay 12 --repeat N BUTTON` when a point is set, or `click` alone when it is not. Buttons are 4 up, 5 down, 6 left, and 7 right, and `N` is the same notch count ydotool would pass to `mousemove --wheel` (five per page). ydotool's absolute move warps through (0, 0); GTK 3 then drops the single following wheel event because re-entry resets its XI2 scroll valuators. XTEST has no scroll valuators, so GTK takes the button path. Missing or failed xdotool commands return an error without a system-wide fallback. `COMPUTER_USE_LINUX_FORCE_YDOTOOL_POINTER=1` skips this path. - **Drag motion.** XTEST, uinput and portal drags use intermediate points paced 30 ms apart. Native X11 uses XTEST on `DISPLAY`; uinput and portal paths use the same trajectory. A failed press or [TRUNCATED]

items.description: Self-hosted mission control for AI coding agents: run Claude Code, OpenCode, Pi, Codex, and Antigravity & Gemini CLI 24/7, from any device, watch every subagent live
items.readme_text:
Mission control for AI coding agents

Claude Code • OpenCode • Codex • Antigravity • Gemini • Pi • Grok • DeepSeek • OMP • Copilot • jcode • Terminal - One Dashboard • Any Device


The native Mac app: signed and notarized, Apple Silicon and Intel, macOS 11.3 or later. What it does

English • 简体中文

**Codeman** is a self-hosted mission control for AI coding agents. It spawns Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini, Pi, Grok, DeepSeek Harness, OMP, GitHub Copilot CLI, or jcode inside persistent tmux sessions, streams the real terminal to any browser, and keeps agents productive after you walk away: it re-prompts on idle, resumes when a usage limit resets, runs scheduled jobs, and shows every background agent working in real time. Get started in one line (macOS & Linux, Windows via WSL): ```bash curl -fsSL https://getcodeman.com/install | bash ``` ```bash codeman web # Open http://localhost:3000 and start your first session ``` The installer asks before every system change, and re-running the same line updates in place. Full details: [Quick Start - Installation](#quick-start---installation). On a Mac you can skip the terminal: [download Codeman.dmg](https://github.com/Ark0N/Codeman/releases/latest/download/Codeman.dmg), and the app installs Codeman for you, opens the one already running, or connects to one on another machine. --- ## Quick Start - Installation ```bash curl -fsSL https://getcodeman.com/install | bash ``` This installs Node.js, tmux and a build toolchain if missing (node-pty ships no Linux prebuilds, so it compiles from source), clones Codeman to `~/.codeman/app`, and builds it. It looks at what is already on the machine, asks at most three questions, then does all the work unattended and ends on the URL with a QR code for your phone. A few things worth knowing: - **Three questions, all up front.** How the dashboard is reached, optionally what to call this machine on your tailnet, and whether to run Codeman as a background service (systemd/launchd, auto-start on boot; Enter says yes). Everything that needs you, including one consent for all missing packages, one sudo password, and the Tailscale login, happens before the build, so you can walk away while it compiles. - **How it's reachable, your choice.** **Tailscale** (loopback bind fronted by `tailscale serve`, so you get `https://..ts.net` with a real certificate and your tailnet as the login, no password needed), **any device on your network** (`0.0.0.0`, with a strongly recommended password prompt), or **this machine only** (`127.0.0.1`, safest). Skipping the password on a network bind requires an explicit confirmation and ends with a loud warning. The highlighted default reflects what is already on the machine (Tailscale when it is already connected, your existing binding on a re-run), and a bare Enter never pulls in new software. If another app already owns `:443` on your node, Codeman goes under `https://..ts.net/codeman` or on a second port instead of replacing it. A bare `codeman web` started by hand still defaults to loopback. - **The name is yours to choose.** By default the URL uses the machine's existing tailnet name. Answering yes to the second question renames the machine to `codeman-` (which also renames it for SSH, so the default is no); `install.sh name` does it later. - **Re-run to update.** The same one-liner updates a finished install in place: local changes in `~/.codeman/app` are stashed (never discarded), and a running service is restarted and verified. If a first install was interrupted, re-running resumes the full setup instead. `install.sh status` prints the URLs and the QR code again; `install.sh update`, `install.sh tailscale` and `install.sh uninstall` also exist. - **No administrator rights needed.** On an account without `sudo`, one whose `sudo` rights the installer cannot confirm (outside the `sudo`, `wheel` and `admin` groups, with a password still required) or a Mac account that is not an administrator and has no Homebrew it can write to, the installer downloads Node.js from nodejs.org and the tmux project's own build into `~/.codeman/runtime`, each checked against its SHA-256, and takes the source as an archive when there is no working git. `--no-admin` forces that route and `CODEMAN_NO_ADMIN=0` turns it off. Two limits: Linux needs make, a C++ compiler and python3 to be there already, and the tmux download needs macOS 15 or newer. Details in the [wiki](https://github.com/Ark0N/Codeman/wiki/Installation#without-administrator-rights). - **Flags for the impatient.** `curl -fsSL https://getcodeman.com/install | bash -s -- --tailscale --service` answers the questions from the command line (`--lan`, `--local`, `--run`, `--no-start`, `--name `, `--port `, `--yes` too). **CI / headless:** without a terminal attached, steps that would change your system abort with instructions instead of running silently; set `CODEMAN_NONINTERACTIVE=1` to approve them for automation. You'll need at least one AI coding CLI installed — [Claude Code](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code), [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai), [Codex](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli), [Antigravity](https://antigravity.google), [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli), [Pi](https://pi.dev), [Grok Build](https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build), [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness), [OMP](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi), [GitHub Copilot CLI](https://github.com/github/copilot-cli), or [jcode](https://jcode.sh) (any combination works; Gemini CLI is enterprise-only since Google's consumer cutover, and Antigravity is its successor). The installer detects whichever of the eleven is present; if none is found, it offers to install any of them from a menu (DeepSeek excepted, since its npm package installs only a launcher with no runnable profile), or you can skip and install one yourself later. After install: ```bash codeman web # Open http://localhost:3000 and start your first session ``` **Sharing with a small team?** Start it in multi-user mode instead: each person gets their own login and workspace. ```bash codeman users add alice --admin # create the first admin account codeman web --multiuser # named logins + per-user case spaces ``` Details in [Multi-User Mode](#multi-user-mode-opt-in) below. **Prefer Docker Compose?** Clone the repo and run one script (Linux, Docker with the Compose v2 plugin): ```bash git clone https://github.com/Ark0N/Codeman.git && cd Codeman bash docker/Start-Codeman.sh ``` The first run asks three questions (data folder, port, password; Enter takes the default, including a generated password), writes `docker/.env` for you, builds the image and ends on the URL once Codeman answers. The image already includes Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode. Codeman runs in a container and spawns Docker cases as sibling containers through the host socket. To update, use **App Settings → Updates**, or `git pull` and run the script again rather than a plain `docker compose up`, so the rebuilt image, refreshed volumes and entrypoint arrive together. See the [Docker deployment guide](docker/README.md) for Unraid, direct Compose commands, storage and networking options. ### On a Mac: the Codeman app **[Download Codeman.dmg](https://github.com/Ark0N/Codeman/releases/latest/download/Codeman.dmg)** · one universal app for Apple Silicon and Intel · macOS 11.3 or later A small native app that opens Codeman in its own window. On a Mac without Codeman it installs it for you, with no Terminal and no administrator password, shows the install as a checklist, and offers to install a coding agent if the Mac has none yet. On a Mac that already runs Codeman it finds the server and opens it, or starts it when it is stopped. Under **Another machine** it connects to Codeman on your Mac mini, a home server or your tailnet, with the password kept in the Keychain, and can start an install over there through SSH. On a MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display, whose lid logo lights up, **View > Blink Apple Logo** makes the logo show what your agents are doing: it breathes while they work, blinks when one waits for you and flashes when one needs permission, and each state can take a style of your own. It stays off until you turn it on. To turn the logo off, dim it or give it effects the rest of the time, there's [LogoLight](https://github.com/Ark0N/LogoLight) (`brew install --cask ark0n/tap/logolight`), which steps aside while Codeman blinks the logo. The app is Rust around macOS's own WebKit, not a bundled browser, so the download is under 5 MB. Open `Codeman.dmg`, drag Codeman into Applications and open it from there. macOS asks once whether to open an app downloaded from the internet: click **Open**. - **Quitting the app doesn't stop Codeman.** An install from the app runs Codeman as a LaunchAgent that starts at login, so your agents keep working with the window closed, and your browser and phone reach it as before. - **Codeman's page needs the WebKit of Safari 16.4.** The app starts on macOS 11.3, but Codeman itself needs macOS 13.3 or later, or macOS 11 or 12 with Safari 16.4 or later installed. On an older WebKit the app says so and does not connect. - **The install from the app needs macOS 15, or a tmux that is already there.** tmux comes from the tmux project's own builds, which need macOS 15. On an older Mac without tmux the app offers Terminal instead, where Homebrew installs it (that takes an administrator once). - **Updating.** The app doesn't update itself yet: download the new `Codeman.dmg` and drag it over the old copy. First launch, known limits and how to build it yourself: [Installation](https://github.com/Ark0N/Codeman/wiki/Installation#on-a-mac-the-codeman-app) in the wiki and [packages/desktop/README.md](packages/desktop/README.md).
Keep it running in the background To outlive the shell you started it in, without setting anything up: ```bash codeman web -d # detach; logs to ~/.codeman/web.log codeman web --status # is it up, and on which pid codeman web --stop # graceful SIGTERM; agents keep running in tmux ``` `-d` waits until the server actually answers before reporting success, and refuses to start a second one on the same data dir (two servers sharing a tmux socket attach to each other's sessions). To have it come back after a reboot, install it as a service instead. The installer's final menu does this for you (option 2); `codeman service` is the equivalent for an `npm i -g aicodeman` install: ```bash codeman service install # systemd user unit (Linux) or LaunchAgent (macOS) codeman service status codeman service uninstall ``` `service install` writes the unit with your current PATH baked in, which matters more than it sounds: launchd hands a job `/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`, so a Homebrew or nvm `node`, `tmux` or `claude` is invisible to a hand-written plist. It never copies `CODEMAN_PASSWORD` into the unit file; add that yourself if the service needs auth. To write the unit by hand instead: **Linux (systemd):** ```bash mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user cat > ~/.config/systemd/user/codeman-web.service << EOF [Unit] Description=Codeman Web Server After=network.target [Service] Type=simple ExecStart=$(which node) $HOME/.codeman/app/dist/index.js web Restart=always RestartSec=10 [Install] WantedBy=default.target EOF systemctl --user daemon-reload systemctl --user enable --now codeman-web loginctl enable-linger $USER ``` **macOS (launchd):** ```bash mkdir -p ~/Library/LaunchAgents cat > ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.codeman.web.plist << EOF Label com.codeman.web ProgramArguments $(which node) $HOME/.codeman/app/dist/index.js web RunAtLoad KeepAlive StandardOutPath /tmp/codeman.log StandardErrorPath /tmp/codeman.log EOF launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.codeman.web.plist ```
Windows (WSL) ```powershell wsl bash -c "curl -fsSL https://getcodeman.com/install | bash" ``` Codeman requires tmux, so Windows users need [WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install). If you don't have WSL yet: run `wsl --install` in an admin PowerShell, reboot, open Ubuntu, then install your preferred AI coding CLI inside WSL ([Claude Code](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code), [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai), [Codex](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli), [Antigravity](https://antigravity.google), [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli), [Pi](https://pi.dev), [Grok Build](https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build), [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness), or [OMP](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi)). After installing, `http://localhost:3000` is accessible from your Windows browser.

- **Keyboard accessory bar** — `/init`, `/clear`, `/compact` quick-action buttons above the virtual keyboard; destructive commands require a double-press to confirm, so you never fire one by accident; on Codex sessions the bar also shows `⇧←` / `⇧→` (Shift+Left / Shift+Right: edit the last queued message / return through the prompt stack) - **Dedicated Enter button** — replays the keypress through the terminal, so text buffered by local echo is flushed first rather than stranded - **Attach button**: the picture icon beside the mic opens the system photo and file sheet without raising the keyboard. Photos and camera-roll videos (mp4, mov, webm, up to 1 GB) upload into the session's folder and their path lands on your prompt, unsent - **Paste in a shell**: a multi-line paste goes in as one block and waits for your Enter, instead of running line by line as it arrives - **Swipe navigation & smart keyboard handling** — swipe left/right to switch sessions; toolbar and terminal shift up when the keyboard opens (`visualViewport` API) - **Built for phones** — safe-area insets for notch and home indicator, 44px touch targets, bottom-sheet case picker, native momentum scrolling; on a folding phone (iPhone Duo) dialogs stay clear of the hinge, and opening or closing the device is never mistaken for the keyboard ```bash codeman web --https # Open on your phone: https://:3000 ``` > `localhost` works over plain HTTP. Use `--https` when accessing from another device, or use [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com/) (recommended): the installer can set it up for you (choose **Tailscale** at the network-access prompt, or run `bash ~/.codeman/app/install.sh tailscale` on an existing install). That gives you `https://..ts.net` with a real certificate: private to your tailnet, no password required, and PWA install + push notifications work on your phone. The installer ends on that URL with a QR code to scan, and `bash ~/.codeman/app/install.sh status` prints it again any time. ### Secure QR Code Authentication Typing passwords on a phone keyboard is miserable. Codeman replaces it with **cryptographically secure single-use QR tokens** — scan the code displayed on your desktop and your phone is authenticated instantly. Each QR encodes a URL containing a 6-character short code that maps to a 256-bit secret (`crypto.randomBytes(32)`) on the server. Tokens auto-rotate every **60 seconds**, are **atomically consumed on first scan** (replays always fail), and use **hash-based `Map.get()` lookup** that leaks nothing through response timing. The short code is an opaque pointer — the real secret never appears in browser history, `Referer` headers, or Cloudflare edge logs. The security design addresses all 6 critical QR auth flaws identified in ["Demystifying the (In)Security of QR Code-based Login"](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/zhang-xin) (USENIX Security 2025, which found 47 of the top-100 websites vulnerable): single-use enforcement, short TTL, cryptographic randomness, server-side generation, real-time desktop notification on scan (QRLjacking detection), and IP + User-Agent session binding with manual revocation. Dual-layer rate limiting (per-IP + global) makes brute force infeasible across 62^6 = 56.8 billion possible codes. Full security analysis: [`docs/qr-auth-plan.md`](docs/qr-auth-plan.md) --- ## Using Codeman — A Human's Guide A start-to-finish walkthrough for driving Codeman from the browser. When accessing your coding agent remotely (VPN, Tailscale, SSH tunnel), every keystroke normally takes 200-300ms to round-trip. Codeman implements a **Mosh-inspired local echo system** that makes typing feel instant regardless of latency. A pixel-perfect DOM overlay inside xterm.js renders keystrokes at 0ms. Background forwarding silently sends every character to the PTY in 50ms debounced batches, so Tab completion, `Ctrl+R` history search, and all shell features work normally. When the server echo arrives 200-300ms later, the overlay seamlessly disappears and the real terminal text takes over — the transition is invisible. - **Ink-proof architecture** — lives as a `` at z-index 7 inside `.xterm-screen`, completely immune to Ink's constant screen redraws (two previous attempts using `terminal.write()` failed because Ink corrupts injected buffer content) - **Font-matched rendering** — reads `fontFamily`, `fontSize`, `fontWeight`, and `letterSpacing` from xterm.js computed styles so overlay text is visually indistinguishable from real terminal output - **Full editing** — backspace, retype, paste (multi-char), cursor tracking, multi-line wrap when input exceeds terminal width - **Persistent across reconnects** — unsent input survives page reloads via localStorage - **Enabled by default** — works on both desktop and mobile, during idle and busy sessions > Extracted as a standalone library: [`xterm-zerolag-input`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/xterm-zerolag-input) — see [Published Packages](#published-packages). --- ## Live Agent Visualization Watch background agents work in real-time. Codeman monitors agent activity and displays each agent in a draggable floating window with animated Matrix-style connection lines back to the parent session.

- **Floating terminal windows** — draggable, resizable panels for each agent with a live activity log showing every tool call, file read, and progress update as it happens - **Connection lines** — animated green lines linking parent sessions to their child agents, updating in real-time as agents spawn and complete - **Status & model badges** — green (active), yellow (idle), blue (completed) indicators with Haiku/Sonnet/Opus model color coding - **Auto-behavior** — windows auto-open on spawn, auto-minimize on completion, tab badge shows "AGENT" or "AGENTS (n)" count - **Nested agents** — supports 3-level hierarchies (lead session -> teammate agents -> sub-subagents) Multi-agent Workflow runs ("ultracode") get the same treatment: a floating run window tracks the whole workflow live, with phases, per-agent token counts, and the current tool of every agent:

**Agent Teams** — first-class support for Claude Code's native multi-agent teams (`CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`). `TeamWatcher` polls `~/.claude/teams/`, matches teammates to their lead session, and surfaces them as live subagent windows with **team-aware idle detection** — so the Respawn Controller won't fire while teammates are still working. See [`docs/agent-teams/`](docs/agent-teams/). --- ## Respawn Controller The core of autonomous work. When the agent goes idle, the Respawn Controller detects it, sends a continue prompt, cycles context management commands for fresh context, and resumes — running **24+ hours** completely unattended. ``` WATCHING → IDLE DETECTED → SEND UPDATE → /clear → /init → CONTINUE → WATCHING ``` - **Multi-layer idle detection** — completion messages, AI-powered idle check, output silence, token stability - **Auto-resume on usage limit** _(opt-in, off by default)_ — when Claude halts on a subscription limit ("You've hit your limit · resets 3pm"), Codeman parses the reset time, waits it out plus a 2-minute safety buffer, then dismisses the rate-limit dialog and sends `continue` — so an overnight run survives the 5-hour window instead of stalling until morning. Recognizes every Claude Code limit-message format, retries if still limited, survives Codeman restarts, and holds respawn cycles while paused so `/clear` can't wipe the waiting conversation. Enable per session at the top of the Respawn tab - **Circuit breaker** — prevents respawn thrashing when Claude is stuck (CLOSED -> HALF_OPEN -> OPEN states, tracks consecutive no-progress and repeated errors) - **Health scoring** — 0-100 health score with component scores for cycle success, circuit breaker state, iteration progress, and stuck recovery - **Built-in presets** — `solo-work` (3s idle, 60min), `subagent-workflow` (45s, 240min), `team-lead` (90s, 480min), `ralph-todo` (8s, 480min), `overnight-autonomous` (10s, 480min) --- ## Orchestrator Loop Beyond single-session respawn, the **Orchestrator** turns a high-level goal into a phased plan and drives it to completion across multiple agents — a state machine that runs `idle → planning → approval → executing → verifying → (replanning) → completed`. - **Plan, then execute** — generates a phased plan from your goal and pauses for approval before touching anything; reject with feedback to regenerate - **Per-phase verification gates** — each phase is verified before the next begins; on failure the orchestrator replans instead of barreling ahead - **Multi-agent execution** — fans phases out to team agents / a task queue, coordinating work too big for one session - **Crash-safe** — full state persists under the `orchestrator` key in `state.json`, so it survives restarts - **Driven from the UI or API** — the Orchestrator panel, or `POST /api/orchestrator/start` → `/approve` → `/status` (10 endpoints) > Full design: [`docs/orchestrator-loop-architecture.md`](docs/orchestrator-loop-architecture.md). --- ## Multi-Session Dashboard Run **20 parallel sessions** with full visibility — real-time xterm.js terminals at 60fps, per-session token and cost tracking, tab-based navigation, and one-click management. ### Tile Grid

Watch and drive up to **six sessions side by side** in one window. Click **Tiles** in the header (or press `Ctrl+Shift+G`) and your sessions open as a grid of live terminals: every tile takes your keystrokes and shows its agent's logo, model and state in its header. Right-click **Tiles** to choose 2, 4 or 6 tiles, and drag a tile by its header to move it. Click **Tiles** again to return to a single session. Desktop only (a window about 1180px wide or more). Every tab tells you its state at a glance. A running session keeps its green status dot. When a session stops and waits for input, its tab turns **yellow**: steady ring, tinted background, yellow dot, with a slow breathing glow on top. When a permission prompt or question is **blocking** the agent, the tab turns **red** with a faster pulse. The base tint never blinks off, so even a split-second glance (or a screenshot) reads the true state; the ring stays visible while the tab is selected, and a page reload re-arms pending alerts from the server, so a blocked session can never hide behind a fresh-looking tab. ### Notifications Real-time desktop alerts when sessions need attention — `permission_prompt` and `elicitation_dialog` trigger critical red tab blinks, `idle_prompt` triggers yellow blinks. Click any notification to jump directly to the affected session. Hooks auto-configured per case directory. ### Run Summary Click the chart icon on any session tab to see a timeline of everything that happened — respawn cycles, token milestones, auto-compact triggers, idle/working transitions, hook events, errors, and more. ### Zero-Flicker Terminal Terminal-based AI agents (Claude Code's Ink, OpenCode's Bubble Tea) redraw the screen on every state change.
