### QR Code Authentication Typing a password on a phone keyboard is terrible. Codeman solves this with **ephemeral single-use QR tokens** — scan the code on your desktop, and your phone is instantly authenticated. No password prompt, no typing, no clipboard. ``` Desktop displays QR → Phone scans → GET /q/Xk9mQ3 → Server validates → Token atomically consumed (single-use) → Session cookie issued → 302 to / → Desktop notified: "Device authenticated via QR" → New QR auto-generated ``` Someone who only has the bare tunnel URL (without the QR) still hits the standard password prompt. The QR is the fast path; the password is the fallback. #### How It Works The server maintains a rotating pool of short-lived, single-use tokens. Each token consists of a 256-bit secret (`crypto.randomBytes(32)`) paired with a 6-character base62 short code used as an opaque lookup key in the URL path. The QR code encodes a URL like `https://abc-xyz.trycloudflare.com/q/Xk9mQ3` — the short code is a pointer, not the secret itself, so it never leaks through browser history, `Referer` headers, or Cloudflare edge logs. Every **60 seconds**, the server automatically rotates to a fresh token. The previous token remains valid for a **90-second grace period** to handle the race where you scan right as rotation happens — after that, it's dead. Each token is **single-use**: the moment a phone successfully scans it, the token is atomically consumed and a new one is immediately generated for the desktop display. #### Security Design The design is informed by ["Demystifying the (In)Security of QR Code-based Login"](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/zhang-xin) (USENIX Security 2025), which found 47 of the top-100 websites vulnerable to QR auth attacks due to 6 critical design flaws across 42 CVEs. Codeman addresses all six: | USENIX Flaw | Mitigation | | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Flaw-1**: Missing single-use enforcement | Token atomically consumed on first scan — replays always fail | | **Flaw-2**: Long-lived tokens | 60s TTL with 90s grace, auto-rotation via timer | | **Flaw-3**: Predictable token generation | `crypto.randomBytes(32)` — 256-bit entropy. Short codes use rejection sampling to eliminate modulo bias | | **Flaw-4**: Client-side token generation | Server-side only — tokens never leave the server until embedded in the QR | | **Flaw-5**: Missing status notification | Desktop toast: _"Device [IP] authenticated via QR (Safari). Not you? [Revoke]"_ — real-time QRLjacking detection | | **Flaw-6**: Inadequate session binding | IP + User-Agent stored for audit. Manual session revocation via API. HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=lax cookies | #### Timing-Safe Lookup Short codes are stored in a `Map`. Validation uses `Map.get()` — a hash-based O(1) lookup that reveals nothing about the target string through response timing. There is no character-by-character string comparison anywhere in the hot path, eliminating timing side-channel attacks entirely. #### Rate Limiting (Dual Layer) QR auth has its own rate limiting, completely independent from password auth: - **Per-IP**: 10 failed QR attempts per IP trigger a 429 block (15-minute decay window) — separate counter from Basic Auth failures, so a fat-fingered password doesn't burn your QR budget - **Global**: 30 QR attempts per minute across all IPs combined — defends against distributed brute force. With 62^6 = 56.8 billion possible short codes and only ~2 valid at any time, brute force is computationally infeasible regardless #### QR Code Size Optimization The URL is kept deliberately short (`/q/` path + 6-char code = ~53-56 total characters) to target **QR Version 4** (33x33 modules) instead of Version 5 (37x37). Smaller QR codes scan faster on budget phones — modern devices read Version 4 in 100-300ms. The `/q/` prefix saves 7 bytes compared to `/qr-auth/`, which alone is the difference between QR versions. #### Desktop Experience The QR display auto-refreshes every 60 seconds via SSE with the SVG embedded directly in the event payload (~2-5KB) — no extra HTTP fetch, sub-50ms refresh. A countdown timer shows time remaining. A "Regenerate" button instantly invalidates all existing tokens and creates a fresh one (useful if you suspect the QR was photographed). When someone authenticates via QR, the desktop shows a notification toast with the device's IP and browser — if it wasn't you, one click revokes all sessions. #### Threat Coverage | Threat | Why it doesn't work | | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **QR screenshot shared** | Single-use: consumed on first scan. 60s TTL: expired before the attacker can act. Desktop notification alerts you immediately. | | **Replay attack** | Atomic single-use consumption + 60s TTL. Old URLs always return 401. | | **Cloudflare edge logs** | Short code is an opaque 6-char lookup key, not the real 256-bit token. Single-use means replaying from logs always fails. | | **Brute force** | 56.8 billion combinations, ~2 valid at any time, dual-layer rate limiting blocks well before statistical feasibility. | | **QRLjacking** | 60s rotation forces real-time relay. Desktop toast provides instant detection. Self-hosted single-user context makes phishing implausible. | | **Timing attack** | Hash-based Map lookup — no string comparison timing leak. | | **Session cookie theft** | HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=lax + 24h TTL. Manual revocation at `POST /api/auth/revoke`. | #### How It Compares | Platform | Model | Comparison | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Discord** | Long-lived token, no confirmation, [repeatedly exploited](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Qrljacking) | Codeman: single-use + TTL + notification | | **WhatsApp Web** | Phone confirms "Link device?", ~60s rotation | Comparable rotation; WhatsApp adds explicit confirmation (acceptable tradeoff for single-user) | | **Signal** | Ephemeral public key, E2E encrypted channel | Stronger crypto, but [exploited by Russian state actors in 2025](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger) via social engineering despite it | > Full design rationale, security analysis, and implementation details: [`docs/qr-auth-plan.md`](docs/qr-auth-plan.md) --- ## Security By default Codeman launches sessions with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, so the web UI is by design a remote-code-execution surface for whoever can reach it — the whole security model exists to control _who_ that is. (The startup permission mode is configurable; see below.) Recent hardening (v0.9.0 + v0.9.5) closes the browser-driven attack paths that bite self-hosted dev tools. Full model: [`docs/security-architecture.md`](docs/security-architecture.md). **Found a vulnerability?** See [`SECURITY.md`](.github/SECURITY.md) for private disclosure and the list of known limitations. ### Network & access - **Loopback by default** — the server binary binds `127.0.0.1`, reachable only from the same machine, so the no-password default is safe out of the box (the guided installer asks about network access and configures the binding + password for you). Binding a non-loopback host without `CODEMAN_PASSWORD` _starts but prints a loud warning_ with three concrete fixes (set a password, loopback + an authenticated tunnel, or explicitly acknowledge with `--allow-unauthenticated-network`) - **Optional auth, real sessions** — HTTP Basic via `CODEMAN_USERNAME` (default `admin`) / `CODEMAN_PASSWORD`. Success issues an opaque 256-bit `codeman_session` cookie (`randomBytes(32)`) — validated server-side, not client-signed, so it can't be forged offline (24h TTL, auto-extend, device-context audit log) - **Per-IP rate limiting** — 10 failed attempts → `429` with `Retry-After` (15-min decay). A valid cookie or correct password recovers _immediately_ even while an attacker hammers the same IP — important because all tunnel traffic shares one loopback IP. Multi-user mode allows 50 failures per IP instead, plus 10 failed guesses per account from one IP; both are checked before the password, so past either a correct password from that IP also waits for the decay, while the account still logs in from another IP. QR auth has its own separate limiter - **Configurable permission mode** - `--dangerously-skip-permissions` is only the default. **App Settings → Agents & CLIs → Claude → Startup Mode** can switch new sessions to Anthropic's classifier-guarded `auto` mode (low-prompt, needs Claude Code 2.1.207+), `normal` prompting, or an explicit allowed-tools list. In multi-user mode, non-granted users are forced to `auto`, and shell sessions / skip-permissions require an explicit per-user grant ### Always-on browser hardening (v0.9.5) These run for **every** request — before auth, even on the default no-password loopback install: - **Host-header allowlist → blocks DNS rebinding.** A custom domain rebound to `127.0.0.1` is rejected with `403 host not allowed` before any handler runs. Allowed: `localhost`, any IP literal, the bind host, `.ts.net` / `.trycloudflare.com` / `.cfargotunnel.com`, the active managed tunnel, and `CODEMAN_ALLOWED_HOSTS` (add custom reverse-proxy domains here — comma-separated; exact host or leading-dot `.suffix` for subdomains) - **Cross-site Origin / CSRF guard.** On state-changing methods (`POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE`) the `Origin` must pass the same allowlist, else `403 cross-site request blocked`. A _missing_ Origin is allowed (so `curl`, the CLI, and Claude Code hooks keep working); only a present-but-foreign or opaque `null` origin is rejected - **Raw `text/plain` bodies.** The global parser no longer JSON-parses `text/plain`, closing the CORS "simple request" CSRF vector where a cross-site `fetch` could smuggle JSON into a write route with no preflight - **WebSocket origin validation.** The terminal WS upgrade runs the same Host + Origin check and closes with code `4003` on failure (anti-CSWSH) - **XSS-escaped agent output.** AI-derived strings (tool names, command arguments, subagent descriptions) are HTML-escaped at every injection site before rendering in the subagent / activity panels ### Input, files & headers - **Schema-validated inputs** — every API body is checked with Zod v4 schemas; a `CLAUDE_CODE_*` / `OPENCODE_*` / `CODEX_*` / `ANTIGRAVITY_*` / `GEMINI_*` / `GOOGLE_*` / `PI_*` / `GROK_*` / `XAI_*` / `DSH_*` / `DEEPSEEK_*` / `OMP_*` / `COPILOT_*` env-prefix allowlist gates which settings each CLI can receive, and the keys that could redirect a CLI's traffic (base URLs, config homes) are clamped for non-admin users - **Path containment** — file routes `realpath` before boundary checks (no TOCTOU); `..`, absolute paths, and symlinks resolving outside the working dir are rejected. Caps: 10 MB text preview / 2 GB raw & download (`CODEMAN_MAX_DOWNLOAD_BYTES`; bodies stream and answer `Range` requests, so the cap is a sanity bound rather than memory protection); `/api/download` blocklists sensitive paths (`.env`, `*credentials*`, `~/.ssh/`, `.aws/credentials`). SVG/HTML is served `octet-stream` + `nosniff` + attachment so it downloads rather than executes. The one place HTML renders is the File Viewer's page view: a separate `/html-view//` address scoped to the file's own folder, served under `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox` without `allow-same-origin`, so the page has an opaque origin and can never read Codeman's cookies or drive its API; hidden folders and broad roots (`/`, home, `/tmp`) are refused, and the capabilities are revoked on logout - **Security headers** — `Content-Security-Policy` (`default-src 'self'`, every exception enumerated), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, HSTS over HTTPS, and CORS reflected **only** for `localhost` / `127.0.0.1` / `::1` ### Supply chain & isolation - **Pinned & verified deps** — security-sensitive transitive deps are forced to patched versions via npm `overrides`; lockfile integrity is checked on every commit/PR (all entries resolve to `registry.npmjs.org` with `sha512` hashes). Public assets are NUL-byte-scanned and `node --check`-validated in CI - **Multi-instance isolation** — `CODEMAN_INSTANCE` scopes both the tmux socket (`-L codeman-`) and data dir (`~/.codeman-`) so two instances never attach each other's live sessions > Mobile login uses single-use, 60-second QR tokens — see [QR Code Authentication](#qr-code-authentication) above for the full design (it addresses all 6 flaws from USENIX Security 2025's QR-login study). --- ## Terminal UI (`codeman tui`) A full-screen dashboard for your sessions, in the terminal. Same states as the web UI, because it is a client of the same server: ```bash codeman tui # the dashboard codeman tui --list # numbered session list, then exit (scriptable) codeman tui 2 # attach straight to session 2 of that list codeman tui api-docs # attach straight to the live session named api-docs ``` Sessions are grouped **NEEDS YOU → WORKING → IDLE → RECENT**, longest-waiting first. `↑↓`/`j`/`k` select, `1`-`9` and `[`/`]` switch between sessions, `Enter` attaches into the tmux pane (**`F1`** to come back). Inside a pane the bar across the top keeps the session strip visible and `Alt+1`-`Alt+9` switch without leaving. `y`/`n`/digit answer a pending permission dialog right from the list, `p` sends a one-line prompt, `n` starts a session and opens straight into it, `x` kills one (`y` confirms), `/` searches, `g` shows the away digest, `?` is help, `q` quits. Below 72 columns it drops the preview pane and becomes a single-column list, so it stays usable in Termius on a phone. With no server running it still starts in attach-only degraded mode. The web UI remains the primary surface; see **[docs/tui.md](docs/tui.md)** for the full guide. --- ## Keyboard Shortcuts > Ctrl bindings also accept Cmd on macOS. | Shortcut | Action | | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | `Ctrl+W` | Not a Codeman shortcut: it reaches the terminal (delete the previous word). **Close Session** has no default key and can be bound in App Settings → Shortcuts | | `Ctrl/Cmd/Option+K` | Find open session or start a new one | | `Ctrl/Cmd+Tab` | Next session | | `Alt/Option+[` / `Alt/Option+]` | Previous / next session | | `Alt/Option+1`-`Alt/Option+9` | Switch to tab N (physical keys, so macOS Option layouts work) | | `Alt/Option+B` | Collapse / expand the session sidebar (sidebar layout only) | | `Ctrl+Shift+{` / `Ctrl+Shift+}` | Move active tab left / right | | `Ctrl/Cmd+C` | Copy selection, or interrupt when nothing is selected | | `Ctrl+Shift+C` | Copy selection (never interrupts) | | `Ctrl/Cmd+V` | Paste, or upload a clipboard image and paste its path | | `Ctrl/Cmd+L` | Clear terminal | | `Ctrl+Shift+R` | Restore terminal size | | `Ctrl+Shift+V` | Toggle voice input | | `Ctrl+Shift+G` | Open or close the tile grid | | `Alt+Shift+Arrows` | Focus the tile to the left, right, above or below | | `Ctrl+Shift+Arrows` | Move the focused tile one place (into an empty cell, or swap) | | `Alt+Shift+Enter` | Zoom the focused tile, or restore the grid | | `Ctrl/Cmd +` / `-` | Font size | | `Ctrl/Cmd+?` | Keyboard help | | `Shift+Enter` | Insert newline (sent to terminal) | | `Shift+drag` | Select text in a pane whose mouse events go to the CLI | | Right-click | Copy the selection (the native menu stays when nothing is selected) | | `Shift+Wheel` | Scroll the local scrollback while the wheel is forwarded to the CLI | | `Ctrl+Z` | Swallowed in agent sessions so a running CLI cannot be suspended; normal job control in a shell | | `Escape` | Close panels & modals | --- ## Driving Codeman from an Agent — Programmatic Guide For AI agents and automation that control Codeman without a browser: an agent that spins up worker sessions, a CI bot, or **Claude Code running _inside_ a Codeman session orchestrating other sessions**. Everything the UI does is HTTP + a CLI, so an agent can do it too. ### The agent skill (start here) Everything in this section also ships as an **agent skill**, [`skills/codeman`](skills/codeman/SKILL.md), in the `SKILL.md` format Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Grok, OMP and most other agent CLIs read. Install it once and you never paste API docs into a prompt again. You ask for what you want in plain English, and the agent already sitting inside a Codeman session loads the recipes and drives the API itself. Full guide, with every install route, the recordings and what it will and will not do on its own: [The Codeman Skill](https://github.com/Ark0N/Codeman/wiki/Codeman-Skill).

#### Step 1: install it Usually there is nothing to install: since 1.50.0 every new session gets the skill in its folder, where its CLI looks for skills (the web UI row below, on by default). The copy ignores itself in git, so your repository never lists it as a new file. The other routes are for pi, or for a copy that does not depend on that setting. | How | Command | Scope | | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | Skills CLI | `npx skills add Ark0N/Codeman --skill codeman -g` | Global, for any skills-aware agent ([skills.sh](https://skills.sh)); the way to give it to pi | | Claude Code plugin | `/plugin marketplace add Ark0N/Codeman` then `/plugin install codeman@codeman` | Global, through Claude Code's plugin manager; `/plugin update codeman` follows releases. Pick this OR a `codeman skill install`, not both: a Claude Code with both lists the skill twice (`codeman` and `codeman:codeman`). | | Bundled CLI | `codeman skill install` | Global (`~/.claude/skills/codeman`), for npm installs that never cloned the repo | | Bundled CLI | `codeman skill install --case [--mode ]` | One case only; `--mode codex` (or any other run mode) writes it where that CLI looks for skills | | Web UI | App Settings → Agents & CLIs → All agent CLIs → **Codeman Agent Skill** | Auto-injects into each case on session create, where that session's CLI looks: `.claude/skills/` for Claude Code, `.agents/skills/` for Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Antigravity, Grok, DeepSeek and OMP; not pi, whose project skills trigger a trust prompt (`agentSkillEnabled`, SYNCED, **on by default** since 1.50.0; a Claude Code that also has the plugin lists the skill twice, both work, so drop one if the duplicate bothers you) | `codeman skill uninstall [--case ]` reverses the CLI installs (with `--case`, every Codeman-managed copy in that case, whichever CLI's directory it sits in), and never touches a `skills/codeman` you wrote yourself. #### Step 2: ask for things That is the entire interface. No curl, no endpoint names, no session ids. These prompts work as written: | You say | The skill does | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | _"What sessions are running right now?"_ | Lists them with name, mode and status. Read-only, safe to ask anytime. | | _"Start a shell worker on the `myapp` case, run the test suite, tell me if it passes."_ | Spawns, waits on a split completion marker, reads back the exit code, cleans up. | | _"Spin up 3 workers for lint, typecheck and tests. Run them in parallel, report failures."_ | The fan-out flow: one session per task, all started first, then gathered as each finishes. | | _"Have a claude worker on `refactor-auth` summarize `src/session.ts`, then close it."_ | Spawns, runs the readiness ladder (first-run trust dialog included), send-and-wait, reads the clean transcript answer, deletes. | | _"Use the local model to summarize every file in `docs/`, then check its summaries."_ | Starts a worker on the model Codeman installed on this Mac, gives it the files, reads its answer back and reviews it in the cloud. Says why instead when no local model is installed. | | _"Watch session w4 and tell me if it gets stuck on a permission prompt."_ | Blocks on the `blocked` signal and surfaces the question to **you**. It never answers another session's prompt itself. | One short line is enough. Here a Claude Code lead gets `use codeman to start 5 claude workers, one per TODO item`, and five real Claude Code workers power on, shown side by side in the tile grid:

#### Step 3: nothing The agent deletes every session it started. Watch the tabs appear and disappear in the dashboard while it works. With eight workers, each one gets its own tab, and a lineage line runs back to the lead that spawned it:

#### A real run, start to finish > **You:** spin up 3 shell workers, run lint / typecheck / the frontend syntax check in parallel, and tell me which failed. ```text lint -> 9f2d8e5f dispatched typecheck -> aff9c691 dispatched 3 tabs appear in the dashboard syntax -> be9f1f15 dispatched lint DONE_lint_17909 rc=0 typecheck DONE_typecheck_3409 rc=0 gathered as each one finishes syntax DONE_syntax_18501 rc=0 deleted 9f2d8e5f, aff9c691, be9f1f15 tabs disappear ``` Those `DONE__` strings are the skill's **split marker** trick, and they are why the fan-out is reliable on hook-less `shell` sessions: the typed line contains `${M}_17909`, so only the command's real *output* ever contains `DONE_17909`. An unsplit marker would match the echo of your own keystrokes before the command had even run. #### What's in the box | File | Contents | | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [`SKILL.md`](skills/codeman/SKILL.md) | Safety rules, the ready-made fast path (spawn N workers, task them, collect), and the verb index. Always loaded. | | [`reference/verbs.md`](skills/codeman/reference/verbs.md) | The 14 verbs in detail: readiness, send-and-wait, markers, interrupts, cleanup. On demand. | | [`reference/recipes.md`](skills/codeman/reference/recipes.md) | 8 worked flows: claude, DeepSeek Harness and shell workers, fan-out, blocked-worker watch, messaging fan-out. On demand. | | [`reference/endpoints.md`](skills/codeman/reference/endpoints.md) | Full endpoint tables, error codes, per-mode signal table, capacity limits. On demand. | | [`reference/messaging.md`](skills/codeman/reference/messaging.md) | Talking to claude workers directly via Claude Code cross-session messaging. On demand. | | [`reference/history.md`](skills/codeman/reference/history.md) | Reading saved Codex conversations offline with `codeman history read`: selectors, filters, forks, budgets. On demand. | | [`reference/inspection-and-staging.md`](skills/codeman/reference/inspection-and-staging.md) | Experimental and opt-in: bounded pane inspection and guarded submission with `codeman agent inspect`, `stage` and `submit`. On demand. | Every recipe in there was verified against a live server, and the comments record the failure modes that were measured rather than guessed. #### Two things worth knowing - **It self-gates.** It acts inside a Codeman-managed session. Outside one (`CODEMAN_MUX` unset) it only reads saved Codex conversations offline (`codeman history read`) and refuses everything else, and it never guesses an API URL, so a global install costs an unrelated Claude Code session nothing. - **It is deliberately conservative.** Unprompted, it may only spawn sessions, prompt them, and delete ones **it created in that same conversation, by exact id**, through a fail-closed guard that refuses to delete the agent's own session. Deleting a case (which erases a real directory of your code), bulk kills, respawn/ralph/cron/orchestrator changes and settings writes all require you to ask, naming the target. ⚠️ The web UI injection is **on by default** since 1.50.0. A `settings.json` without the `agentSkillEnabled` key means on. Existing installs that stored off are switched on once at the first 1.50.0 start (every App Settings save on 1.49.0 or earlier wrote the old default, `false`, whether or not you touched this switch); turning it off afterwards sticks. Turning it off **does [TRUNCATED]

items.name: nanocode
items.description: SDK for Frontier Embedded Agents.
items.readme_text:
nanocode

Site · Docs · Experiments · Cloudflare Demo · Vercel Demo

SDK for frontier embedded agents, in Rust. One runtime for the Codex and Claude harnesses, with their own prompts and tools, that runs in a terminal, a server, a Worker, a browser tab, or an app.

- **Durable.** Every model call and tool call is journaled, so a turn finishes after its process dies. - **Code Mode.** The model writes one program that calls every tool, and only its result enters the context. - **Hands.** No sandbox per session. A turn reaches a laptop, a server, or a browser tab only for the calls that need one. - **Subagents.** A cell spawns children, each a durable session of its own. - **Any payer.** A ChatGPT or Claude subscription, an API key, or Machine Payments from a Tempo account you sign in to with Tempo ID. ## The CLI ```sh curl -fsSL https://nanocode.xyz/install | sh nc ``` ## The SDK ```toml [dependencies] nanocode = { git = "https://github.com/nanocodexyz/nanocode" } ``` The same code runs in other languages: | Language | Repository | | --- | --- | | TypeScript, as one WebAssembly module | [nanocode-ts](https://github.com/nanocodexyz/nanocode-ts) | | Swift, for macOS and iOS | [nanocode-swift](https://github.com/nanocodexyz/nanocode-swift) | | C, for a game engine or any other host | [libnanocode](https://github.com/nanocodexyz/libnanocode) | [The crate layout](crates/README.md) describes the workspace; git history records what each change established. ## License [MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](LICENSE-APACHE).

items.name: kwant
items.description: Your own team of AI bots in one self-hosted binary: spaces, every account you have, handoffs, approvals and routines. Open-source, self-hosted alternative to Grok Bot, Claude Duet and OpenAI dots. Rust + React.
items.readme_text:
Your own team of AI bots that check each other’s work before saying “done”.

Website · Docs · Features · Compare · Changelog · Discussions


macOS: one app for Apple silicon and Intel · Linux x86_64 (beta): .deb or AppImage · A server: binary or Docker · Phone: add it to your Home Screen · All downloads


Free and open source. A ⭐ helps others find kwant.

kwant has no token. Official X account is @kwantbot.

kwant gives you a team of bots that share chats, hand work to each other with an @mention and get it done on their own, on a schedule or while you're away. Each message goes to the bot that fits, and the reply says why. Work shows up as cards on a Mission board, and a task turns **Verified** only when kwant runs the check itself, never on a bot's word. Keep separate spaces for work and home, each with its own bots and accounts. Run it as an app on your Mac, Linux or Windows (beta) PC, or on a server, with the Claude, Codex or Grok CLI you already use, or your own API keys. It's written in Rust (Tokio, Axum, SQLite) with a React web app embedded in the binary. ![A kwant channel: Designer answers a question about empty states, then @mentions QA, and QA checks it on a 360 pixel screen.](docs/media/handoff.webp) --- ## New in 0.9 - **Review a bot's work in the Inbox** (0.9.0). Inbox › New has a **To review** group, highest risk first. Each item shows a verdict (Pass, Fail, Needs you or Not checked yet), what done looks like, the evidence, and a **Couldn't check** list with the reason for each. Press **Approve**, **Send back** with a note, or **Roll back**. Low-risk items that passed every check can be approved together with **Approve all**. - **A second check before you approve** (0.9.0). When a Mission board task moves to review, a teammate on another model runs its checks again in a clean copy of the files and never writes to the task's folder. For high-risk work it also changes the code in small ways to see if the tests notice. It says Pass only when kwant ran a check again itself. A task can say what done means and what must not change, and rolling back work you approved moves the bot down one Flight School tier. - **Point at the part of the page you mean** (0.9.0). In Watch live, press **Point** and click part of the page. The bot gets the page address, a selector, the element's HTML, its size and styles, and a picture of it. Point only reads the page: it never clicks or types. - **Notes on diff lines, and CI back to the bot** (0.9.0). On a Dev desk review card, add notes on lines and send them to the bot as one message; after its next push, each note says whether those lines changed. Failed CI checks and review comments on a bot's PR go back to that bot as one Fix-it item, and when the PR goes green a fresh-eyes reviewer gives its advice. Nothing is posted to GitHub, and nothing is merged. - **A worktree for each bot task** (0.9.0). The Dev desk's **Worktrees** tab makes a worktree from a new or existing branch, for a bot or just for you, and the bot works in its folder. **Remove** never deletes the branch and asks before it loses changes. An hour after a task finishes, kwant deletes build folders git ignores, such as `node_modules` and `target`, unless you keep them. - **Watch a mission** (0.9.0). Pick a bot to check a mission's claims when it stops. A claim that doesn't hold sends its task back, and the report shows what was claimed and what was checked. - **One order for what needs you** (0.9.0). The sidebar, the Inbox and the phone's Chats tab sort the same way: needs you, stuck or failed, to review, finished, working, waiting. A message to a busy or stuck bot is kept and says why it waits, and you get one notification when a turn shows no step for 15 minutes. Also: bots leave notes about their tools in Settings › Connections, and a bot can have a monthly budget (set through the API for now). - **Fixed in 0.9.1.** Bots hand work to each other as often as the work needs, with no stop at 4 hand-offs to one teammate or 16 per message. Exact repeats and a teammate that failed 3 times in a row are skipped with the reason. You press **Continue** only after 64 hand-offs for one message. Hand-off cards catch up after a lost connection, and TikTok's QR sign-in no longer freezes the bot's browser. - **New in 0.9.2.** Teams keep going until the job is done, so you no longer type "continue" when a lead stops halfway. After a teammate reports back, a lead that stops without handing on, asking you or writing a `Done:` line gets up to 2 more turns, then you get one **Keep going?** card. "Continue with Google" and other sign-in popups now open in the bot's live browser view, and the view goes back to the page when the popup closes. Bitwarden accounts with two-step login connect, and a Telegram approval card sent as you switch off Allow approvals from Telegram no longer keeps a dead Allow once button. - **New in 0.9.3.** Each bot job gets its own page in its team's browser, so a sign-in or CAPTCHA that one bot waits on no longer stops the team's other bots. The pages share the team's sign-ins. When a team has 2 or more pages, the browser view lists them by bot and site, marks the one that needs you and goes to it. A team has at most 4 job pages at once, and a page nobody has used for 30 minutes closes. - **New in 0.9.4.** Bots don't stop after a failed step. When a step fails or is refused, a bot tries it again, then tries another way; a step you declined isn't tried again. If nothing works, its last line starts with `Blocked:` and says what would unblock it, and from a team's lead that line comes to you as a question card. A reply that still ends on "I'll…" after a failed step gets one more turn. - **New in 0.9.5.** Apps & accounts puts apps, AI accounts, MCP servers and Telegram on one settings page, and connecting an app takes 3 steps: open Composio, paste your link, pick the bots. Each bot can have a monthly budget in tokens or dollars: at 80% you get a heads-up, and at 100% it pauses with **Raise the limit** and **Continue this month**. When a bot's connection fails, its chat gets one line that says which one and why, with **Reconnect** when only you can fix it. The team browser frees idle pages and retries for up to 45 seconds when it's busy, and Dev mode no longer stops at 30 model calls a day. - **New in 0.9.6.** Describe what your bots should do, press **Suggest a team**, and get 2 to 6 bots to untick or rename before you create them. The Inbox has a **Done while you were away** group next to **Needs you**: each item shows the answer, what the bot did and why, with **Looks good**, or ask the bot to redo it. Items stay for 7 days. A reply in your chat that stops before it's done either continues by itself or leaves one line in the chat and one item in **Needs you**, with **Retry** or **Continue**. Settings has one **kwant bots** card that says whether you're on the latest version, with **Update** when you're not. kwant's Chrome now presents itself as normal Chrome, and when Google refuses a sign-in without a window, **Sign in in Chrome** opens one for it on a computer with a screen. - **New in 0.9.7.** While a reply is coming, the chat shows the bot's own avatar typing at a pixel laptop, with **Ben is working on it**, and the words take its place without a jump. Each bot's avatar has a small mark for the AI it runs on, live while it works, and a greyed mark with the reason when its engine can't run. One **Find a tool** box searches built-in tools, Composio apps and the public MCP directory, forgives typos, and installs a directory tool in one step. - **New in 0.9.8.** A fresh install starts with **@helpers** (Assistant, Researcher, Writer), and #general asks **What do you want done?**; Dev mode and Approvals move to Settings › This space › General. A done item in the Inbox says what **checked** it (Checked, Partly checked, Failed or Not checked), with the checks and their evidence. Pressing **Ask Ben to try again** on a pre-push card lets Ben's next clean push of that branch go with no second card; the card follows it to **Pushed**. A mission check can **wait** for an outside service (exit 75): it re-runs every 15 minutes without bot turns and tells you after 72 hours. A chat that only needs your answer says **Waiting for you** in one amber line, with **Answer**; press a choice or just type. Bots @mention each other to hand work on, and a team lead runs short discussions and posts one summary. In a channel, kwant picks the bot that fits each message and shows why. The [Laya](#laya-model-router) router picks the model and effort for bots set to `auto`. - **"Done" means checked.** The [Mission board](docs/mission-control.md) turns work into cards, one per hand-off. A card turns **Verified** only when kwant runs the check itself, such as a test or a file check, and the card keeps the receipt. Files a bot attaches are evidence to look at, never proof on their own. - **Dev mode for code.** When bots write code, the [Dev desk](docs/dev-mode.md) shows what landed in each team's repo in plain words, and a bot that didn't write a pull request reviews it, tests and secrets included. Pushes to main, deploys and other production steps always ask first. - **Facts with sources.** Bots back web facts with a link that opens the page at the exact quote. kwant checks the quote is on the page word for word and refuses one that isn't. - **Spaces.** Separate spaces for work, a side project and home. Each has its own bots, teams, channels, routines, accounts, approval rule and hiring rule. - **Every account you have.** Several accounts per engine: Claude, Codex or Grok CLI logins, Anthropic, OpenAI or xAI keys, and your own OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible server. Set a default and a priority order. When an account runs out of usage, the turn moves to the next one and the chat says so. You can pin a bot to one account. - **Works while you're away.** Routines on a schedule (bots can set them up when you ask, with an Undo button), follow-ups bots schedule for themselves, and an **Inbox** with what's waiting on you, what finished and what failed. Turn on Automation Discovery and kwant suggests a routine for a task you keep asking for, which you accept or dismiss. - **Autonomous, with a safety net you control.** Ordinary work runs without stopping. On *Ask only when risky*, the default for new spaces, only risky steps such as `git push`, network calls, unknown commands or changes outside the bot's folder show an approval card with the exact command: *Allow once*, *Always allow* or *Deny*. Per space or per bot, switch to ask every time or don't ask. **Payments always ask**, in every mode: a payment command in the shell, or a checkout in the bot's browser, even behind a plain "Continue". Turn on Flight School and each bot earns more freedom per kind of work, but only you grant it. - **Rules per bot.** Say what each bot is good for and what it should never get, and which sites its browser may open. Blocked sites always win. - **Loose ends and letters.** kwant reads your chats and, if you add them, an IMAP inbox and your GitHub issues and pull requests, read-only, and finds what you started and never finished. Photograph a bill or a form and it pulls out the sender, the ask and the deadline and drafts a reply. It never sends anything. - **Parallel Universe.** Compare up to three ways to deploy an app with local container tests and dated price estimates. Every number is tagged as verified, an estimate or speculation. No cloud account and no spending. - **No telemetry.** kwant sends nothing to us, and its interface loads nothing from other servers. The one download you don't set up yourself is the [Laya](#laya-model-router) router on first start: its Python packages and its model from PyPI and Hugging Face (`--no-laya` turns it off). Everything else goes only to the AI providers and services you add. - **And more:** memory and skills per bot (you approve new skills), bots that propose hiring a teammate, import a bot from a Claude Code subagent, a SKILL.md, a character card or a JSON export, search across a space's chats, MCP tool servers, a shared browser for bots, saved passwords with an optional Bitwarden store, and Local or VM computer mode. See every feature, with screenshots, on [kwant.si/features](https://kwant.si/features).

Who answers: the bot that fits, and why. Wrong bot? teaches it.
Mission board: verified results, their cost and what needs you (with Truth Ledger and Flight School on).

Verified: only when kwant runs the check, with a receipt.
Payments always ask, in every approval mode.

Rules per bot: Good for, Not for and Browser sites.
