Screenshots come from a demo space with sample data. --- ## Quickstart The quickest way is the app for Mac, Linux or Windows (beta): download it, add an AI account you already have and ask your first question. There's nothing to build. On a server, see [Self-hosting on a VPS](#self-hosting-on-a-vps). ### What you need - **A Mac** (Apple silicon or Intel) **or a Linux x86_64 desktop** for the app. - **At least one AI account.** Any one of these is enough: - a Claude, ChatGPT or Grok account. You don't need to install or sign in to anything first: the **Get started** card installs the AI when it's missing, and you sign in from the app; - an Anthropic, OpenAI or xAI API key, which you add in the card or under **Settings → This space → Accounts**. - To [build from source](#run-from-a-fresh-clone) instead: **Rust** (stable), installed with [rustup](https://rustup.rs), and **Node.js 20 or newer** with npm, to build the web app. The finished binary doesn't need Node. - Optional: **Docker** for VM mode and the bots' shared browser, and [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) or `python3` for the Laya router. If you build from source, `kwnt doctor` (`cargo run -- doctor` from a clone) checks all of these and prints the install command for whatever is missing on your machine; `kwnt setup` installs it (see [Without Docker](#without-docker-kwnt-setup)). ### On a Mac: the app [Download the Mac app](https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant/releases/latest/download/kwant_universal.dmg) (a universal `.dmg` for Apple silicon and Intel) and drag kwant to Applications. It runs its own kwant on your Mac, with the same `~/.kwnt` data folder as `kwnt serve`, and stays in the menu bar when you close the window. Build it yourself from [`apps/mac`](apps/mac/README.md). The app is signed ad hoc, not notarized by Apple, so macOS stops it the first time. Click **Done**, open **System Settings → Privacy & Security**, scroll down and click **Open Anyway**. On macOS 14 or earlier, right-click the app and choose **Open** instead. ### On Linux: the app (beta) The Linux app is for x86_64. Like the Mac app, it runs its own kwant, uses the same `~/.kwnt` data folder and puts an icon in the tray. - **Ubuntu 22.04 or newer, Debian 12 or newer:** download [`kwant_amd64.deb`](https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant/releases/latest/download/kwant_amd64.deb), then run `sudo apt install ./kwant_amd64.deb`. - **Other distributions:** download [`kwant_x86_64.AppImage`](https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant/releases/latest/download/kwant_x86_64.AppImage), then `chmod +x kwant_x86_64.AppImage` and run it. It needs a normal GTK desktop and FUSE. Updates arrive in the app, which checks each one's signature before it installs it; with the `.deb`, your system asks for your password. `sudo apt remove kwant` removes the `.deb`, and your data in `~/.kwnt` stays. It's a beta: tested in containers on Ubuntu 22.04, Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12, not yet on real desktops, so the tray icon, Wayland and HiDPI may vary. There's no ARM Linux app yet. ### On Windows: the app (beta) Download `kwant_X.Y.Z_windows_x64_beta_setup.exe` from the [latest release](https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant/releases/latest) (its SHA-256 is next to it) and run it. It's for 64-bit Windows, installs for your user only with no admin rights, and runs kwant on your PC with the same `.kwnt` data folder in your user folder as `kwnt serve`. The installer isn't code-signed yet, so the first time Windows SmartScreen warns about an unrecognized app: click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. In the beta, the app doesn't update itself (a new version is a new installer), and Grok, the VM and looking inside videos aren't available on Windows yet. In a folder OneDrive syncs with Files On-Demand, Dev mode asks before every push. ### On your phone: iPhone and Android kwant has a phone app with no app store: you install it from the phone's browser, and it opens full screen from its own Home Screen icon. You need a kwant server your phone can reach over **https** (a [VPS or Docker](#self-hosting-on-a-vps) behind an HTTPS reverse proxy). The desktop apps run kwant at `127.0.0.1`, which a phone can't reach. 1. **Open kwant on the phone.** On a computer signed in to your kwant at its https address, open **Settings → All spaces → Signed-in devices → Add a phone or browser** and scan the QR code with the phone's camera. It opens your kwant and signs the phone in once. Or open your server's address on the phone, tap **Sign in from another device**, and approve the code it shows from a signed-in device. 2. **Add it to the Home Screen.** iPhone and iPad: in Safari, tap **Share → Add to Home Screen**. Android: in Chrome, tap **⋮ → Add to Home screen** (or **Install app**). 3. **Open "kwant bots" from the Home Screen** and turn on **Settings → All spaces → Notifications → Notify me on this device**, so approvals and questions reach you with the app closed. It loads from your server, so it updates when the server does. Step by step, with fixes for when it won't install: [kwant on your phone](https://kwant.si/docs/phone). ### Run from a fresh clone ```bash git clone https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant.git cd kwant make run # builds the web app (frontend/dist), then runs `cargo run -- serve` ``` Open **http://127.0.0.1:8799**. A new person's `#general` opens with the **Get started** card: choose your AI, sign in, pick a team ([guide](https://kwant.si/docs/quickstart#get-started)). A fresh install starts with three bots in `#general`: Architect, TechLead and DevOps. Make more with **New bot**, from a ready-made persona or blank. The binary embeds `frontend/dist`, so on a fresh clone `cargo build`, `cargo test` and `cargo run -- serve` fail to compile until you've run `make run` or `make frontend` once. **The first start takes a few minutes:** kwant installs its Laya router and downloads its model (about 420 MB) in the background. Bots answer meanwhile, and the routing rules still pick who answers. To skip Laya, run `cargo run -- serve --no-laya`. ### Build a release binary ```bash make build # web app + cargo build --release ./target/release/kwnt serve ``` ### Install the web app In Chrome or Edge, click **Install app** in **Settings → All spaces** (the sidebar also offers it once, as a tip); in Safari on a Mac, **File → Add to Dock**; on a phone, see [On your phone](#on-your-phone-iphone-and-android). Browsers only install pages served over https or from `127.0.0.1`. To get notifications on your phone with kwant closed, install it (on an iPhone, add it to the Home Screen first) and turn on **Settings → All spaces → Notifications → Notify me on this device**. kwant then sends a Web Push notification for each kind you've ticked there, such as an approval or a question. It goes through your browser's push service (Google's for Chrome on Android, Apple's on an iPhone), encrypted so that service can't read it. Signing a browser out under **Signed-in devices** stops its notifications. More in the [quickstart](https://kwant.si/docs/quickstart), [install](https://kwant.si/docs/install) and [phone](https://kwant.si/docs/phone) docs. --- ## Self-hosting on a VPS ### The binary `kwnt` is self-contained: SQLite and the web app are inside it. ```bash scp target/release/kwnt user@your-vps:/usr/local/bin/kwnt ssh user@your-vps "kwnt serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8799" ``` On your own computer there is nothing to sign in to. From another machine, open the one-time link `kwnt serve` prints at startup (it works once, for 15 minutes; with `KWNT_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` set it is ready to open and comes with a QR code), or make a new one with `kwnt signin-link`. The browser stays signed in for a year. To add your phone or another browser later, open **Settings → Signed-in devices → Add a phone or browser** in a signed-in browser and scan the one-time QR code (it also works once, for 15 minutes); the same list lets you sign those browsers out. A new browser can also choose **Sign in from another device** on the sign-in screen: it shows a code for 10 minutes, and a signed-in browser shows **New device wants access** with Approve or Deny. Approve only a code that is on a screen you are holding. Prefer the token? On the server, as the user that runs kwnt, `cat ~/.kwnt/api-token` (or `$KWNT_DATA_DIR/api-token`, e.g. `sudo cat /var/lib/kwnt/api-token` with the systemd unit below) prints the token to paste (`kwnt token --raw` does the same; `./target/release/kwnt` if kwnt isn't on your PATH), and `kwnt token` prints a new one-time link like `kwnt signin-link`. Run them as the same user: as another user they fail, because that user can't read the token file (for the systemd unit use `sudo cat` as above). Each install has its own token, so one copied from your laptop won't open kwnt on the server. Or skip sign-in: `ssh -N -L 8799:127.0.0.1:8799 user@your-vps`, then open http://127.0.0.1:8799 on your computer (not with Docker, where requests always count as remote). A one-time link signs in as you, so keep it private until you've used it; the token never appears in the server's output. Put a TLS reverse proxy in front: see [browser service and VPS hosting](docs/browser-service.md).
A systemd unit ```ini # /etc/systemd/system/kwnt.service [Unit] Description=kwant AI bot platform After=network.target [Service] Type=simple # A dedicated user (useradd --system --create-home --home-dir /var/lib/kwnt kwnt); sign the # claude/codex/grok CLIs in as this user, or add API keys in the app User=kwnt ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/kwnt serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8799 Restart=always Environment=KWNT_DATA_DIR=/var/lib/kwnt [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target ``` ```bash systemctl daemon-reload systemctl enable --now kwnt ```
### VPS in 5 minutes (Docker Compose) One command starts everything kwant needs: kwnt, the **Laya** router (with its model baked in) and a private **Chromium** for the bots (VM mode), with no Docker socket mounted. You need Docker with Compose and about 4 GB of free RAM (Chromium is capped at 1.5 GB). ```bash git clone https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant.git && cd kwant KWNT_CLIS=claude,codex docker compose up -d --build # any of claude,codex,grok; leave out for none docker compose exec kwnt kwnt doctor # what works, and the fix for what doesn't docker compose exec kwnt claude auth login # sign a CLI in (codex login --device-auth, grok login --device-auth) docker compose exec kwnt kwnt signin-link # a one-time sign-in link and QR code (15 minutes) ``` Or skip the CLIs and add an Anthropic, OpenAI or xAI API key in the app under **Settings → This space → Accounts**. CLI sign-ins live in the `kwnt-home` volume and data in `kwnt-data`, so both survive rebuilds. **HTTPS:** the UI is published on `127.0.0.1:8799` only. Put a TLS proxy in front, e.g. [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com) with this `Caddyfile`, and tell kwnt its address: ``` kwant.example.com { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8799 } ``` ```bash echo KWNT_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://kwant.example.com >> .env && docker compose up -d ``` `docker compose exec kwnt kwnt signin-link` prints a one-time sign-in link for your domain and a QR code to scan with your phone. It works once, for 15 minutes; run it again for the next device. `docker compose exec kwnt kwnt token --raw` still prints the API token, as a fallback. - **Image sizes** (measured): kwnt alone 0.2 GB; with `KWNT_CLIS=claude,codex,grok` 1.7 GB (the CLIs add about 0.9 GB, so they are off by default). Laya 3.2 GB, the browser 1.2 GB. Idle RAM: Laya about 1.7–2.3 GB, the browser about 0.4 GB, kwnt about 25 MB. - **kwant's own `execute_shell` tool** runs in per-team Docker containers, so it isn't available inside this stack: that would need the host's Docker socket, which is root on the host. The CLIs' own shell tools work inside the kwnt container. - **Upgrading from an older image:** kwnt now runs as uid 10001, not root. If it says `/data isn't writable`, run once: `docker compose run --rm -u root kwnt chown -R 10001:10001 /data`. ### Render, Railway, CasaOS, Umbrel and Coolify [![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant) [![Deploy on Railway](https://railway.com/button.svg)](https://railway.com/deploy/kwant) The button reads [`render.yaml`](render.yaml): one web service from the released image with a 1 GB disk on `/data`. **Render keeps files only on a disk, and disks need a paid instance** (Starter or up), so the free plan won't work. Render makes the sign-in token: copy `KWNT_API_TOKEN` from the service's **Environment** page and paste it on the sign-in screen. The Railway button builds the same `docker/render.Dockerfile` with a volume on `/data`, plus the bots' private browser from `docker/browser.Dockerfile` on Railway's private network. Railway makes the sign-in token: copy `KWNT_API_TOKEN` from the kwant service's **Variables** tab. For home servers, [`deploy/`](deploy) has a listing for each store, pinned to the release: [CasaOS](deploy/casaos/Kwnt/docker-compose.yml) (sign in with `kwnt token --raw` from the app's **Terminal**), [Umbrel](deploy/umbrel/kwant) (sign in with the password Umbrel shows for kwant) and [Coolify](deploy/coolify/kwnt.yaml) (sign in with `SERVICE_PASSWORD_64_KWNT` from the service's environment variables). Until a store lists kwant, CasaOS can import the file under **Custom Install** and Coolify can run it as a **Docker Compose** resource; Umbrel needs the listing. These run kwnt alone, without Laya or the bots' browser; see [docs/self-host-stores.md](docs/self-host-stores.md). ### Without Docker: `kwnt setup` `kwnt setup` installs what kwant needs on this machine: Chromium or Chrome for the bots' browser, Laya (in kwant's data folder, with its own `uv` if you have no Python), and a CLI (`claude` unless you name others with `--clis`). It asks before each step (`--yes` skips the questions), never runs `sudo` itself (it prints the command for you instead), installs into your home folder where it can, skips Docker unless you pass `--docker`, and running it again changes nothing. `--dry-run` shows the plan. The app has the same checklist under **Setup**. One line per platform, each followed by `kwnt doctor`: | Platform | Install | Then | |---|---|---| | Mac app | Download the `.dmg` from [Releases](https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant/releases) and open it | Run `kwnt doctor` | | Linux app (beta, x86_64) | Download the `.deb` or the AppImage from [Releases](https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant/releases) and [install it](#on-linux-the-app-beta) | Open **Setup** in the app | | Mac, command line | `git clone https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant.git && cd kwant && make build && ./target/release/kwnt setup` (uses Homebrew when you have it) | Run `kwnt doctor` | | Linux desktop or server | The same clone and `make build`, then `kwnt setup`, or `sh scripts/install-linux-deps.sh --clis claude` on Debian/Ubuntu | Run `kwnt doctor` | | VPS with Docker | [Docker Compose](#vps-in-5-minutes-docker-compose) | Run `docker compose exec kwnt kwnt doctor` | On Linux (x86_64 or arm64, glibc 2.35+) you can skip the build: `curl -fsSL https://kwant.si/install.sh | sh` installs the prebuilt `kwnt` from the latest release after checking its `.sha256`, and every release also has `kwnt-linux-x86_64.tar.gz` and `kwnt-linux-aarch64.tar.gz`. There's no prebuilt command-line `kwnt` for macOS yet, so on a Mac the command line needs a clone and a build (Rust and Node). --- ## Laya model router [Laya](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya) picks which model and effort a bot uses when its model is `auto`. When kwant picks which bot answers in a channel, Laya adds its own guess from the bots' titles, but it never picks a bot on its own: kwant's [routing rules](docs/channel-routing.md) do. It runs as a small Python service, and **`kwnt serve` manages it for you**: on first run it installs `laya[serve]` into `~/.kwnt/laya/venv` (with `uv` when present, else `python3 -m venv`), starts it, and restarts it if it exits. The header shows its status. While Laya is unavailable, the rules still pick the bot, the model and effort come from a keyword estimate, and the reason line under a reply says it was a keyword match. | Setting | `config.toml` | Environment | Default | |---|---|---|---| | Laya URL | `laya_url` | `LAYA_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:8000` | | Manage a local Laya | `laya_managed` | `KWNT_LAYA_MANAGED=0` to disable, or `kwnt serve --no-laya` | `true` | | Checkpoints to preload | `laya_models` | `KWNT_LAYA_MODELS` | `english` | | Use an existing `laya-serve` binary | | `KWNT_LAYA_SERVE_BIN` | | The first start needs `huggingface.co`. Behind a proxy that blocks it, start kwant once on an open network or copy `~/.kwnt/laya/hf` from another machine. --- ## FAQ **Is kwant free?** Yes. It's open source under the AGPL-3.0: use it, change it and run it for yourself, your team or your company, at any size. You pay only for the AI accounts you already have. If you want to sell or host kwant without publishing your changes, there's a [commercial license](COMMERCIAL.md). **Can I use my Claude or ChatGPT plan?** Yes. kwant runs the Claude, Codex or Grok CLI you're signed in to, so your plan covers the work. You can also add Anthropic, OpenAI or xAI API keys, or your own OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible server. When one account runs out of usage, the turn moves to the next. **How is it different from Grok Bot, Claude Duet or OpenAI dots?** It's the same idea, a team of named bots you message, but open source, running on your own computer or server, with any of your accounts. And a task counts as done only when kwant runs the check itself. Side by side: [kwant vs Grok Bot](https://kwant.si/alternatives/grok-bot). **Where does my data go?** It stays on your computer or server, in kwant's data folder (`~/.kwnt` by default). kwant has no telemetry and sends nothing to us. Your messages go only to the AI providers and services you add. **Do I need an account with you?** No. There's no sign-up: you run kwant yourself and sign in only to the AI accounts you add. **Which computers can run it?** A Mac (Apple silicon or Intel), a Linux desktop (x86_64, beta), a Windows PC (64-bit, beta) or a Linux server, with the binary or Docker Compose. **Can I run it on a free server?** Yes. [This guide](https://kwant.si/blog/self-host-grok-bot-alternative-free-oracle-cloud) sets kwant up on Oracle Cloud's free tier, step by step. --- ## Documentation - What changed in each release: [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) - Website docs: [kwant.si/docs](https://kwant.si/docs/quickstart): quickstart, install, spaces, bots and teams, Mission board, Flight School, Truth Ledger, models and routing, accounts, routines, approvals, the bots' browser, loose ends, Parallel Universe, memory and skills, MCP. - In this repo: - [Channel routing: who answers](docs/channel-routing.md) - [Mission Control and verified outcomes](docs/mission-control.md) - [Approvals](docs/approvals.md) - [Payments always ask](docs/payments.md) - [How bots use their browser](docs/bot-browser.md) - [Bot actions](docs/bot-actions.md) - [Browser service and VPS hosting](docs/browser-service.md) - [LLM profiles (accounts) and API access](docs/llm-profiles.md) - [Connections API](docs/connections.md) - [Live activity and human steps API](docs/live-activity.md) - [MCP API](docs/mcp-api.md) - [Saved passwords](docs/saved-passwords.md) - [Loose ends (zombie hunter)](docs/zombie-hunter.md) - [Letters (camera to completed)](docs/camera-to-completed.md) - [Parallel Universe](docs/parallel-universe.md) - [Dev mode](docs/dev-mode.md) - [Idea jar](docs/idea-jar.md) - [Dictation](docs/dictation.md): `GET /api/spaces/:id/transcribe` says whether the mic button works in a space; `POST /api/spaces/:id/transcribe` turns a recording into text --- ## Contributing Bug reports, ideas and pull requests are welcome. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for how to build, test and send a change, and follow the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). ```bash make frontend # build the web app once (cargo test needs frontend/dist) cargo test # Rust unit and integration tests cd frontend && npm test # web app tests ``` ## Security kwant runs commands and holds API keys and passwords, so please report vulnerabilities privately. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). Don't open a public issue for a security problem. ## Contact - Email: [contact@kwant.si](mailto:contact@kwant.si), for questions, a commercial license, privacy requests or press. - Bugs and ideas: [GitHub issues](https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant/issues). Questions and setups to share: [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/alexsergivan/kwant/discussions). - Security problems: report them privately, as [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) describes. ## License kwant is open source under the [GNU Affero General Public License v3.0](LICENSE) (AGPL-3.0-only). - **Free for everyone:** use it, change it and run it for yourself, your team or your company, at any size. - **Share your changes if you serve them:** if you change kwant and let others use it over a network, for example as a hosted service, you must publish your changed source code under the AGPL too. - **Commercial license:** if you want to sell kwant, host it or build it into your product without publishing your changes, you can buy a commercial license instead. See [COMMERCIAL.md](COMMERCIAL.md). Code published before the switch, including the mac-v0.1.0 release, stays under MIT OR Apache-2.0. Contributions are accepted under the terms in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#license).

items.name: Cotal
items.description: The open standard for agent coordination
items.readme_text:
**The open pub/sub standard for AI agents.** Connect agents across applications and machines.
Choose the topology that fits your team.

[![CI](https://github.com/Cotal-AI/Cotal/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Cotal-AI/Cotal/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@cotal-ai/core?label=%40cotal-ai%2Fcore)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@cotal-ai/core) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-docs.cotal.ai-e9c46a)](https://docs.cotal.ai) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-join-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/fhPqe3b4qu) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-blue)](LICENSE) [![Node](https://img.shields.io/badge/node-%E2%89%A522-brightgreen)](https://nodejs.org) [Live demo](https://booth.apps.cotal.ai) · [Examples](#examples) · [Supported agents](#supported-agents) · [FAQ](#faq)
## What is Cotal Cotal lets AI agents and software services work together in a shared space, across applications and machines. An agent can find its peers, message a channel, ask a reviewer for help, or call a service. You choose who delegates to whom. Use it for a team of peers, a supervisor with workers, or a workflow with human checkpoints. Agents can join from a laptop, a workstation or a remote host. Separate spaces keep projects and their permissions apart. The open standard defines identity, messaging, presence and endpoint control. The TypeScript implementation runs on [NATS + JetStream](https://nats.io) and includes the CLI, application connectors, a process manager, durable workflows and observation tools. [Read the overview](docs/what-is-cotal.mdx). ## Quick start On minimal Linux images, check the [installer prerequisites](docs/installation.mdx#use-the-shell-installer) first. Rocky Linux 9 needs `sudo dnf install tar` before running the installer. ```bash curl -fsSL https://get.cotal.ai | sh ``` The installer writes to your home directory without sudo and opens guided setup. You can [read the script](https://get.cotal.ai) first or preview it with `| sh -s -- --dry-run`. On Windows, or with an existing Node 22.10+ installation, use npm. With distribution Node on macOS or Linux, npm's default global prefix may be root-owned. Use the shell installer above or follow the [user-owned npm prefix and PATH steps](docs/installation.mdx#install-with-npm) before the npm command. Install Cotal as your own user, without sudo. ```bash npm install -g cotal-ai cotal setup ``` Setup prepares a space, configures your chosen application and seeds a `default` persona. It asks separately whether to start. To prepare only, use `cotal setup --configure-only`. If you leave startup for later, run these from the project folder: ```bash cotal up # start the local mesh, delivery daemon and manager in the background cotal spawn # open your agent in this terminal ``` In another terminal, `cotal console` shows the team and its messages. Press **Ctrl-P** to open its command palette and launch another agent. You can also launch one directly with `cotal spawn --detach`. Ask either agent to introduce itself to its peers. `cotal down` stops the local stack. The [Quickstart](docs/getting-started.mdx) covers requirements, non-interactive setup and troubleshooting. Prefer your coding agent to do the setup? Give it . The CLI sends usage telemetry by default. Disable it with `cotal telemetry off`. [See what is sent](docs/telemetry.mdx). ## Choose how to work | You want to | Start here | |---|---| | Run agents locally or on another machine | [Launch modes and manager selection](https://docs.cotal.ai/api-reference/cli-agents/#spawn) | | Connect a personal Claude Code session | [Existing-session connection and approval](https://docs.cotal.ai/docs/connect-claude/#sessions-cotal-did-not-launch) | | Join a hosted space | [Sign in and select a space](https://docs.cotal.ai/docs/using-cotal/#join-a-hosted-space) | | Declare a team and its channel permissions | [Team manifests](docs/define-a-team.mdx) | | Coordinate work that waits, branches or resumes | [Cotal Lang workflows](docs/workflows.mdx) | | Connect a service or automate Cotal | [API reference](docs/api-reference.mdx) | A personal-session connection needs a signed-in space with a supported approval flow. The approval explains its permissions and activity sharing. For a local static-auth or open space, launch through `cotal spawn` instead. ## Supported agents

Claude Code
plugin + native hooks
OpenCode
in-process plugin
Codex
app-server + TUI
Hermes
gateway + plugin		 Jcode
Harness API + TUI
pi
native extension
The connectors expose mesh tools and deliver peer messages through each application's own mechanisms. Codex, Jcode and pi support directed messages during a live turn; personal native Claude Code sessions receive messages at supported busy boundaries. Resume, events and tool-sharing support differ by application. The [connector matrix](docs/connectors.mdx) lists the details and maturity levels. Managed agents can run in a PTY or a supported terminal runtime: [tmux](extensions/tmux), [cmux](extensions/cmux), [Orca](extensions/orca) or [Herdr](extensions/herdr). See [runtimes](https://docs.cotal.ai/api-reference/cli-agents/#runtimes) for installation and availability. Bring another application by [writing a connector](docs/authoring-a-connector.mdx), or [vote for the next one](https://github.com/Cotal-AI/Cotal/discussions/80). ## How it works Each participant has an identity and reports its presence. Messages have three destinations:

- **Multicast** reaches the subscribers of a channel such as `#review`. - **Unicast** addresses one peer directly. - **Anycast** addresses a role such as `reviewer`, so one available instance can take the work. On authenticated meshes, the durable backstop retains messages for busy or offline agents within the configured retention and lifecycle limits. Presence tells peers who is there; attention modes let an agent control which channel traffic may interrupt it. A heartbeat reports liveness, not proof that a task is progressing. The manager starts and stops processes. It does not sit between agents' messages or choose their work. Agents can request teammates through `cotal_spawn` when their grants allow it. A manifest sets up a team in advance; Cotal Lang coordinates its execution. [Architecture](docs/architecture.mdx) · [Delivery](docs/presence-and-delivery.mdx) · [Channel permissions](docs/channels-and-permissions.mdx) ## Workflow runs Cotal Lang is a small subset of JavaScript for coordinating work over a step journal. A program can launch agents, wait for replies and pause for a person. A supported host can resume an interrupted run from its recorded progress. For example, with `planner` and `builder` personas defined on the manager: ```js const planner = await spawn("planner") const builder = await spawn("builder") await turn(planner, { name: "plan" }) const approval = await checkpoint("approve-plan", "Build the plan?", { timeout: "4h" }) if (approval.value === "yes") { await turn(builder, { name: "build", deadline: "30m" }) } ``` Save the program as `build.cotal.js` and start it on an authenticated mesh with run authority: ```bash cotal run start --file build.cotal.js cotal run # list recorded runs cotal run show # inspect progress and open questions cotal run answer --value '"yes"' ``` The runtime also supports concurrent branches, keyed submissions and authenticated cooperative cancellation. A cancellation record does not prove every external process has stopped. See [Workflow runs](docs/workflows.mdx) for recovery and host limits, and the [language reference](spec/cotal-lang.md) for the full contract. ## Services and integrations Services publish command contracts that authorized callers can discover and invoke. The same endpoint interface serves the manager and integrations such as [Linear](implementations/linear). Agents use `cotal_describe` and `cotal_invoke` where their connector and grants provide them; scripts can use the CLI's [endpoint commands](https://docs.cotal.ai/api-reference/cli-endpoints/#endpoint-control) and structured output. The Linear adapter serves an upstream account on static-auth meshes or through an approved user-auth service registration. A hosted deployment still needs to configure its authority, endpoint binding and caller grants. Installing an adapter does not grant access to an account or make a service available in every space. For your own integration, choose among the [TypeScript libraries](docs/embedding.mdx), [agent tools](docs/mcp-tools.mdx) and [HTTP references](docs/api-reference.mdx#http-interfaces). ## Watch the team `cotal console` provides an interactive terminal view of peers, channels and messages. Its command palette can launch agents and perform authorized operator actions. `cotal watch` streams observations; commands such as `who`, `ps` and `status` answer specific questions about peers, managed agents and the local machine. The browser dashboard is a separately configured read-only service. It uses an explicit protected credential for a registered static-auth space and shows only what that credential may read. It does not mint its own access. Follow the [dashboard setup](https://docs.cotal.ai/docs/web-dashboard/#web-dashboard) before starting it.

Channel membership and live message flow.


The roster, channel messages and agents that need attention.
## Identity and access `cotal up` authenticates by default. The broker checks the sender identity in each message's subject and enforces per-agent permissions. Spaces use separate NATS accounts. User-auth deployments let people sign in and issue access under their current grants. The broker, operator and admin credentials are trusted. Direct messages are protected from unauthorized peers, but are not end-to-end encrypted against those trusted parties. `cotal up --open` is a loopback-only, live-only mode without authentication, for local experiments. [Read the security model](docs/security.mdx). Personal-session activity sharing, mesh permissions and CLI telemetry are separate settings. Review the connection approval before sharing a conversation's activity, and see [Telemetry](docs/telemetry.mdx) for CLI usage reporting. ## Examples Try the [browser demo](https://booth.apps.cotal.ai) without installing anything. Its four scripted scenes cover a mixed-agent team, the delivery modes, changing topologies and a workflow that resumes on another machine.
Lateral coordination

Role-specialized peers in one space: presence, all three addressing modes, live state, graceful leave, and late join, each in its own terminal.

the raw protocol · plain terminals
A swarm rebuilds Cotal's console

Four Claude Code agents coordinate on one mesh while an orchestrator launches workers in cmux tabs. They build an Ink/React console for watching the team.

four coding agents · cmux tabs
Frontier Tower faces

Ten panelist personas as animated pixel-art OpenCode agents: each thinks, lip-syncs its streamed reply, and steers its own 32×32 expression, and on the mesh they coordinate as lateral peers in one space.

ten OpenCode faces · OpenCode · tmux wall + browser
[All examples](docs/examples.mdx), including their own setup instructions and limitations. ## Documentation The docs are at **[docs.cotal.ai](https://docs.cotal.ai)**. Pages also have Markdown versions for agents, and installed connectors expose a versioned `cotal_docs` bundle. - [Choose a workflow](docs/using-cotal.mdx): local teams, hosted spaces, personal sessions and integrations. - [CLI reference](docs/cli.mdx#find-a-command): commands grouped by task, with flags and output contracts. - [API reference](docs/api-reference.mdx): libraries, endpoint commands, agent tools and HTTP. - [Spec](SPEC.md): the normative wire contract. - [Upgrading](docs/UPGRADING.md): package-specific migration steps. ## FAQ
How does Cotal relate to MCP and A2A? MCP connects applications to tools. A2A defines agent communication using its own request/response and task model. Cotal provides a shared pub/sub space with presence, channels, durable delivery and role-based addressing. It reuses A2A's `AgentCard` and `Message`/`Part` shapes, but uses the NATS binding rather than A2A's HTTP transport. Reusing those shapes does not make Cotal an A2A transport bridge.
Is Cotal TypeScript-only? TypeScript is the reference implementation. The standard is a wire contract, so another language can implement it with a NATS client and the required identity, delivery and presence behavior. [Build a client](docs/build-a-client.mdx) gives the implementation order.
Can agents run on different machines? Yes. They connect to the same space through a reachable broker. A laptop, workstation and remote host can participate together. Remote launches need an authorized manager; the host controls which agents and services may run there. See [remote supervision](https://docs.cotal.ai/docs/remote-supervision/#remote-supervised-agents).
Is the browser dashboard the hosted Cotal product? The dashboard in this repository is a read-only observer configured with a static credential. Hosted Cotal has its own deployment and account flows. Support in a library or adapter does not mean every hosted deployment has enabled it.
## Sponsors & partners

Building Web-A, the web for agents. We're part of it and share the vision.
San Francisco's hub for frontier technologies.

Runs the sandboxes behind hosted Cotal.
Cotal is part of the Cloudflare® for Startups program.
We're looking for more design partners building multi-agent systems. [Reach out](#team). Contributions are welcome: implement the contract in your language, build a connector, or open an issue. See [Running the smoke gate](bin/smoke/README.md) for local and CI testing. ## Team

David Farah
Sven Jonscher
Building something on Cotal, or want to? Email hello@cotal.ai. We read everything. ## License [Apache-2.0](LICENSE) for everything in this repo: the wire protocol, core, every extension, and the CLI. See [LICENSING.md](LICENSING.md) for the trademark note and the hosted-server plan. Cloudflare and the Cloudflare logo are trademarks and/or registered trademarks of Cloudflare, Inc. in the United States and other jurisdictions. ---

Made with ❤️ by Cotal, in Switzerland and San Francisco.

items.name: chrome-agent
items.description: CLI that gives AI coding agents direct access to Chrome via the DevTools Protocol. Many agents and humans can share one browser, each with isolated event subscriptions.
items.readme_text:
# chrome-agent [![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/chrome-agent)](https://pypi.org/project/chrome-agent/) [![PyPI downloads](https://img.shields.io/pepy/dt/chrome-agent)](https://pepy.tech/projects/chrome-agent) [![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/chrome-agent)](https://pypi.org/project/chrome-agent/) [![License](https://img.shields.io/pypi/l/chrome-agent)](https://github.com/captivus/chrome-agent/blob/main/LICENSE) A CLI tool that gives AI coding agents the ability to observe and interact with Chrome browsers via the [Chrome DevTools Protocol](https://chromedevtools.github.io/devtools-protocol/). Multiple agents and humans can share the same browser simultaneously, each with isolated event subscriptions. One agent drives while another observes network traffic. A human browses while an agent watches for errors. Four agents run a coordinated test suite against a single browser. Each participant sees only the events they subscribed to -- no interference. **I teach a live course on this:** [Building AI Agents for the Web](https://agentsfortheweb.com/?c=now-a-course-readme). Next free live lesson, Tuesday, November 24: [Find the hidden API behind any web app](https://agentsfortheweb.com/live/?c=now-a-course-readme).

Used by engineers at





## Why this exists AI coding agents need to see and interact with browsers -- to test their code, debug automation, inspect page state. The standard approach (browser MCP tools) uses a persistent server with protocol negotiation and verbose response formatting. `chrome-agent` takes a different approach: direct access to Chrome's DevTools Protocol with no abstraction layer. This means full CDP protocol access -- every command, every event, every domain Chrome exposes. Not a curated subset of capabilities, but the complete protocol. Agents compose interactions from CDP primitives the same way DevTools does. ## Tracks the running browser, not its own version Because there is no abstraction layer, chrome-agent tracks your browser rather than its own release. The CLI sends the method name and parameters you give it straight to Chrome and streams back the events you subscribe to -- nothing is validated against a bundled schema. So **any command, event, or domain your installed Chrome supports just works**, including protocol surface added *after* the version of chrome-agent you installed. There is no curated subset to fall behind. For example, the `CrashReportContext` and `WebMCP` domains (added to CDP in later Chrome releases) are both absent from an older chrome-agent's typed bindings, yet a method on one returns a normal result through the CLI, with no change to chrome-agent: ```bash chrome-agent myproject-01 CrashReportContext.getEntries # {"entries": []} ``` The one point-in-time artifact is the typed Python classes (see [Python API](#python-api)) -- an optional convenience layer that snapshots the schema at generation time. They never gate access: `CDPClient.send(method=..., params=...)` reaches any method regardless. And `help` reads the protocol schema live from the running browser, so its documentation is always as current as your Chrome. ## Installation ```bash uv tool install chrome-agent ``` Or add to a project: ```bash uv add chrome-agent ``` Requires Google Chrome or Chromium installed on the system. Runtime dependencies are `websockets`, plus `cryptography` and `keyring` for encrypting saved sessions. No Playwright, no browser downloads. ## Quick Start ```bash # Launch a browser -- auto-allocates a port and names the instance. From your # terminal it opens on your desktop; from an AI agent, on a virtual display # (see "Agent browsers" below) chrome-agent launch # {"name": "myproject-01", "port": 9222, "pid": 58469, "browser_version": "Chrome/147", "display": {"kind": "desktop", "display": ":1"}, "owner": null} # Check what's running chrome-agent status # myproject-01 port 9222 [desktop :1] kept # [1] 956FD3C2 https://example.com "Example Domain" # Read the page title chrome-agent myproject-01 Runtime.evaluate '{"expression": "document.title", "returnByValue": true}' # Navigate chrome-agent myproject-01 Page.navigate '{"url": "https://example.com"}' # Take a screenshot (returns base64 PNG in JSON) chrome-agent myproject-01 Page.captureScreenshot '{"format": "png"}' # Discover available commands chrome-agent help myproject-01 Page chrome-agent help myproject-01 Page.navigate # Stop the browser when done chrome-agent stop myproject-01 # Or stop a whole related set at once (quote the pattern -- see Instance Patterns) chrome-agent stop 'myproject-*' ``` ## Instance Patterns Anywhere an instance name is accepted, a glob works instead -- `*`, `?`, `[abc]`, matched case-sensitively against the registered names. ```bash chrome-agent stop 'myproject-*' # stops every match, printing the names first chrome-agent status 'myproject-*' # lists every match chrome-agent 'myproject-0[2]' Page.navigate '{"url": "https://example.com"}' ``` `stop` and `status` act on every match. The single-browser commands -- `attach`, `help` and one-shot CDP calls -- resolve a pattern that matches exactly one instance and otherwise error with the candidates listed, rather than picking one. A pattern matching nothing is an error, not a silent no-op. **Quote the pattern.** Your shell expands an unquoted glob before chrome-agent sees it, and zsh aborts the command outright when nothing in the working directory matches (`zsh: no matches found: myproject-*`). A literal name is never treated as a pattern, so `chrome-agent stop myproject-01` cannot sweep up `myproject-02`. Because `stop --target` closes one tab, combining it with a pattern that matches several instances is refused. ## Tab Completion zsh only, for now. Two ways to install it; pick one. **Sourced from `.zshrc`** -- one line, works anywhere, costs one subprocess (~60 ms) at shell startup. It must come *after* `compinit`: ```bash source <(chrome-agent completions zsh) ``` **Installed as a file** -- no startup cost, but the directory has to be on `$fpath` *before* `compinit` runs, which is the step that is easy to miss: ```bash mkdir -p ~/.config/zsh/completions chrome-agent completions zsh > ~/.config/zsh/completions/_chrome-agent ``` ```bash fpath=(~/.config/zsh/completions $fpath) autoload -Uz compinit && compinit ``` That second block goes in `.zshrc`, in that order. If the directory is not on `$fpath`, the file is simply never read and Tab does nothing -- there is no error to tell you so. Either way, open a new shell and check it took: ```bash chrome-agent ``` You should get the subcommands and your running instances, each with a description. If nothing happens, `echo $_comps[chrome-agent]` should print `_chrome-agent`; an empty result means the completion was never registered. The generated file is a snapshot of the completion logic, so regenerate it after upgrading chrome-agent (the *candidates* it offers are always read live; the function itself is not). Sourcing from `.zshrc` avoids that entirely. Completes the subcommands, their flags, the **live instance names**, and **CDP method and event names**: ``` chrome-agent stop reader -> ensorcell-reader-01, described by port and tab count chrome-agent taleb-01 Page.nav -> Page.navigate chrome-agent attach taleb-01 +Page.load -> +Page.loadEventFired ``` Instance names are read from the registry as you type, so they are what is actually registered rather than a list baked in at install time. Methods and events come from the running browser's own `/json/protocol` -- the protocol *this* Chrome implements, not a snapshot shipped with chrome-agent -- cached on disk under the browser version, so a Chrome upgrade invalidates it. Without a running browser you simply get no candidates. The protocol cache lives under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/chrome-agent` (default `~/.cache/chrome-agent`), one file per browser version; deleting it is safe and costs one 7 ms refetch. ## Two Channels chrome-agent uses a two-channel pattern for browser interaction: ### One-shot mode (commands) Send a single CDP command. Connects, sends, prints JSON response, disconnects. ```bash chrome-agent Domain.method '{"param": "value"}' ``` Good for spot checks, screenshots, quick queries. ~50-80ms per call. If only one instance is running, the instance name can be omitted. ### Attach mode (events) Persistent connection with isolated event subscriptions. Streams events to stdout as JSON lines. ```bash chrome-agent attach +Page.loadEventFired +Network.requestWillBeSent ``` Run it in the background while sending one-shot commands: ```bash # Background: observe events chrome-agent attach myproject-01 +Page.loadEventFired +Network.requestWillBeSent > /tmp/events.jsonl & # Foreground: send commands -- events appear in the attach stream chrome-agent myproject-01 Page.navigate '{"url": "https://example.com"}' ``` Subscribe to exactly the events you need. Each attach session is isolated -- subscribing to Network events in one session does not affect other sessions. An attach session **exits on its own once it has outlived its purpose** -- when its instance is retired from the registry, or its browser is gone or no longer reachable -- so a backgrounded observer never lingers indefinitely after the thing it was watching is gone. It also shuts down cleanly (detaching its CDP session) on `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT`, even while idle with no events arriving. A transient registry read or CDP-port blip is ridden out rather than acted on. ## Operational Commands ``` chrome-agent launch [--display virtual|desktop] [--keep] [--headless] [--fingerprint PATH] [--port PORT] [--no-window-border] chrome-agent status [] chrome-agent attach [+Event ...] [--target SPEC | --target-id ID | --target-index N | --url SUBSTRING] chrome-agent stop [--target SPEC | --target-id ID | --target-index N | --url SUBSTRING] chrome-agent stop --orphans chrome-agent keep chrome-agent move --to desktop|virtual chrome-agent help [] [Domain | Domain.method] chrome-agent cleanup chrome-agent save ... | --all [--stop] [--as NAME] [--overwrite | --keep-both] chrome-agent restore [...] | --all [--here] [--any-port] [--desktop saved|terminal] [--display virtual|desktop] [--keep] [--no-reattach] [--replace-profile] [--start-display] chrome-agent restore --as NEW-NAME [...] chrome-agent snapshots [list [] | show | rm ... [--older-than AGE] [--yes] | export-key | import-key [--replace]] chrome-agent completions [] chrome-agent --version ``` | Command | Description | |---------|-------------| | `launch` | Find Chrome, launch with CDP enabled. Auto-allocates a port and names the instance from the current directory. From an AI agent's session the browser goes on a managed virtual display and is tied to that session; from your terminal it opens on your desktop and runs until stopped. `--display virtual\|desktop` and `--keep` override -- see [Agent browsers](#agent-browsers-off-your-screen-and-gone-with-the-agent). | | `status` | List running instances with their page targets (IDs, URLs, titles), in the order the tabs sit on screen, window by window, numbered `[1]`, `[2]`, ... left to right -- the numbers `--target N` and `--target-index N` select. If the order cannot be read, `status` says so and numbers tabs by target id instead. Accepts a glob to list a matching subset. Each header says where the browser is -- `[desktop :1]` on your screen, `[Xvfb :100]` on a virtual X display (Xvfb, Xvnc, Xephyr), `[headless]` with no window -- and who it belongs to: `owner claude-code pid 9669` for an agent session's browser (`(yours)` when you are that session), `kept` for one with no owner, `ORPHAN` when its owner has exited. The JSON form carries `display` and `owner` fields for every live instance. | | `attach` | Persistent event observation with isolated subscriptions. Use `--target` (fewer than 8 digits is a tab number, anything else a target-id prefix), `--url substring`, or the explicit `--target-id` / `--target-index` for multi-tab browsers. Tab `N` is the Nth tab on screen, as `status` numbers them. | | `stop` | Gracefully shut down a browser instance (`Browser.close`) or close a specific tab (`Target.closeTarget`). Accepts a glob, stopping every matching instance. Use `--target` or `--url` to close a single tab without affecting the browser; because this closes a tab, prefer `--target-id`: an id never changes, while a tab's number shifts whenever tabs are opened, closed or dragged. | | `help` | Query the browser's protocol schema. Lists domains, commands, events, parameters. | | `stop --orphans` | Stop every browser whose owning agent session has exited. Normally each one's supervisor does this by itself within seconds; this is the sweep for when it could not. | | `keep` | Release an instance from its agent session, so it runs until stopped (like `launch --keep`). | | `move` | Move a running browser between your desktop and a managed virtual display, keeping its name, port, tabs and logins (a `save --stop` and `restore` in one step). | | `cleanup` | Remove stale instances (dead browsers) and their session directories; re-arm the keeper of any managed virtual display that lost its own. | | `save` | Snapshot running instances -- profile, tabs, cookies, launch flags, desktop, observers -- so they can be restored later. See [Saving and Restoring Sessions](#saving-and-restoring-sessions). | | `restore` | Bring snapshots back as running instances under their original names and ports (or one under a new name, with `--as`). From your terminal a session comes back where it was saved; from an agent, on a managed virtual display and owned by the agent's session, like `launch` (`--display`, `--keep` override). | | `snapshots` | List, inspect (`show`) and delete (`rm`) saved snapshots; back up the encryption key. | | `completions` | `zsh` prints a shell completion; `instances`, `methods` and `events` print `name:description` lines for the registered instances and for the running browser's CDP protocol (what the completion reads as you type). | | `--version` | Print the installed chrome-agent version (`-V` alias) and exit. | Instances are tracked in a registry at `/tmp/chrome-agent/registry.json`. A headed browser's instance is **automatically removed from the registry when its window is closed** (its session directory is cleaned up too), so `status` reflects what is actually running. Liveness is determined by **process identity plus port attribution**, not a bare PID-existence check: the recorded PID counts only if it is a live process of the launching user whose start time matches what was recorded at launch (so a recycled or namespace-local PID never masquerades as the browser), and a listening CDP port counts only if a process claiming that port with this instance's profile directory can be found -- so browsers started via wrapper/snap launchers (which fork the real browser into another process) are still reported correctly, while a port since claimed by a *different* browser is not mistaken for this one. A **transient connection drop does not retire a live instance**: a host suspend/resume severs the supervisor's CDP connection while Chrome keeps running, so the supervisor reconnects and keeps supervising; retirement happens only once the CDP port stops listening. `cleanup` removes any entries that remain (headless instances, or browsers that were killed abruptly). Two consequences worth knowing. **Launching from inside a PID-namespaced sandbox** (a container, bubblewrap, some agent-CLI sandboxes) records the sandbox's local PID in the shared registry; the identity check recognizes such an entry as stale once its browser is gone, instead of treating the aliased host PID as a live browser forever. **`stop` verifies its target before acting**: it never sends `Browser.close` to a port that is serving a different browser (it terminates the instance's own verified process instead, or just cleans up the stale entry), and its SIGTERM fallback only ever fires at a PID verified to be the instance's own browser process. ## Agent browsers: off your screen, and gone with the agent Two things go wrong when AI agents launch browsers on a workstation. A headed window opening on your desktop takes your focus in the middle of whatever you were doing. And a browser an agent forgot to stop keeps running after the agent is gone -- for days, at up to a full CPU core each. chrome-agent handles both by default for agents, and leaves your own launches alone. **Who counts as an agent.** A launch or restore is an agent's when it comes from inside an agent session: chrome-agent looks for an agent CLI (`claude`, `codex`) among the launching command's parent processes, and for the environment those CLIs export (`CLAUDECODE`, `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, `AI_AGENT`, ...). Both Claude Code and Codex are recognized with no setup. `chrome-agent launch` typed in your own terminal has neither, so it behaves as it always has. Detection was chosen over a variable each agent launcher must remember to set (the failure being guarded against is exactly a forgotten step) and over a virtual default for everyone (your own `launch` should open where you can see it). For another harness, `CHROME_AGENT_OWNER_PID=` marks its launches as an agent's, owned by that process; `CHROME_AGENT_DISPLAY=virtual|desktop` sets the default display for anyone. **Off your screen: a managed virtual display.** An agent's browser -- launched or restored -- opens on a virtual X display (Xvfb) that chrome-agent starts itself on the first free display from `:100`, shares between every agent browser while it is up, and removes once the last browser on it is gone. It is an ordinary headed Chrome, so sites see nothing unusual (unlike `--headless`); screenshots, input and CDP work the same. A small keeper process per display checks every 2 seconds whether any process still runs on that display -- which catches a browser however it ended: `stop`, a closed window, a crash, a kill -- and stops the Xvfb after two idle checks (never within 30 seconds of a launch claiming it, so a browser still starting is safe). (Xvfb's own `-terminate` is no help: it exits on any connection closing, even a bare probe.) An agent that already runs on a virtual display (`DISPLAY=:95` with an Xvfb behind it) keeps using it. An agent's `restore` -- by name, `--all`, `--here` or `--as` -- puts the session on the managed display whatever it was saved on: the user's desktop, or a particular Xvfb, whose recorded number then plays no part (it only matters when you restore it yourself). A headless snapshot stays headless. If Xvfb is not installed, an agent launch fails and says how to install it rather than falling back to your screen. Linux only; elsewhere the default stays the desktop. **Onto your screen when you need it.** `launch --display desktop` (or `restore --display desktop`) opens on your desktop -- e.g. so you can sign in to a site yourself. `chrome-agent move --to desktop` brings a running browser onto your screen and `--to virtual` takes it off again, keeping its name, port, tabs, logins and cookies: a browser cannot change X display while it runs, so this is `save --stop` and `restore` in one step, through a snapshot that is deleted once the browser is back (it needs the snapshot key, see below). **Gone with the agent: owners.** An agent's launch or restore records the agent session's process as the instance's **owner** -- pid, start time and PID namespace, so a recycled PID never passes for it. The per-instance supervisor checks the owner every 5 seconds and stops the browser after two checks find it gone, so an agent browser outlives its session by about 10 seconds. A browser launched or restored with `--keep`, released with `chrome-agent keep`, or launched or restored from your terminal has no owner and runs until stopped. Restores are owned too because agents routinely restore logged-in sessions to work in them, and such a browser would otherwise never be stopped; stopping it loses only what changed since the snapshot, which is left as it was. An agent bringing a session back *for you* should pass `--keep` (and usually `--display desktop`). Nothing ever stops a browser on an uncertain answer, and there is no age-based sweep: a browser is stopped because the session it belongs to ended, never because it has been running a long time. - **Sub-agents.** Claude Code runs sub-agents inside the session's own process, so their browsers belong to the session and last until it ends. An agent that runs as its own process (an agent-collab worker, a nested `claude -p`) owns its browsers itself, and they end with it; it can hand one on with `keep`. - **PID-namespaced sandboxes.** Codex runs each command in a bubblewrap sandbox with its own PID namespace, where no process outside it is visible. Everything started in there -- browser, supervisor, a virtual display of its own -- dies with the sandbox regardless, so the owner recorded is the sandbox itself; `status` on the host finds it by namespace. A check made from inside a different sandbox cannot see the owner and reports it as unknown, never as gone. - **Suspend and resume.** Process identity survives a suspend, and the supervisor already rides out the CDP drop a resume causes, so a sleeping laptop stops nothing. - **When the supervisor itself was killed**, no one stops the browser: `status` shows it as `ORPHAN`, and `chrome-agent stop --orphans` stops every such browser. ## Saving and Restoring Sessions A launched browser's profile lives under `/tmp/chrome-agent/` and is deleted when the browser closes -- and most Linux systems empty `/tmp` at boot anyway. So logins, cookies and open tabs do not survive a restart unless you save them: ```bash chrome-agent save --all --stop # before a reboot: close every instance cleanly and save it chrome-agent restore --all # after: bring them all back ``` A snapshot holds everything needed to bring an instance back as it was: - **The profile** -- cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB, saved logins -- minus caches and components Chrome re-downloads on its own (a real profile is typically 5-20 MB saved). - **Every cookie the browser holds in memory**, including session cookies that are never written to disk; they are set again on restore before any tab loads. - **Windows and tabs**, with each window's size, position and active tab. - **Tab order**, window by window, as the tabs sit on screen. CDP has no command for tab order (`Target.getTargets` lists pages in an order of its own), so `save`, `status` and selecting a tab by number load a tiny bundled extension over CDP for a moment (about a tenth of a second), read the order from Chrome's extension API, and uninstall it; an extension loaded this way does not survive a restart, so it never ends up in a saved profile. Where Chrome refuses (extensions disabled by policy or flag), tabs fall back to target-id order -- for numbering too, so `status` and `--target N` still agree. - **Name, port and working directory**, so an agent or script that addresses `mysite-01` (or its port) carries on unchanged. A fresh `launch` avoids the ports the last `save --all` will restore onto. - **Launch settings** -- headless, extra Chrome flags, fingerprint flags and TZ, window border, and a custom `--user-data-dir` if one was given. - **The virtual desktop** of each window (Linux/X11), or -- for a browser kept off-screen on a virtual X display (Xvfb, Xvnc, Xephyr) -- that display and the command that started its server. - **`attach` observers** subscribed to the instance. One that wrote to a file (including a shell loop that re-attaches) is restarted on restore; one whose output was piped to a reader that is gone is printed as the command to run. ```bash chrome-agent save mysite-01 # live: the browser keeps running chrome-agent save mysite-01 --stop # close it cleanly first -- fully consistent chrome-agent save 'mysite-*' # every matching instance chrome-agent restore mysite-01 # the latest version chrome-agent restore mysite-01@20260927T153000Z chrome-agent restore # everything launched from the current directory chrome-agent restore mysite-04 --as mysite-01 # bring it back under a new name chrome-agent snapshots # list: name@stamp, saved, tabs, size, port, origin dir chrome-agent snapshots show mysite-01 # tabs, observers, launch flags, desktop chrome-agent snapshots rm mysite-01 # every version (asks first; --yes when scripted) chrome-agent snapshots rm --older-than 30d ``` **Versions.** Each save is a timestamped version. When one already exists, an interactive `save` shows when it was saved and its tabs and asks whether to overwrite it; answering no keeps both. Non-interactively, both are kept unless `--overwrite` is given. Nothing is ever deleted automatically -- not by a restore, not by age -- so saving and discarding credentials stays a deliberate act. **Consistency.** `--stop` closes the browser cleanly before copying, so every database is complete on disk; use it before a reboot. A live save copies the files while Chrome runs without taking any lock (Chrome holds most of its SQLite databases exclusively, and a reader's lock on the rest could make Chrome's own writes fail), re-reading any file that changes mid-copy. Cookies are captured from the running browser either way, so they do not depend on what Chrome has flushed to disk. **Encryption.** Snapshots are credential bundles, so every snapshot file except a small plaintext summary (no URLs, no cookies) is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key kept in the OS keyring (GNOME Keyring / KWallet, macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Locker). The keyring unlocks at login, so restores need no prompt; a snapshot that ends up in a backup or a synced folder is unreadable without the key. **If the keyring is lost, the snapshots are unrecoverable** -- back the key up with `chrome-agent snapshots export-key`, and load it on another machine with `chrome-agent snapshots import-key < keyfile`. On a host with no keyring service, set `CHROME_AGENT_SNAPSHOT_KEY` to a base64 32-byte key. Snapshots live in `~/.local/share/chrome-agent/snapshots/` (mode 0700). **Renaming.** `save --as NAME` names the *snapshot*, not the session: the snapshot still records the instance name it was saved from, and a plain `restore` brings that name back. To bring a session back under a different instance name, use `restore --as NEW-NAME`. Everything else -- tabs, logins, port, windows -- comes back as saved, and `attach` observers that named the old instance are restarted against the new one. The snapshot is left unchanged (restoring it without `--as` still gives the old name); the next `save` of the renamed browser is filed under the new name. `--as` restores exactly one snapshot, so it cannot be combined with `--all` or a glob matching several. **Restoring safely.** `restore` refuses when the instance is already running (it was restored already, or the original never closed), when the saved port is taken by something else (`--any-port` picks a new one), or when a custom profile directory already exists (`--replace-profile` moves it aside rather than deleting it). It warns when the installed Chrome is older than the one that saved the snapshot, since an older Chrome may refuse a newer profile. Sites that bind a login to a device or IP, or expire it server-side, may still ask you to sign in again. **Virtual displays.** A browser running on a virtual X display is restored onto that same display, never onto the screen of whoever runs `restore`. A virtual display usually does not survive a reboot, so `restore` refuses while it is down and names the command that starts it; `--start-display` runs that recorded command (e.g. `Xvfb :90 -screen 0 1920x1200x24 -nolisten tcp`) first. A session saved from a display chrome-agent managed is not tied to its number: it comes back on whichever managed display is up, started if need be. A browser on your own desktop is not tied to a display number either -- that can change across a reboot -- and follows the display `restore` runs on. `--display virtual` or `--display desktop` overrides all of this for one restore. All of this describes a restore you run yourself: a session you restore has no owner and runs until stopped. Restored by an AI agent, a session goes on a managed virtual display whatever it was saved on, and belongs to the agent's session unless it passes `--keep` (see [Agent browsers](#agent-browsers-off-your-screen-and-gone-with-the-agent)). **Virtual desktops.** A single restore puts the browser on the current terminal's desktop, alongside the project you just reopened. `restore --all` puts each window back on the desktop it was saved from (`--desktop` overrides either default). With dynamic workspaces (GNOME's default) a window can only go as far as the last workspace that exists -- the window manager deletes empty workspaces in the middle -- so `restore --all` works through the snapshots in desktop order: the original layout comes back where the workspaces in between are occupied, and otherwise windows are packed down, keeping the ones that shared a desktop together and in order. ## Interacting with Elements Agents interact with page elements using a three-step pattern: **locate, act, verify.** ```bash # Locate -- find element coordinates via JavaScript chrome-agent myproject-01 Runtime.evaluate '{"expression": "(() => { const r = document.querySelector(\"#submit\").getBoundingClientRect(); return {x: r.x+r.width/2, y: r.y+r.height/2}; })()", "returnByValue": true}' # Act -- dispatch real input events at those coordinates chrome-agent myproject-01 Input.dispatchMouseEvent '{"type": "mousePressed", "x": 400, "y": 300, "button": "left", "clickCount": 1}' chrome-agent myproject-01 Input.dispatchMouseEvent '{"type": "mouseReleased", "x": 400, "y": 300, "button": "left", "clickCount": 1}' # Verify -- confirm the action worked chrome-agent myproject-01 Runtime.evaluate '{"expression": "document.title", "returnByValue": true}' ``` Chrome processes dispatched input events identically to physical input. A human watching the browser sees the cursor move, buttons depress, text highlight, and pages load in real time. ## Python API ```python from chrome_agent.cdp_client import CDPClient, get_ws_url from chrome_agent.domains.page import Page from chrome_agent.domains.runtime import Runtime async with CDPClient(ws_url=get_ws_url(port=9222)) as cdp: page = Page(client=cdp) runtime = Runtime(client=cdp) await page.navigate(url="https://example.com") result = await runtime.evaluate(expression="document.title", return_by_value=True) print(result["result"]["value"]) ``` 54 typed domain classes with snake_case methods, generated from Chrome's protocol schema. They are an optional convenience layer -- a point-in-time snapshot, not a gate. For any method newer than the snapshot, call `CDPClient.send(method=..., params=...)` directly (see [Tracks the running browser, not its own version](#tracks-the-running-browser-not-its-own-version)). ## Window Border So you can tell an agent-driven window apart from your own Chrome windows, every launched browser is marked by default: a colored border + corner badge around each tab (a stable, per-instance color derived from the instance name), and a title prefix so the window reads as `🤖 — ` in the taskbar / Alt-Tab. The marker is drawn in a closed shadow DOM and adds no automation-detection signal (verified against bot.sannysoft.com and CreepJS). ```bash chrome-agent launch # marked (default) chrome-agent launch --no-window-border # no marker ``` The marker is suppressed automatically when running `--headless` (no visible window) or with `--fingerprint` (the in-page marker is page-observable, and stealth is the point on the sites where fingerprinting is used). ## Browser Fingerprinting For sites that detect automated browsers, launch with a fingerprint profile: ```bash chrome-agent launch --fingerprint profile.json ``` ```json { "userAgent": "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 ...", "platform": "Linux x86_64", "vendor": "Google Inc.", "language": "en-US", "timezone": "America/Chicago", "viewport": {"width": 1920, "height": 1080} } ``` Spoofs the user agent (HTTP header and JavaScript), viewport, language, and timezone via Chrome launch flags -- persistent across navigations, with no JavaScript injection. It deliberately does **not** patch `navigator.webdriver`, `navigator.platform`, `navigator.vendor`, or `window.chrome`. An empirical detection audit found those JS overrides are each independently detectable and make the browser *more* detectable, not less: they flip bot.sannysoft.com's WebDriver test from pass to fail (the override makes `navigator.webdriver` an own property) and raise CreepJS's headless score. A plain CDP-attached Chrome already reports the native `navigator.webdriver === false` and keeps the genuine `window.chrome` shape, so the cleanest profile is one that leaves the JS environment untouched. A profile's `platform`/`vendor` should match the host OS (they are retained in the schema but not spoofed). Note that WebRTC can still leak the real IP regardless of profile. Headless mode has one giveaway that has nothing to do with fingerprinting: Chrome puts `HeadlessChrome/` in the User-Agent (`...HeadlessChrome/151.0.0.0 Safari/537.36`), and some sites block on that string alone. A profile's `userAgent` replaces it. For a lighter fix, derive the ordinary UA from a running headless instance and relaunch with only that flag: ```bash UA=$(chrome-agent Browser.getVersion | sed -n '/"userAgent"/{s/.*"userAgent": "\([^"]*\)".*/\1/;s/HeadlessChrome/Chrome/;p;}') chrome-agent stop chrome-agent launch --headless -- "--user-agent=$UA" ``` Derived this way, the version and platform always match the installed Chrome; a hardcoded UA drifts out of step on the next update, and a UA claiming a different version than the browser is its own signal. ## For AI Agents See [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/captivus/chrome-agent/blob/main/AGENTS.md) for concise agent instructions (the standard for AI agent tool documentation). It covers the mental model (address an instance, send any CDP command), the sense ⇄ act loop, the two channels, the command reference, and gotchas. **The guide ships with the package**, so an agent can reach it from any install without a checkout: ```bash chrome-agent guide # print the guide chrome-agent guide --path # print its path, to read with your own file tools ``` `--path` is usually what you want: reading the file directly beats paging 20+ KB through stdout. The command is listed in `chrome-agent --help`, which is how an agent meeting this tool for the first time finds it. The bundled copy is captured when the release is built, so it always matches the version installed. To make it load automatically -- most agent harnesses read an `AGENTS.md` from the *project* root, not from site-packages -- link it into your project: ```bash ln -s "$(chrome-agent guide --path)" AGENTS-chrome-agent.md ``` **`AGENTS.md` is a tailorable example, not gospel.** Its *mechanics* are exact, but the operating judgment in it is general -- adapt it to your own sites, tasks, and constraints. A good pattern is to keep a private, project-specific layer on top -- site-specific field notes, extraction playbooks, hard-won gotchas -- that *references* this public manual and extends it, rather than forking a separate set of instructions. Grow yours the same way. ## Collaboration Multiple participants -- humans, AI agents, or both -- can share a browser simultaneously. Each participant creates an independent CDP session with isolated event subscriptions. One agent enabling Network observation does not flood another agent's event stream. See [docs/collaboration-guide.md](https://github.com/captivus/chrome-agent/blob/main/docs/collaboration-guide.md) for: - Human-agent collaboration patterns (you browse, agent watches) - Agent-driven workflows (agent drives, you supervise) - Multi-agent setups with isolated event subscriptions - The observation gap (what CDP sees vs what it misses) - Full interaction observation via the binding bridge For real-time observation using Claude Code's Monitor tool, see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#reacting-to-events-as-they-happen-monitor) for the practical usage path (subscribing, discovering events via `help`, the gotchas), and [docs/monitor-integration.md](https://github.com/captivus/chrome-agent/blob/main/docs/monitor-integration.md) for the architecture and usage patterns in depth. Monitor is specific to Claude Code. Agents on other harnesses can still be event-driven rather than falling back to fixed sleeps -- background `attach` to a file once, then block on [`scripts/cdp-wait.py`](https://github.com/captivus/chrome-agent/blob/main/scripts/cdp-wait.py), which returns the instant a matching event lands and also catches events that fired before the wait began. See [docs/event-driven-without-monitor.md](https://github.com/captivus/chrome-agent/blob/main/docs/event-driven-without-monitor.md). ## Requirements - Python >= 3.11 - Google Chrome or Chromium (system-installed) - Linux with xdotool (optional, for virtual desktop pinning) - Xvfb on Linux, for agent launches (`sudo apt install xvfb`); without it an agent must launch with `--display desktop` or `--headless` ## Releasing (maintainer) Releases are cut from the project root with `release X.Y.Z` (or `release` for an interactive version prompt). The tool bumps `pyproject.toml`, commits, tags, pushes -- which triggers the PyPI publish workflow via GitHub Actions Trusted Publishing. Release notes auto-generate from commit messages between tags, so commits should read well as changelog entries. ## License MIT
